When night fell, he set up the tripod, adjusted the angle and the focus, and did everything with meticulous care. Yet however he adjusted it, all he could see was a blurry haze of light. He changed the eyepiece, cleaned the lenses, and fiddled for two hours before he finally discovered that his finderscope had never been lined up in the first place. Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: nothing was wrong with the equipment, nothing was wrong with his technique, nothing was wrong with his effort. Only the focus was wrong. And when the focus is wrong, the harder you try, the further you get from your target. Today’s church doesn’t lack methods or strategies. We only need to stop and ask: who is our focus aimed at?

Let me tell you something else that really happened. It was 24 December 1968, Christmas Eve, and Apollo 8 was orbiting the moon. As the spacecraft came out from behind the moon, the astronaut Bill Anders looked out through the window and saw a sight no one had ever seen before: above the grey, desolate horizon of the moon, a blue planet was slowly rising. He grabbed his camera and took the photograph that would stun the world — “Earthrise”. That night, in a live broadcast, the three astronauts read Genesis chapter 1: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.” Brothers and sisters, they flew three hundred and eighty thousand kilometres to look at the moon, and what they truly saw was creation, was God. This is revival: you go looking for one thing and are seized by a far greater focus.

Let’s look at today’s theme verse. Paul wrote Philippians from prison in Rome, around AD 61 to 62. He was in chains and didn’t know how his trial would end, yet this letter speaks of joy again and again. Why? Because his focus was not on the chains. Philippi was a Roman colony whose people took pride in Roman citizenship; status and glory were in the very air of that city. So Paul first lays out his assets: a pure bloodline, a noble tribe, a strict religious party, a blameless moral record. Then he writes verse 7: all of this I now consider a loss for Christ. In the original, “gain” means profit and “loss” means deficit — this is a profit-and-loss statement. Brothers and sisters, those things were not bad; they blocked out Jesus.

The first key point: Jesus is the focal point of the Bible. In John chapter 5 the Lord heals, at the Pool of Bethesda, a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years — and that day was the Sabbath. At the climax of the dispute, the Lord says to people who had studied the Scriptures all their lives: “These are they which testify about me.” John 5:39. Brothers and sisters, the word “search” in the original is the word for a hunter bending low and tracking footprints inch by inch. The Lord acknowledges that they were in earnest. They could recite the law; they could count how many letters there were in the Scriptures. But brothers and sisters, earnestness is not the same as focus.

Then the Lord says something extremely weighty: “Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.” John 5:40. They spent their whole lives tracking the footprints, yet refused to recognise the One standing in front of them. In 1999, the psychologists Simons and Chabris asked participants to watch a video and count how many passes the team in white made. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked through the middle of the scene and even stopped to thump its chest. About half the people didn’t see it at all. This is called inattentional blindness. Brothers and sisters, although a person’s eyes are wide open, they see only what they are looking for. So the key to reading the Bible is not how many times you’ve read it, but who your heart is looking for when you open it.

Let’s take it one item at a time. First, he is the centre of the four Gospels. John says, “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.” John 20:31. Brothers and sisters, the four Gospels are not biographies. A biography gives a balanced account of a whole life, but the Gospels devote an enormous amount of space to the last week. Mark has sixteen chapters, and six of them are about Passion Week. That is why the German theologian Martin Kähler called the Gospels “passion narratives with extended introductions”. Why? Because the cross and the empty tomb are the focus of the focus. Paul says, “For I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.”

Second, he is the protagonist of the New Testament. Peter says, “There is salvation in no one else.” Acts 4:12. Paul says, “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord.” 2 Corinthians 4:5. Brothers and sisters, listen to this phrase — we don’t preach ourselves. This is the watershed between revival and religious movements. Religious movements preach their own experiences, methods and results; revival preaches Jesus. When a religious movement is over, what people remember is the speaker; when a revival has passed, what people remember is the Lord. John the Baptist put it best: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” It’s like a see-saw. We often want both ends to rise, but there is only one focus.

Third, he is the Messiah to whom Old Testament prophecy points. On the day he rose again, on the road to Emmaus, the Lord “beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself”. Luke 24:27. That evening he said again that everything written about him in the law of Moses, the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled — that is, the whole Old Testament. Genesis 3:15 says the offspring of the woman will bruise the serpent’s head; Isaiah 53:5 says by his wounds we are healed — and seven hundred years later, at Golgotha, it was fulfilled to the letter. In the original, “Christ” means the anointed one. In the Old Testament, prophets, priests and kings were anointed, but no one ever held all three offices fully at once — until Jesus came.

Fourth, the Bible has only one theme. Theologians down the ages have tried to find a unifying theme: some say promise, some covenant, some Kingdom. Brothers and sisters, each of these has value, but they all finally flow into the same person. Who is the content of the promise? Christ. Who is the mediator of the covenant? Christ. Who is the King of the Kingdom? Christ. Revelation says, “for the testimony of Jesus is the Spirit of Prophecy.” Sixty-six books, more than forty authors, spanning over fifteen hundred years, together tell only one story. Martin Luther is generally credited with saying, “The whole of Scripture everywhere speaks only of Christ.” 321 says the Bible is my standard — because it bears witness to the living Lord.

The second key point: Jesus is the focal point of the universe. “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things.” Romans 11:36. Brothers and sisters, the original uses three prepositions, like three pillars holding up the whole universe. Of him — the source; through him — the way; to him — the destination. The starting point is him, the process is him, and the end point is him too. This is the doxology that bursts out of Paul after eleven chapters on salvation. And straight away, in chapter 12, verse 1, he says: therefore, present your bodies a living sacrifice. Did you see that “therefore”? Knowing the focal point inevitably leads to offering ourselves. This is what 321 says: change the mindset and you change the life.

He is the Lord of creation. “All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.” John 1:3. One sentence positive, one negative, sealing off every exception. Colossians declares even more: all things were created by him and through him, “and for him”. Brothers and sisters, notice that phrase — and for him. Creation is not only through him; even more, it is for him. The galaxies turn for him, the seasons change for him, and your heart beats for him. In his Confessions Augustine wrote the words repeated for sixteen hundred years: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

He is also the Lord who upholds all things. “In him all things are held together.” Colossians 1:17. In the original, “held together” means bound together, held in place so they do not fall apart. Hebrews says he is “upholding all things by the word of his power”, and “upholding” is a present participle in the original, meaning he keeps on holding them up. Paul said in Athens, “For in him we live, move, and have our being.” And the Lord himself said, “apart from me you can do nothing.” Brothers and sisters, we often treat Jesus as one item in our lives, ranked before or after work, family and finances. No. He is not an item; he is the table holding up the whole list.

Let me use a piece of the history of science to explain. From Ptolemy onwards, for fourteen hundred years, humanity believed the earth was the centre of the universe. The trouble was the planets. Mars would sometimes suddenly go backwards; this is called retrograde motion. To explain it, astronomers had to add a small circle on top of the circular orbit, called an epicycle; when that didn’t work, they added another layer. The system became astonishingly complicated, and still it couldn’t predict accurately. In 1543 Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, putting forward a simple proposal: put the sun at the centre. Once it was put in the right place, everything fell into place. Brothers and sisters, they weren’t lazy; they got only one thing wrong — they put the wrong thing at the centre. The sun accounts for 99.86 per cent of the total mass of the solar system. His first place is not a courtesy from us; it is simply how things are.

One more illustration. In pilot training there is a lesson called instrument flying. When an aircraft enters cloud and there is no horizon outside to refer to, the inner ear produces serious illusions: you are clearly descending, yet you feel you are climbing. This is called spatial disorientation. The training materials of the US Federal Aviation Administration stress again and again that at such times the only way to survive is to trust the instruments, not your feelings. Brothers and sisters, our lives also have times when we fly into cloud. Then our feelings will say: God doesn’t love you any more. The only way to survive is to move our focus back to God’s word. “Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith.” Hebrews 12:2. In the original, “looking” is “away from elsewhere” plus “to gaze” — to gaze at this One, you have to turn away from those other things.

Psychology offers supporting evidence too. In 2002, Mor and Winquist published in Psychological Bulletin a meta-analysis drawing together more than two hundred studies, and the conclusion was clear: self-focused attention is significantly and consistently associated with depression and anxiety. 321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Being self-centred means putting yourself at the centre, and people who put themselves at the centre live exhausting lives, because the whole weight of the universe presses down on their shoulders. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living it out. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Galatians 2:20. Brothers and sisters, this verse is the move from an earth-centred to a sun-centred universe: I have stepped down, and he is at the centre.

Next come the three practices for daily living. First, make Jesus the focus of your daily devotions. Three steps: before you read, pray one sentence, “Lord, please reveal yourself to me today” — that is lining up the finderscope; after you read, write down one sentence, “what kind of Lord the Jesus I saw today is”; then carry that sentence into the day. Second, turn to Jesus and make the choice of sovereignty. When facing conflict, don’t first ask how you should respond; first ask how this can bring Jesus glory. 321 says: pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility inspires humility and both sides win. With money, first ask: Lord, is this money building your Kingdom, or building my name?

The third practice: let Jesus be glorified through your actions. Every day, look for one thing through which people can see Jesus in you. It might be a word of comfort, an act of help, a choice. Be willing to turn the spotlight onto Jesus, not seeking to be seen yourself, but letting Jesus alone be lifted up. The Lord says, “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” Matthew 5:16. Look carefully at the order: the glory goes to the Father. If the applause comes to me, it isn’t light at all; it’s a stage spotlight. These three practices need to be fixed firmly in place with the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Brothers and sisters, let’s go through 321 once more. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — the focus is his life; the Bible is my standard — the focus is his word; the Holy Spirit is my guide — the focus is his Spirit. The Lord said, “He will glorify me.” So a person truly filled with the Holy Spirit will only exalt Jesus. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — that is Practice 2; let Jesus receive all the glory — that is Practice 3. The Goal: establish God’s system — a system that runs with Jesus at its centre. The fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry, and the order cannot be reversed: life first, then relationships, then ministry. 920 says: towards every “2”, live out selflessness and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit — and fruit is for others to eat, not for the tree to eat itself.

Let’s go back to that telescope at the very beginning. Nothing was wrong with the equipment, nothing was wrong with the effort; only the focus was wrong. The Lord Jesus said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” John 12:32. Brothers and sisters, if what is lifted up is a method, people will follow the method; if it is a person, people will follow that person — and people fall. Only when it is Jesus who is lifted up will people be drawn to him, and never be disappointed. So this morning I issue this call: move him back to the centre. In your devotions, look for his heart; in your decisions, ask his will first; in your reputation, let him alone be lifted up; in your church, boast not in size, not in strategy, but boast only in Christ.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You are not merely one part of our faith; you are the very reason and centre of our living. Lord, we confess that we often push you to the side. We are busy reading the Bible, yet we do not meet you; we are busy serving, yet we do not look to you. Please forgive us. Cleanse our eyes today, we pray, and move our focus back onto you. When we open the Bible, reveal yourself to us; when we face decisions, help us to ask your will first; when we do anything good, help us to turn the spotlight onto you. May you have first place in everything. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, today, let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Introduction: Jesus Is Not an Option but the Focus
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to do something very simple: close your eyes for three seconds, then open them and look at the room in front of you.

You’ll notice something remarkable. Although your eyes “see” the whole room, the only part that is truly sharp is the small patch you are looking straight at. That isn’t an illusion; it’s a fact of the Creator’s design. On the retina of the human eye there is a tiny area called the fovea centralis — less than a millimetre across — and yet it holds the great majority of the cells that give us high-resolution sight. In other words, the field we truly see clearly at any one moment is only about one or two degrees wide — roughly the size of your thumbnail held at arm’s length.

God never made the human eye to “see everything clearly at once”. He made it to “focus clearly on one”.

But what kind of age are we living in? It’s an age that leans on reason, prizes efficiency, and is crammed with images and noise. The phone lights up and a dozen red dots pop up at once; we open the computer and twenty tabs are waiting for us. Our hearts are easily scattered, our eyes easily blurred — and even in our faith we have slipped into the confusion of having many focal points.

We need to admit something honestly: for many Christians, the problem isn’t that we fail to see Jesus; it’s that we see too much. He hasn’t disappeared — he has simply been pushed to one side. He has gone from being “the only one” to being “one of many”.

Where does Jesus rank on the list of our lives? Family, work, health, finances, relationships, dreams … and then Jesus. We haven’t denied him; we’ve just filed him under “also very important”.

But brothers and sisters, the Bible reminds us plainly: Jesus is not an optional extra on the journey of faith, nor is he some kind of spiritual supplement. He is not one dish on the platter of our lives; he is the host of the whole table. He is the centre of our lives, the one focus we should be fixing our eyes on every day.

Astronomers describe the solar system like this: the sun makes up about 99.8 per cent of the total mass of the entire solar system. That isn’t a religious claim; it is basic astronomical data. It is precisely because the sun’s mass is so overwhelming that every planet is held firmly in its orbit. If one day the sun were moved out of place, the solar system wouldn’t merely become less convenient — it would collapse altogether.

As early as 1609, the German astronomer Johannes Kepler set out, in his New Astronomy, the first law of planetary motion: a planet travels around the sun in an elliptical orbit, with the sun at one “focus” of that ellipse. Notice that word — focus. An orbit is an orbit not because the planet runs well, but because the focus is where it is. Shift the focus and the orbit is thrown into chaos.

Our lives are just the same. We often think our spiritual problem is “I’m not trying hard enough”, when far more often it is “my focus has drifted”. With the wrong focus, the harder you try, the further you stray; with the right focus, your whole life naturally falls back into place.

Today’s message comes down to one sentence: Jesus is not an option; he is the focus. May we refocus on him this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Scene on the Mount of Transfiguration
sections.html:
Our theme verse today is Matthew 17:8. To really understand this verse, we first need to know something about this book, its author, and the passage around it.

The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, whose former name was Levi. He had been a tax collector in Capernaum, and when the Lord called him he followed him (Matthew 9:9). This Gospel is generally thought to have been written somewhere between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish readers. That is why Matthew keeps quoting the Old Testament and repeatedly uses phrases like “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet”. His aim was to prove one thing to his fellow Jews: this Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament — the Son of David, the offspring of Abraham, the King.

Once we grasp that purpose, we understand why the scene on the Mount of Transfiguration matters so much to Matthew.

In time, the transfiguration follows hard on the heels of a major event. In Matthew 16, in the region of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his disciples, “Who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:16) The Lord commended him, saying that flesh and blood had not revealed this to him, but his Father in heaven.

Yet in that very same chapter, the Lord began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and be raised on the third day. Peter immediately took hold of him and rebuked him: “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.” And the Lord turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” (Matthew 16:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, take note of those words. The same Peter who one moment received revelation from the Father was, the next moment, being used by Satan. What made the difference? The Lord himself put it plainly: “You are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” That is exactly a problem of focus — a shift from God’s point of view to man’s.

Then Matthew 17:1 says, “After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light.” (Matthew 17:1–2)

“After six days” — these three words are not thrown in casually. They bind the transfiguration tightly to the battle over focus that came just before. The disciples had just stumbled over their focus, and the Lord took them up the mountain to refocus them himself.

Geographically, tradition places the transfiguration on Mount Tabor in Galilee, but the context suggests it was more likely Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi — around 2,800 metres high and the tallest mountain in that region. Whichever it was, the point is that they went up “into a high mountain by themselves” — away from the crowds, away from the noise, away from every distraction, until only the Lord and these three disciples remained.

Culturally, the appearance of Moses and Elijah carried deep meaning for the Jews. Moses stood for the law: he led Israel out of Egypt and met God on Mount Sinai. Elijah stood for the prophets: he heard the gentle whisper on Mount Horeb and was later taken up by chariots and horses of fire. “The Law and the Prophets” was how the Jews referred to the whole of the Old Testament.

So the meaning of this scene is this: here the entire Old Testament hands the baton to this one man, Jesus.

Then three things happened, and they form the heart of today’s lesson. First, Peter proposed making three tents. Second, a bright cloud overshadowed them and the Father himself spoke. Third, the disciples lifted up their eyes and saw no one, except Jesus alone.

Brothers and sisters, this is not a romantic religious experience; it is a “refocusing operation” performed by God himself. This morning, let us go up the mountain together.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Jesus Is the Centre of History and Eternity
sections.html:
Jesus is not merely a great man within one stretch of history; he is the source and the end of history.

Paul says it with great clarity in Colossians: “For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.” (Colossians 1:16–17)

Notice the three prepositions here: “created through him”, “created for him”, and “held together in him”. The first speaks of origin, the second of purpose, the third of continuance. All things come from him, all things exist for him, all things hold together in him. Once those three statements are spoken, there is no way left to put Jesus in the position of “one among many”.

The word for “held together” in Greek is sunistemi, meaning “to bring together and keep from falling apart”. In today’s language, Jesus is the power that keeps all things from flying to pieces. Scientists tell us that the positively charged protons in the nucleus of an atom repel one another, yet some force binds them tightly together; they call it the “strong nuclear force”. The Bible doesn’t teach us physics, but it does tell us who it is that holds everything in his hand — “in him all things are held together”.

In the chronology of world history there is a well-known fact: most civilisations number their years from the birth of Jesus. The years before his birth are called “before Christ” (BC), and those after it “AD” — from the Latin Anno Domini, “in the year of the Lord”. This way of reckoning was proposed in AD 525 by a monk named Dionysius Exiguus. It gradually spread throughout the world, and to this day it remains the international standard for dating.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: today, whether or not a person believes in Jesus, the moment they write down the date they are already acknowledging one thing — that history divides at the birth of this man. Jesus did not merely influence one religion; he has touched the course and the very core of all human history.

More importantly, Jesus is not only the focus of the past. The writer of Hebrews says, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.” (Hebrews 13:8)

We often take this verse to comfort ourselves that the Lord does not change. That is certainly true. But its deeper meaning is that all three dimensions of time — past, present and future — are centred on him. He is not a single point living within history; he is the line that runs through the whole of it.

In the days to come, he will be the focus before whom every nation and people bows in worship: “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:10–11)

In eternity he will still be the centre of worship. John saw the New Jerusalem in Revelation, and he said: “The city has no need for the sun or moon to shine, for the very glory of God illuminated it, and its lamp is the Lamb.” (Revelation 21:23)

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? In eternity even the sun leaves the stage, because by then the true source of light has come in person. The Lord himself says, “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.” (Revelation 22:13)

Let me use an everyday picture. Have you ever played with a magnifying glass in the sunshine? The same sunlight, spread out, only gives warmth; gathered to a single point, it can start a fire. The sun’s energy hasn’t increased — only the focus has changed.

Many Christians today are not short of grace; their grace is simply too scattered. Our time, energy and passion are all there; they just aren’t focused on one person. The Bible says “in him all things are held together”, and our lives are the same: when Jesus becomes the focus, everything that was scattered begins to come together; when Jesus is not the focus, everything that was together begins to fall apart.

Seen through the eyes of the 321 vision, this is exactly “a shift of perspective”. Our natural perspective is human, earthly, temporary and worldly: I look at my years of service, I look at the difficulties in front of me, I look at whether this season is a success or a failure. God wants us to turn to a perspective that is divine, heavenly, eternal and of God: I look to the Lord who is the author and perfecter, I look to the Christ who never changes, I look to the kingdom that is coming.

Once our perspective shifts, our life begins to change. As the 321 vision puts it so well: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: See No One but Jesus
sections.html:
Now we come to the heart of this lesson.

Matthew 17 records a supremely glorious scene. The Lord took Peter, James and John up the mountain and was transfigured before them; his face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light. Then, “Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him.” (Matthew 17:3)

Brothers and sisters, try to picture the scene. Three fishermen from Galilee, who had read the law and heard the prophets all their lives, suddenly find the giver of the law and the representative of the prophets standing before their eyes — and their Teacher standing in the middle, his face shining like the sun.

Peter’s response was deeply human, and deeply sincere. He said, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (Matthew 17:4)

Peter meant no harm. He was eager; he wanted to hold on to this glory. When Luke records the event, he adds a very honest comment: “not knowing what he said.” (Luke 9:33)

So where was the problem? It lay in the number — three tents.

Three tents means three focal points. Peter put Moses, Elijah and Jesus on the same level. He didn’t reject Jesus; he simply made Jesus “one of the three”.

Brothers and sisters, this is the mistake we make most often and notice least. We rarely deny Jesus outright; we just keep “pitching tents” for other people and other things. We pitch a tent for our achievements, a tent for our family, a tent for some spiritual mentor, and then a tent for Jesus too — usually the finest one of all. We think this is honouring him; in fact it is losing our focus.

How did the Father respond? The Bible says: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’” (Matthew 17:5)

Notice two actions. The first is “overshadowing”. The Father didn’t argue with Peter or explain theology; he simply covered everything with the cloud. The second is “speaking”. He moved the disciples’ attention from their eyes to their ears, from the scene to the word.

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” — the Father had already said this once, at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:17). But this time the Father added three more words: “Listen to him.”

Those three words have a long history behind them. In Deuteronomy, Moses had long ago prophesied: “Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from among you, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.” (Deuteronomy 18:15)

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The “Listen to him” the Father spoke on the mountain points to the very one Moses himself had pointed to more than a thousand years earlier. Moses never wanted people to listen to Moses; he wanted them to listen to the prophet who was to come. So when the Father said, “Listen to him”, Moses’ task was complete.

Then verse 8: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.”

This is no coincidence; it is a deliberate revelation from God. Even Moses, the representative of the law, even Elijah, the representative of the prophets, had to leave the stage, because now the focus belonged to Jesus alone.

Hebrews describes this as a grand history of salvation: “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds.” (Hebrews 1:1–2)

John says as well: “For the law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realized through Jesus Christ.” (John 1:17)

Paul puts it more vividly still: “So that the law has become our tutor to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” (Galatians 3:24)

The word “tutor” in Greek is paidagogos: in a Greek or Roman household, the servant whose job was to take the children to school and bring them home. His task was to bring the child safely to the teacher and then step aside. He was important, but he was not the teacher. Moses and Elijah are the servant who brings us to Jesus. Once the child stands before the teacher, if the servant is still standing in the middle, he is in the way.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: God covered Moses and Elijah not because they weren’t good, but precisely because they were so good. It is exactly because they were glorious enough, weighty enough and worthy enough of honour that they were the most likely to steal our gaze from Jesus.

Even spiritual leaders, signs of grace and great figures of the past — if they rob us of our focus on Jesus, God himself will cover them and remind us: “Listen to him.”

There is a tender detail here that we often miss. When the disciples heard the Father’s voice, “they fell on their faces, and were very afraid.” Then the Bible says, “Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid.’” (Matthew 17:6–7)

Brothers and sisters, the Lord of glory who made them afraid is the same Jesus who came and touched them. Refocusing is not a frightening thing. When everything else is covered over, what remains is not judgement but a hand resting on your shoulder, and the words, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.”

Paul says: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18)

This is the single most important verse in the whole Bible on “gazing”. It tells us a spiritual law: what you gaze upon, you become. On the mountain the disciples saw the Lord transfigured; after they came down, they themselves began to be transformed.

Psychology offers an interesting confirmation. A study by Phillippa Lally and colleagues at University College London, published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit, with wide variation between individuals. This reminds us that gazing on Jesus isn’t accomplished by one moving moment on a mountain; it takes refocusing day after day.

Seen through the eyes of the 321 vision, Peter’s “three tents” are an expression of the self-centred life. Being self-centred doesn’t necessarily mean doing evil; very often it means “I’ve got a good idea”. Within Peter’s zeal lay his own arrangements, his own plans, the glory he himself wanted to hold on to. And the Father’s cloud came to cover that “self”, so that a selfless life might be revealed.

The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. When all three tents are taken down and only one Christ remains, that is not a loss; it is entering into fullness without limit. Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

This is precisely the 321 vision’s Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. “See no one but Jesus” is the most beautiful picture of those Two Core Values.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: When Our Focus Drifts, We Easily Lose Our Way
sections.html:
Our spiritual life often isn’t without the Lord; it’s that we see too many “other people”.

We follow those who teach us, we admire the servants God uses, we honour the spiritual elders who led us to faith. All of these are good; all of them are grace God has given. But if they cause us to put our focus in the wrong place, our faith has lost its focus.

The church in Corinth is the clearest example. Paul says: “Now I mean this, that each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ.’” (1 Corinthians 1:12)

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Corinthians’ problem wasn’t that they were unspiritual but that they were too spiritual — every one of them was clutching a very impressive name. Paul, Apollos, Cephas — which of them wasn’t good? Which of them wasn’t a servant God greatly used? Yet when these names were put in the place of focus, the church split apart.

Paul’s answer is utterly decisive: “Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed, and each as the Lord gave to him? I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:5–7)

“Neither he who plants is anything” — that is how Paul speaks of himself. This isn’t low self-esteem; it’s clear-sightedness. Paul knew he was the “tutor”: his task was to bring people to Jesus and then step aside.

John the Baptist took this to its very limit: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

There is a phenomenon in psychology that helps us understand how scarce focus is. In 1953 Colin Cherry, a scholar at Imperial College London, conducted a classic experiment that later gave its name to the “cocktail party effect”. He found that in a room full of voices, a person can lock on to one voice and listen intently — but at the cost of hearing almost nothing of what the other voices are saying; and the moment their attention is pulled away, the original voice immediately grows blurred.

That tells us something very important: human attention is a limited resource, not something that can be shared out without end. So “listening closely to Jesus” is not an emotional form of piety; it is a choice that costs something — if you choose to listen to him, you must stop listening to other things at the same time.

The Lord himself puts it even more directly: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

He also says: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.” (Matthew 6:22)

The word “sound” in Greek is haplous, which literally means “single, undivided, simple”. The Lord’s meaning is that if the eye is single, the whole body is full of light. The Danish thinker Kierkegaard wrote a book whose title is Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. He was right — a pure heart is a single-minded heart.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask an honest question: this morning, who takes up the most space in your heart?

Is it the person who hurt you? The message that still hasn’t had a reply? The test result that still hasn’t come back? The co-worker who is moving ahead faster than you?

When our focus drifts, it isn’t necessarily because we love the world. More often it’s because we care too much — too much about what people think, too much about our own performance, too much about the changes in our circumstances.

The 321 vision has a saying that hits the mark exactly: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

When the focus is on ourselves, we fall into pride or into feelings of inferiority — two sides of the same coin, both of them the self-centred life. When the focus is on other people, we fall into comparison and criticism — which was exactly the state of the church in Corinth. When the focus is on our circumstances, we fall into fear and anxiety — which is the story of Peter on the sea that we’ll come to shortly.

The Lord’s heart comes down to one sentence: “Listen to him.” Only Jesus is worthy of our whole-hearted gaze, our single-minded following and our complete obedience.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: How to Actually Live a Life That Sees “Jesus Alone”
sections.html:
“Jesus alone” isn’t a romantic religious slogan; it is a deliberately chosen way of life.

This doesn’t mean we no longer see anyone else. The Lord hasn’t told us to close our eyes; he has told us to fix our focus. Truly seeing “Jesus alone” means having a clear centre within: I live for him; I act relying on him; I think with my eyes fixed on him.

Paul describes this life in full: “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:1–2)

The word “set your mind” in Greek is phroneo. It doesn’t mean thinking of something now and then, but “continually orienting the mind towards it”. It speaks of a habit of the mind, an inner compass needle pointing north.

He also says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

Brothers and sisters, there’s a beautiful picture that can help us here. Why don’t ballet dancers get dizzy when they spin? They use a technique called “spotting”: the body keeps turning, but the eyes stay locked on a single point on the wall; when the body can turn no further, the head whips round and the eyes find that same point again. The body spins, but the focus doesn’t move.

Brothers and sisters, our lives are often spinning just like that. Our schedules spin, our emotions spin, our relationships spin, the times we live in spin. God has never promised that we won’t spin, but he has promised that we can have a fixed point that doesn’t move.

David says, “I have set Yahweh always before me. Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.” (Psalm 16:8)

He also says, “One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.” (Psalm 27:4)

“One thing.” Not ten things, not three things — one thing. Paul says the same: “but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal.” (Philippians 3:13–14)

C. S. Lewis is generally credited with saying something like this in Mere Christianity: aim at heaven and you will get earth thrown in; aim at earth and you will get neither. That captures the secret of seeing “Jesus alone” — it isn’t giving up everything on earth, but first fixing our aim on the One in heaven, and then everything else falls into its proper place.

The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

Brothers and sisters, this order must not be reversed. Many weary servants are worn out not because they are doing too much but because their order is upside down — first things, then people, and only then God. By the time God’s turn comes, there is no strength left.

Seeing “Jesus alone” means setting the order right. When he is in first place, everything else returns to where it belongs.

A Gentle Reminder: Focus Comes Not by “Effort” but by “Turning”

Before we move on to putting this into practice, there is one vital reminder.

Focusing on Jesus doesn’t come from staring at him anxiously; it comes from turning to him straight away whenever you notice your focus has drifted.

There is a scene in the Bible that makes this as clear as it could be. The Lord was walking on the water, and Peter said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.” The Lord said, “Come!” And the Bible records: “Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus. But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” (Matthew 14:29–30)

Brothers and sisters, notice that Peter didn’t sink because the wind and waves got bigger. The wind and waves had been there from the moment he stepped out of the boat. He sank because “he saw that the wind was strong”. His eyes changed what they were looking at.

And how did the Lord respond? “Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’” (Matthew 14:31)

“Immediately.” The Lord didn’t wait until Peter had sunk to the bottom before giving him a lecture; he stretched out his hand at once. Brothers and sisters, how gentle our Lord is towards those who lose their focus.

So it isn’t about how spiritual you are; it’s about whether you are willing to keep “coming back to him one more time”.

Hebrews gives us the whole movement: “Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith.” (Hebrews 12:1–2)

Lay aside, throw off, persevere, run — and finally, “looking”. The word for “looking” in Greek is aphorao. The prefix apo means “away from”, and horao means “to see”. So the word literally means: to take your eyes off everything else and fix them on one thing.

True looking to Jesus always includes the act of “looking away”.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Seeing Jesus Alone Is 321
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s lesson is in fact the most central picture of the whole 321 vision.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. On the mountain the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” That one sentence establishes three things at once: Jesus is the role model we are to follow; his word is the standard we are to listen to; and the one who enables us truly to hear him and truly to recognise him is the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The words “see no one but Jesus” are a picture of those Two Core Values. When my eyes see only him, he reigns as King in my heart; when my lips proclaim only him, all the glory goes to him.

The Goal — establish God’s system. God’s system is not propped up by one very strong leader; it is built together by a company of people who “see no one but Jesus”. Any system propped up by a person collapses when that person falls; only a system with Christ as its cornerstone will never fall.

Now look at the self-centred life and selflessness. Peter wanting to build three tents was the self-centred life; the Father covering it with the cloud was turning the self-centred life into selflessness. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Moses and Elijah leaving the stage is the most beautiful demonstration of “returning to our originally intended position”. They were not rejected; they simply returned to the place of creatures and servants.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Think of Matthew 16: Peter set his mind on the things of men, and the Lord said, “Get behind me, Satan!” Six days later, on the mountain, the Father himself dealt with the same problem through the cloud. What Satan fears most is not that we are busy, but that our eyes turn away from everything he has laid out and back to Jesus.

Now look at the five-fold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Today’s lesson starts with mindset — Jesus is not an option; he is the focus. Change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. The order cannot be reversed, nor can any step be skipped.

Now look at the shift of perspective: from the human to the divine, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to what is of God. On the mountain Peter was “not knowing what he said”, because he was still viewing the scene from a human perspective. Many years later he wrote 2 Peter, and said: “For he received from God the Father honor and glory when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’ We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.” (2 Peter 1:17–18) Years later, he finally understood. A shift of perspective is the lesson of a lifetime.

Now look at the 920 practice. Every person we are in relationship with is our “2”. As we practise living a selfless (0) life, we can bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions in these relationships. Brothers and sisters, think about it: why are we so easily hurt in relationships? Often it’s because we look for our focus in those relationships — I need to be seen, I need to be affirmed, I need to be understood. But when our focus is on Jesus alone, we no longer need to take anything from other people; instead we are able to give. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control — all nine of these fruits grow naturally out of a life that is in focus.

Finally, look at the 235 relationships. With selfless people we become a “2” — spiritual companions who hold each other up; we build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; we become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, notice how many people were on the Mount of Transfiguration — the Lord took three disciples up the mountain. He didn’t take one, nor did he take twelve. The spiritual mountaintop experience is never meant to be enjoyed by a lone bird; it is to be experienced together among companions, witnessed together, and carried down the mountain together into service.

And after coming down the mountain? From Matthew 17:14 onwards, at the foot of the mountain a boy possessed by a demon was waiting for them. The glory on the mountain was for the service below it. The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Receiving life on the mountain, building relationships among companions, doing ministry at the foot of the mountain — the order is perfectly clear.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Make Jesus Your Focus Every Day
sections.html:
In an age with too many voices and too many options, “focusing on Jesus” is not just an emotional longing; it is a spiritual rhythm that has to be deliberately cultivated.

One classic study deserves our attention. In research published in 2000 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Sheena Iyengar of Columbia University and Mark Lepper of Stanford University found that when a store displayed only six kinds of jam, the proportion of people who stopped to taste and went on to buy was far higher than when it displayed twenty-four. The more options people had, the harder they found it to decide, and the less satisfied they were with their decision.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the spiritual situation of our generation. We’re not short of options; what we’re short of is focus.

Here are three concrete practices to help you refocus in everyday life and live as a disciple who sees “Jesus alone”. We’ll deepen each practice through the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Your First Glance in the Morning Goes to Jesus

When you get up each day, don’t rush to check your phone, scroll social media or dive into your schedule. First be still for one minute and give your heart to Jesus.

You can say to him quietly, “Lord Jesus, today I long to see you alone, and not to let anyone or anything take my eyes off you.”

This is a deliberate beginning — letting faith define your day instead of letting the world define it. Let Jesus be the first focus of your day, so that even as the sun is rising, your heart has already turned towards him.

The Lord himself did exactly this: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.” (Mark 1:35)

David did the same: “Yahweh, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.” (Psalm 5:3)

Lamentations says, “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” (Lamentations 3:23)

Brothers and sisters, your first glance in the morning sets the direction of your day.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Stage 1, Information — recognise a fact: the focus of your day is decided in its first ten minutes.

Stage 2, Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to let you truly see that every morning you are already worshipping something, though it may not be the Lord.

Stage 3, Conviction — say sincerely in your heart: I believe that a day that begins by seeing Jesus and a day that begins by seeing my phone are two completely different days.

Stage 4, Implementation — today, move the place where your phone charges out of reach of your bed, and put a Bible by your bedside.

Stage 5, Evaluation — in the evening, ask honestly: whom did I give my first glance to this morning?

Stage 6, Correction — if you failed, don’t condemn yourself; simply turn again tomorrow.

Stage 7, Repetition — keep it up for at least forty days. Remember that study: forming a new habit takes an average of sixty-six days.

Stage 8, Multiplication — find a brother or sister, make a commitment together, remind each other, and pass this practice on.

Practice 2: When Facing a Choice, Pause and Ask Jesus

Before you make any important decision, give Jesus thirty seconds.

Whether it’s a choice at work, how to respond to someone, or an emotional reaction, you can ask in your heart, “Lord Jesus, how do you want me to choose? How do you see this?”

This simple pause is an act of surrender and refocusing. You aren’t reacting on emotion; you are choosing to invite Jesus in and let his will lead you forward. Very often he will give you unexpected guidance through a verse of Scripture, a word, or a sense of peace.

The Bible says, “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

James also says, “But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.” (James 1:5)

The 321 vision puts it well: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll worry, rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice. Those thirty seconds are the switch that moves you from relying on the brain to relying on the heart.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Stage 1, Information — know that you make far more decisions every day than you think, and that most of them are made out of habit.

Stage 2, Revelation — ask the Lord to shine his light so you can see what you most often base your decisions on: fear, saving face, efficiency — or the Lord.

Stage 3, Conviction — believe that the Lord has a will for every small decision you make today; he isn’t a God who only cares about the big things.

Stage 4, Implementation — pick the situation where you most easily lose control, such as “wanting to reply at once to a message that has made me angry”, and deliberately pause for thirty seconds there.

Stage 5, Evaluation — after a week, look back: which times did I pause? What turned out differently?

Stage 6, Correction — shorten or lengthen the thirty seconds until you find a length you can really keep to.

Stage 7, Repetition — let the pause become a reflex.

Stage 8, Multiplication — share a testimony in your small group: “I paused for thirty seconds, and it turned out differently.”

Practice 3: After Sunset, Review Whether You Saw “Jesus Alone”

Before the day ends, set aside five minutes to look back quietly over your walk with the Lord. Ask yourself three questions:

First, at what moment today was I especially fixed on Jesus, especially drawn to him?

Second, at what moments did my eyes drift from the Lord and fix instead on what people thought of me, on the pressure of work, or on my own emotions?

Third, in which situation of daily living am I willing, tomorrow, to fix my eyes on Jesus more simply?

This kind of spiritual review will help you gradually develop a sensitivity of life that is “alert to Jesus”. You’ll find that the more often you review, the more easily you “see” him in everyday life.

David’s prayer can serve as the pattern for our review: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Lamentations also says, “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to Yahweh.” (Lamentations 3:40)

Notice the order: first search, then turn again. The purpose of review isn’t condemnation; it is turning back.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Stage 1, Information — recognise that this kind of review is a spiritual tradition of the saints through the ages, not a new invention.

Stage 2, Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to remind you of the truly decisive moments of your day, not just the most dramatic one.

Stage 3, Conviction — believe that an unexamined life will, without your noticing, be refocused by the world.

Stage 4, Implementation — try five minutes tonight; three lines written down is enough.

Stage 5, Evaluation — at the weekend, look over the week’s notes and find the patterns of losing focus that keep recurring.

Stage 6, Correction — for that pattern, ask the Lord for a verse to be your “fixed point”.

Stage 7, Repetition — let the review become the full stop of your day, as natural as switching off the light.

Stage 8, Multiplication — in the 920 practice, pray for every “2” around you, asking the Lord to let them see Jesus too.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: May Your Whole Life See “Jesus Alone”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the central reminder of this whole course rests on the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. But the deeper aim is that we would not merely know about Jesus, but see “Jesus alone” every day.

Knowing him is a matter of the head; seeing him alone is a matter of the eyes and the heart. Many people have known about Jesus for years, yet have seldom truly “seen” him.

May we not let achievement steal our focus, nor relationships, nor service, nor expectations, pressure or disappointment — but keep our eyes fixed on him always.

When Stephen was martyred, the Bible says: “But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God.” (Acts 7:55) Brothers and sisters, the stones were raining down on him, yet he saw Jesus. When a person truly sees “Jesus alone”, not even death can take away their focus.

Those Greeks who came to Philip spoke words that have become the cry of the church through every age: “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” (John 12:21)

This morning, that is our cry too.

May our families let people see Jesus; may our church let people see Jesus; may our workplaces let people see Jesus; and when we come to the end of this life, may those who look back on it see no one but Jesus.

Because — he is worthy of all our focus and all our worship.

In his vision John heard the song of heaven: “To him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb be the blessing, the honor, the glory, and the dominion, forever and ever! Amen!” (Revelation 5:13)

keyVerses: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
practices: First glance in the morning: fix your eyes on Jesus
Facing a choice: pause and ask Jesus
After sunset: review whether you saw “Jesus alone”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that this morning you have brought us up the mountain.

Lord, we confess that our hearts are so often scattered and our eyes so often blurred. Like Peter, we have eagerly wanted to pitch tents for many people and many things, and without even noticing we have made you just one among them. Please forgive us.
We ask you, like that bright cloud, to cover everything in our lives that steals our focus; and we ask you, like the voice of the Father, to speak to us: This is my beloved Son; listen to him.
Lord, when we see that the wind is strong and we begin to sink, stretch out your hand at once and take hold of us.

Holy Spirit, help us, from tomorrow morning onwards, to give our first glance to you; to pause and ask you before every choice; and at the close of every day to look back quietly and turn to you once again.

May our mindset be changed by you, our life changed by you, our daily living changed by you, our relationships changed by you, and our ministry changed by you too. Reign as King among us, and may all the glory be yours.
We lift up our eyes and see no one else; we long to see only you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 17:4: “Peter answered, and said to Jesus, ‘Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.’” Take a quiet moment to reflect: in your life right now, which “tent” stands side by side with Jesus? It may be an achievement, a person, an expectation, or a sense of security. Share with your group, and pray together, asking the Lord to cover it with his cloud.

Matthew 14:30: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” Which “wind” has lately been most likely to pull your eyes away from the Lord? Which concrete practice (your first glance in the morning, thirty seconds before a decision, a review after sunset) do you plan to use to help yourself turn back? Make a commitment to one another in your group, and become each other’s spiritual companion.

blog.title: Your Eyes Can Only See One Focus Clearly at a Time

blocks.x: See No One but Jesus
Have you ever tried closing your eyes for three seconds, then opening them and looking at the room in front of you?
You’ll notice something remarkable: although your eyes “see” the whole room, the only part that is truly sharp is the small patch you are looking straight at.

That isn’t an illusion. On the human retina there is a tiny area called the fovea centralis — less than a millimetre across — and yet it holds the great majority of the cells that give us high-resolution sight. The field we truly see clearly at any one moment is only about one or two degrees wide — roughly the size of your thumbnail held at arm’s length.
God never made the human eye to “see everything clearly at once”. He made it to “focus clearly on one”.

But we live in an age when the phone lights up and a dozen red dots pop up at once, and we open the computer to find twenty tabs waiting for us. Our hearts are easily scattered, our eyes easily blurred — and even in our faith we have slipped into the confusion of having many focal points.
And so a fact emerges that few of us are willing to admit: very often the problem isn’t that we fail to see Jesus; it’s that we see too much.
He hasn’t disappeared. He has simply been pushed to one side. He has gone from being “the only one” to being “one of many”.
Peter’s Three Tents

Matthew 17 records a supremely glorious scene. Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain and was transfigured before them; his face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light. Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared to them.
Moses stood for the law, Elijah for the prophets. To a Jew, it was as if the whole Old Testament were standing before their eyes.

Peter’s response was deeply human, and deeply sincere. He said, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (Matthew 17:4)
Peter meant no harm. He was eager. When Luke records the event, he adds just one very honest comment: “not knowing what he said.”
So where was the problem? It lay in the number — three tents.
Three tents means three focal points. Peter didn’t reject Jesus; he simply made Jesus “one of the three”.

We are just the same. We rarely deny Jesus outright; we just keep pitching tents for other people and other things: a tent for our achievements, a tent for our family, a tent for some spiritual mentor, and then a tent for Jesus too — usually the finest one of all.
We think this is honouring him. In fact it is losing our focus.

How did the Father respond? The Bible says: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’” (Matthew 17:5)
The Father didn’t argue with Peter or explain theology. He simply covered everything with the cloud.
Then the disciples lifted up their eyes and saw no one, except Jesus alone.

Notice this: God covered Moses and Elijah not because they weren’t good, but precisely because they were so good. It is exactly because they were glorious enough, weighty enough and worthy enough of honour that they were the most likely to steal our gaze from Jesus.
Focus Comes Not by Effort but by Turning
This is the most important sentence in this whole piece.
Focusing on Jesus doesn’t come from staring at him anxiously; it comes from turning to him straight away whenever you notice your focus has drifted.

Peter once walked on the water and then began to sink. He didn’t sink because the wind and waves got bigger — they had been there from the moment he stepped out of the boat. The Bible puts it precisely: “when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid.” His eyes changed what they were looking at.
And how did the Lord respond? “Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him.” Immediately. How gentle our Lord is towards those who lose their focus.

Why don’t ballet dancers get dizzy when they spin? Because they use a technique called “spotting”: the body keeps turning, but the eyes stay locked on a single point on the wall; when the body can turn no further, the head whips round and the eyes find that same point again.
The body spins, but the focus doesn’t move.

God has never promised that our lives won’t spin. Our schedules spin, our emotions spin, our relationships spin, the times we live in spin. But he has promised that we can have a fixed point that doesn’t move.
If you’d like to start today, you can try three very small practices:
1. Your first glance in the morning goes to Jesus. When you get up, don’t check your phone first; be still for one minute.
2. When facing a choice, give Jesus thirty seconds and ask in your heart: Lord, how do you want me to choose?
3. After sunset, take five minutes to look back: at what moment today was I especially fixed on him? At what moments did I drift?

Don’t underestimate these small actions. Research published in 2010 by Phillippa Lally and colleagues at University College London found that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit. So please don’t stop after three days.
May we not let achievement steal our focus, nor relationships, nor service, nor expectations, pressure or disappointment.
And when we come to the end of this life, may those who look back on it see no one but Jesus.
Because he is worthy of all our focus and all our worship.
Reflection question: if a cloud came down today and covered everything in your life that steals your focus, what do you think would be the first thing to be covered?
