blog.title: If the Donkey’s Colt Lifted Up Its Head

blocks.x: Lift Up No One — Lift Up Only Jesus

The sun is roughly four hundred times the size of the moon. Yet the sun is also roughly four hundred times further from the earth than the moon is. And so, to our eyes, the two look exactly the same size.

That is why, every so often, people on earth witness something astonishing: broad daylight suddenly turns dark, birds fly back to their nests, and stars appear on the horizon. And what has blotted out the sun entirely is that very moon, four hundred times smaller.

The moon gives off no light of its own. Every bit of its light is borrowed. A rock like that — giving no light, not burning — can nonetheless hide the sun. Not because it is big, but because it is standing in the wrong place.

Brothers and sisters, each of us is like that moon. We have no light of our own; all our light is borrowed from the Lord. But the moment we move ourselves in between the Lord and the people, we can hide the Lord, who is infinitely greater than we are, so that people can no longer see him.
Three Tents on the Mountain

On the day of the transfiguration, Peter saw Jesus’ face shining like the sun, and saw Moses and Elijah appear. He said excitedly, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (Matthew 17:4)
Three tents. The same size, the same height, side by side in a row.

Peter meant no harm; he spoke out of eagerness. But hidden in what he said was a fatal distortion — he set the Creator alongside the created, the source of light alongside the things that merely reflect it.
God the Father interrupted him before he had finished: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.”
Then the cloud lifted. The Bible records a short but stunning sentence:
“Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
Moses was gone; Elijah was gone. Not because they didn’t matter, but because their task was to point to that One.
I Am the Donkey’s Colt; He Is the King

On Palm Sunday, the Lord sent his disciples to fetch a donkey’s colt. It was no thoroughbred, no warhorse; no one had ever ridden it; it had no track record at all. The disciples said just four words, and it was brought to him: “The Lord needs him.”
That day the crowds spread their clothes on the road, spread branches on the road, and shouts of praise shook the whole city.
So let me ask: whom were the people welcoming? The colt, or Jesus?
The colt walked right in the middle of it all — cloaks on its back, branches under its hooves, cheering in its ears. It was present for all the pageantry; not one bit of the glory was its own.
What would have happened if it had lifted up its head amid the crowd’s cheers? Jesus would have fallen off its back, and the focus would have changed.
The colt’s job is to keep its head down, to carry the load, to keep walking forward. If its head comes up, its back tilts, and the one riding on it can’t sit steady.
Brothers and sisters, the posture of our service determines whether the Lord can sit steady.

The most dangerous thing is not great sin or scandal, but the quietest drift of all. A brother who led worship received praise from the whole congregation the very first time he served. By the second week he had started paying attention to whether he was in tune; by the fourth week he found that when he prayed, what came to mind was not the face of the Lord but the applause of the congregation. Later, with tears in his eyes, he said, “I didn’t fall. I just slowly moved myself into the middle.”
Three Practices You Can Start Right Away

First, give the glory to Jesus straight after you serve. When you’ve finished preaching, praying or visiting, go back to your inner room within ten minutes and say to the Lord: Lord, you did all this, not me.

Second, after a meeting, ask yourself one question: do I love Jesus more? Or do I only remember the speaker, the lines and the atmosphere? You can write two lines — what did this meeting show me about Jesus? What am I going to change this week because of it?
Third, each week meditate on one sentence: I am the colt. And ask honestly: did I lift my head this week? Did I block the glory of Jesus?
Remember: you are not the star; you are a bridge. The church needs bridges, not stars on a stage. God wants to use you to bring people to Jesus, not to bring them to you.
The Lord himself said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” (John 12:32)

What truly draws people’s hearts is not events, not programmes, not speakers, but Jesus himself. If a church relies only on events to draw people, it will wear itself out; but if it relies on the glory of Jesus to draw people, the result is a revival that is real, lasting and transforms hearts.
God has never looked for famous people; he looks for people willing to make Jesus famous.
Lower yourself, and lift Jesus high. See no one but Jesus — this is the Father’s heart, and the direction of our whole lives.
Reflection
Was there a moment this week when you “lifted your head”? At that moment, whose light were you blocking?

Greet the brothers and sisters and explain that today is Lesson 13 of Morning Devotion 321: Lift Up No One — Lift Up Only Jesus.
Read the theme verse, Matthew 17:8: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.”
State the main thread of the lesson: we are all vessels, and being used is no reason to be exalted.
Introduce the subtitle, “I am the donkey’s colt; he is the King” — the most important picture in the whole lesson.
A small moon hides a great sun
The sun is 400 times the moon’s size
and exactly 400 times further away
In the wrong place, the moon hides the sun
We too can block the Lord’s light
Start with the astronomical facts: the sun is about 1.39 million km across, the moon about 3,474 km — a factor of four hundred.
The sun is about 150 million km from the earth, the moon about 384,000 km — also four hundred times — so they look the same size.
Conclusion: the moon hides the sun not because it is big but because it stands in the wrong place.
Apply it: we have no light of our own; our light is borrowed from the Lord; standing in the wrong place, we block him.
Optional testimony: a worship leader who said, “I didn’t fall. I just slowly moved myself into the middle.”
Three tents on the Mount of Transfiguration
Peter wants three tents (Matthew 17:4)
The Father says: Listen to him!
The cloud lifts; Moses and Elijah are gone
They saw no one, except Jesus alone
Background: Matthew was written around AD 50–70 for Jewish readers, to prove that Jesus is the Messiah and the King.
Six days before the transfiguration, Peter had just recognised the Christ, then was rebuked: “You are not setting your mind on the things of God” (Matthew 16:23).
Peter wants three tents, setting Jesus alongside Moses and Elijah — putting the source of light alongside its reflectors.
The Father interrupts: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” (Matthew 17:5)
The cloud lifts, Moses and Elijah are gone, only Jesus remains — the final destiny and the glory of every vessel.
Point 1 · People are not the focus
Treasure in clay vessels (2 Corinthians 4:7)
A vessel’s worth lies in who uses it
The bronze serpent exalted became an idol
Old self self-centred, new self selfless
Quote 2 Corinthians 4:7; explain that “clay” (Greek ostrakinos) means the cheapest earthenware.
Illustration: a stick in Moses’ hand became God’s rod; the rod didn’t change — what changed was who was holding it.
A warning: the bronze serpent was God’s vessel (Numbers 21:9), but Israel later burned incense to it and Hezekiah had to break it (2 Kings 18:4).
Supporting psychology: Gilovich and colleagues at Cornell (1999–2000), the “spotlight effect” — people overestimate how much others notice them by about double.
321 application: the old self is self-centred, the new self selfless; humility is returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.
Point 2 · The lesson of the colt
The Lord needs him (Mark 11:3)
The crowds welcomed Jesus, not the donkey
If the colt lifts its head, the Lord falls
The focus is Jesus, not ourselves
Tell the scene of the colt: Mark 11:2–3, “on which no one has sat”; its only credential was “The Lord needs him”.
This fulfilled Zechariah 9:9: your King comes to you, lowly, riding on the colt of a donkey.
On Palm Sunday the crowds spread clothes and branches and shouted Hosanna (Matthew 21:8–9) — the colt was present for all the pageantry, yet none of the glory was its own.
The lesson’s picture: if the colt lifts its head, Jesus falls off and the focus changes.
321 application: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.
Point 3 · Head down, not head up
We don’t preach ourselves (2 Corinthians 4:5)
Not to be remembered, but to help people meet the Lord
It is Jesus working through me
Humility inspires humility: both win
Quote 2 Corinthians 4:5: “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord.”
Give three self-check questions: who is the subject of the sentence? Where are the listeners being led? If my name were removed, would I still do it?
Clarify: true humility doesn’t deny what God has done; it knows it is Jesus doing the work through me (1 Corinthians 15:10).
Jim Collins, Good to Great (2001), Level 5 leaders: in success they look out of the window and credit others; in failure they look in the mirror and take responsibility.
321 application: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.
Point 4 · Exalt people and the church splits
I follow Paul (1 Corinthians 3:4)
Neither planter nor waterer is anything
Paul tore his clothes; Herod was eaten by worms
The church exists to exalt Christ
Factions in Corinth: “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos” (1 Corinthians 3:4).
Paul says they are nothing to speak of; only God gives the increase (1 Corinthians 3:5–7); “servant” originally meant one who waits at table.
Lystra: Paul and Barnabas tore their clothes and cried, “We also are men” (Acts 14:14–15).
Caesarea: Herod didn’t give God the glory and was eaten by worms and died (Acts 12:22–23).
Point out: Herod’s sin was not seizing the glory but not giving the glory; silence can sometimes be consent.

If I am lifted up from the earth (John 12:32)
Drawing with events wears us out
Drawing with his glory brings lasting change
Look at the bronze serpent and live

The bronze serpent as a type: “when he looked at the serpent of bronze, he lived” (Numbers 21:9); a vessel’s function is to turn eyes to the one point God has appointed.
Contrast: people drawn by events are loyal to events and you must keep staging bigger ones; people drawn by Jesus are loyal to Jesus.
Optional: the Welsh Revival of 1904 and the Great Pyongyang Revival of 1907 — revival is never something you can organise.
You are not the star; you are a bridge
The church needs bridges, not stars
Bring people to Jesus
What people truly need is not you, but him
Life first, then relationships, then ministry

Two characteristics of a bridge: it is there to be walked across; it sits low, stooping over the gap.
The Lord Jesus himself is that bridge: he came down from heaven to the lowest place to carry us across to God.
321 application: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships more than things.
Close with one line: what people truly need is not you, but him.

The Father interrupts: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” (Matthew 17:5)
The cloud lifts and only Jesus remains — the Law and the Prophets step aside once their task is done.
Point 1 · We are all vessels
“We have this treasure in clay vessels”
2 Corinthians 4:7
Clay jars were the cheapest containers
So the power may be shown to be of God
Read 2 Corinthians 4:7; explain that “clay” (Greek ostrakinos) means the cheapest earthenware.
Paul gives the answer himself: that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.
Illustration: put the treasure in a golden vessel and eyes stop at the gold; put it in a clay jar and people can see the treasure.
Application: God uses ordinary people precisely so that his glory is beyond dispute.
A vessel’s worth lies in who uses it
A stick in Moses’ hand became God’s rod
The rod didn’t change — the hand did
The bronze serpent saved, then got incense
Hezekiah had to break it in pieces
The staff illustration: an ordinary stick is worth next to nothing, but in Moses’ hand it became God’s rod (Exodus 4:20).
The rod didn’t change; what changed was who was holding it.
The bronze serpent warning: a vessel God commanded (Numbers 21:9), yet more than seven hundred years later Israel burned incense to it.
Hezekiah broke the bronze serpent Moses had made (2 Kings 18:4) — a vessel that is exalted will sooner or later be broken.
Close with one line: a vessel has no worth in itself; who uses it determines its glory and function.
From self-centred to selfless
Spotlight effect: we overestimate attention
Not exalting self never happens automatically
Humility is returning to our originally intended position
Selflessness overcomes Satan
Supporting psychology: Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky at Cornell (1999–2000) described the spotlight effect.
Participants overestimated how many people noticed them — about twice the actual number.
Two reminders: we are not as important as we imagine; not exalting ourselves never happens automatically — it must be a deliberate choice made relying on the Holy Spirit.
Andrew Murray, Humility: humility is nothing other than the creature taking its rightful place before God.
321: the old self is self-centred, the new self selfless; humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan (Galatians 2:20).
Point 2 · The Lord needs him
“On which no one has sat”
Mark 11:2–3
No credentials — just one sentence
The Lord needs him
Read Mark 11:2–3, stressing “on which no one has sat”.
The colt was no thoroughbred or warhorse, with no training and no track record; its only credential was “The Lord needs him”.
It fulfilled Zechariah 9:9: your King comes, lowly, riding on the colt of a donkey (around 520 BC).
Application: we were chosen not because we were good enough; we are used not because we are strong enough.
Whom were the crowds welcoming?
Clothes on the road, branches on the road
Hosanna to the son of David
Present for all the pageantry
Not one bit of the glory was its own
Read Matthew 21:8–9: clothes on the road, branches on the road, shouts of Hosanna.
The lesson’s question: whom were the people welcoming? The colt, or Jesus?
The colt walked right in the middle — cloaks on its back, branches under its hooves, cheering in its ears.
Present for all the pageantry, yet none of the glory was its own — exactly the situation of everyone who serves.
If the colt lifts its head, the Lord falls
The colt’s job: head down, carry the load
Head up, back tilts
Lifting its head feels like being affirmed
The focus is Jesus, not ourselves
Read the lesson: if it lifted its head amid the cheers, Jesus would fall off its back.
The colt’s job is to keep its head down, carry the load and walk on; head up, back tilts, and the Lord can’t sit steady.
The most dangerous thing: when it lifts its head, it feels like being affirmed, being effective, being used by God.
321: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.
Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice, rely on the brain and you’ll worry.
Point 3 · We don’t preach ourselves
“We don’t preach ourselves”
2 Corinthians 4:5
The mission isn’t to be remembered
but to help people meet the Lord
Read 2 Corinthians 4:5: “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord.”
Two roads: people remember me — heavier the further I go; people meet the Lord — lighter the further I go.
Three self-check questions: who is the subject of the sentence? Where are the listeners being led? If my name were removed, would I still do it?
Matthew 5:16: people see our good works, but the glory goes to our Father in heaven.
Acknowledge the facts; give back the glory
“Yet not I, but the grace of God”
1 Corinthians 15:10
Level 5 leaders: success — look out of the window
Failure — look in the mirror
Clear up a misunderstanding: true humility doesn’t deny what God has done, nor rush to say “I was terrible”.
Paul’s standard sentence pattern: acknowledge the facts, give back the glory (1 Corinthians 15:10).
Jim Collins, Good to Great (2001): from more than 1,400 companies, eleven great ones were identified.
The window and the mirror of Level 5 leaders: in success they look out of the window and credit others; in failure they look in the mirror and take responsibility.
James 4:6: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.
Point 4 · Exalt people and factions form
“I follow Paul”
1 Corinthians 3:4
Neither planter nor waterer is anything
But God gives the increase
Factions in Corinth: “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos” (1 Corinthians 3:4).
Paul says they are nothing to speak of; only God gives the increase (1 Corinthians 3:5–7).
“Servant” (Greek diakonos) originally meant one who waits at table — no guest remembers who carried the dishes in.
Exalting people never leads to unity but to factions; once the focus is scattered, it is no longer a focus.
Two responses, two endings
Paul tore his clothes: we also are men
Herod didn’t give God the glory
He was eaten by worms and died
The church exists to exalt Christ
Lystra: the crowd called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes (Acts 14:11–12).
The two apostles tore their clothes, sprang into the crowd and cried, “We also are men” (Acts 14:14–15).
Caesarea: Herod put on his royal robes, the people shouted, “The voice of a god”, and he didn’t give God the glory (Acts 12:22–23).
Herod’s sin was not seizing the glory but not giving the glory — silence can sometimes be consent.
Colossians 1:18: that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Point 5 · If I am lifted up
“Will draw all people to myself”
John 12:32
Signifying by what kind of death he should die
What truly draws people is the cross
Read John 12:32, then verse 33: “But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die.”
“Draw” (Greek helkuō) means to pull or drag, like hauling a boat up onto the shore.
A tremendous reversal: the world’s exaltation is being looked up to; the Lord’s is being nailed to wood.
The bronze serpent as a type: look and live (John 3:14–15; Numbers 21:9) — turning eyes to the one point God has appointed.
By glory, not by events
Drawing with events wears us out
Drawing with his glory brings lasting change
Only in totality can you see the corona
When self is covered, the Lord is revealed
The lesson: drawing people with events wears us out; only the glory of Jesus brings lasting revival.
People drawn by events are loyal to events, people drawn by a speaker to the speaker — and all of that passes.
The Welsh Revival of 1904 and the Great Pyongyang Revival of 1907 shared deep confession and worship.
In a total eclipse the moon blocks the photosphere and the corona becomes visible; in 1919 Eddington used this to observe starlight being bent.
Spiritual lesson: when self is covered, the Lord’s glory is revealed.
Practices 1 and 2
Give the glory to the Lord straight after serving
“Lord, you did all this, not me”
After a meeting ask: do I love Jesus more?
Or do I only remember the speaker and atmosphere?
Practice 1: within ten minutes of finishing your service, go back to your inner room and say, “Lord, you did all this, not me.”
Add the eight stages: Information (the glory was never mine), Revelation (see that faint longing), Conviction, Implementation.
Practice 2: after a meeting ask, “Do I love Jesus more?” — or do I only remember the speaker, the lines and the atmosphere?
Practical step: after a meeting write two lines — what did I see of Jesus? What will I change this week?
Practice 3 · I am the colt
Each week meditate: I am the colt
Did I lift my head this week?
Did I block the Lord’s glory?
Eight stages: Implementation, Repetition, Multiplication
Practice 3: each week quietly meditate on one sentence — “I am the colt.”
Answer the lesson’s three questions: did I lift my head this week? Did I block the Lord’s glory? Am I willing to be more humble?
Information stage: read Mark 11:1–11 and remember those four words, “The Lord needs him.”
Evaluation and Correction: find your pattern of “lifting your head” — when praised, when comparing, or when overlooked.
Repetition and Multiplication: make this sentence your silent prayer before stepping up, and teach it to your spiritual children.
The 3-2-1 vision in summary
Jesus my role model, the Bible my standard
The Holy Spirit my guide; let Jesus be King
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
You are not the star; you are a bridge
The Three Foundations: Jesus my role model (Philippians 2:6–8, he emptied himself), the Bible my standard (Isaiah 42:8), the Holy Spirit my guide (John 16:14).
Point out especially: even the Holy Spirit does not exalt himself; the Spirit’s work is to glorify Jesus.
The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory; the Goal: establish God’s system.
The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; life first, then relationships, then ministry.
The 920 practice and 235 relationships: being praised is exactly the moment to practise the “0”; become spiritual companions with selfless people.
Exalt Jesus alone, and revival will come
God looks for people who will make Jesus famous
Lower yourself; lift Jesus high
Let Jesus receive all the glory
See no one but Jesus
Read the lesson’s closing words: God has never looked for famous people; he looks for people willing to make Jesus famous.
Examples: John the Baptist went down into prison, Paul wrote from a cell, the colt vanished from the story — they all disappeared.
Yet the One they pointed to is still praised by hundreds of millions two thousand years later.
Give a threefold call: to those serving, those who have been hurt, and those praying for revival.
Revival doesn’t begin with a bigger event; it begins with a company of people willing to bow their heads.
Prayer and blessing
Lord, I am not the star
Be exalted
May all people come to see you because of me
Amen
Lead the congregation in declaring together: Lord, I am not the star. Be exalted, and may all people come to see you because of me.
Pray for those who serve, asking the Lord to keep them standing in the right place.
Pray for the church, asking the Lord that we would not block his light but reflect it.
Close with “See no one but Jesus” and bless the congregation in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re reading Lesson 13 of Morning Devotion 321 together: Lift Up No One — Lift Up Only Jesus. Our theme verse is Matthew 17:8: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” No one, except Jesus alone. Today’s lesson has a subtitle, and it is the most important picture in the whole lesson: I am the donkey’s colt; he is the King. May the Lord engrave this picture on our hearts this morning.

Brothers and sisters, let me begin with something that happens in the sky. The sun is roughly four hundred times the size of the moon. Yet the sun is also roughly four hundred times further away from us than the moon. So to our eyes, they look exactly the same size. As long as the moon stands on that line in between, a small moon can cover the whole sun completely. Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: the moon can hide the sun not because it is big, but because it is standing in the wrong place. We are just the same. We have no light of our own; all our light is borrowed from the Lord. But the moment we move ourselves in between the Lord and the people, we can hide the Lord so that people can no longer see him.

Let’s go up the Mount of Transfiguration. That day Jesus’ face shone like the sun, and Moses and Elijah appeared to the disciples. As soon as Peter saw them he said, Lord, let me make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah. Brothers and sisters, Peter meant no harm; he spoke out of eagerness. But he set the Creator alongside the created. How did God the Father respond? He interrupted Peter and said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” Then the cloud lifted; Moses was gone, Elijah was gone. “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.”

Key point one: people are not the focus; Jesus is the focus. Paul says, “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” 2 Corinthians 4:7. Clay jars were the cheapest earthenware; nobody grieved when one broke. Think of that wooden staff: in Moses’ hand, stretched out over the Red Sea, the waters parted. Did the staff change? No — what changed was who was holding it. Brothers and sisters, our gifts, our eloquence, our music are all that staff; they have worth because they are held in the Lord’s hand.

Key point two: the lesson of the donkey’s colt. On the day Jesus entered Jerusalem, the disciples went to fetch a donkey’s colt. They said just one thing: “The Lord needs him.” That colt was no thoroughbred, no warhorse; no one had ever ridden it. Its only credentials in all its life were those four words: the Lord needs him. That day the crowds spread their clothes on the road and spread branches on the road. Let me ask: whom were the people welcoming? The colt, or Jesus? Jesus! The colt was present for all the pageantry; not one bit of the glory was its own. Brothers and sisters, the colt’s job is to keep its head down; if its head comes up, its back tilts, and the one riding on it can’t sit steady.

Key point three: the attitude of service is head down, not head up. Paul says, “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord.” 2 Corinthians 4:5. We don’t preach ourselves. Brothers and sisters, ask yourself three questions. First, when I talk about this, who is the subject of the sentence? Second, where are my listeners being led? Third, if my name were removed from this, would I still be willing to do it? True humility isn’t denying what God has done; it is knowing clearly that it is Jesus who is doing the work through me. The 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Key point four: what happens when the church starts exalting people? In the church at Corinth some said, I follow Paul, and others, I follow Apollos. Paul answered: neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase. Exalting people never leads to unity; it leads to factions. In Lystra the crowds wanted to worship Paul and Barnabas, and they tore their clothes and cried out: we also are men! In Caesarea Herod didn’t give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and died. Brothers and sisters, notice: Herod’s sin was not seizing the glory but not giving the glory. Silence can sometimes be consent.

Key point five: what draws people is not us but Jesus lifted up. The Lord says, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” John 12:32. The next verse makes it clear that he said this signifying by what kind of death he should die. Brothers and sisters, what truly draws people’s hearts is the cross — not the stage, not the lighting, not the pageantry. How were the people bitten by serpents in the wilderness healed? They looked at the bronze serpent and lived. If a church relies only on events to draw people, it will wear itself out; but if it relies on the glory of Jesus to draw people, the result is a revival that is real, lasting and transforms hearts.

Brothers and sisters, the lesson gives us a gentle reminder: you are not the star; you are a bridge. The church needs bridges, not stars on a stage. A bridge has two characteristics. First, a bridge is there to be walked across; nobody holds a celebration in the middle of a bridge. Second, a bridge sits low; it has to stoop over the chasm. The Lord Jesus himself is that bridge: he came down from heaven to the very lowest place to carry us across to God. The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. What people truly need is not you, but him.

Now let’s practise. First, give the glory to Jesus straight after you serve; within ten minutes, go back to your inner room and say: Lord, you did all this, not me. Second, after a meeting, ask yourself: do I love Jesus more? Or do I only remember the speaker and the atmosphere? Third, each week meditate on one sentence: I am the colt; and ask: did I lift my head this week? Did I block the glory of Jesus? Brothers and sisters, put down deep roots through the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s closing words are beautiful: God has never looked for famous people; he looks for people willing to make Jesus famous. Lowering and lifting are two sides of the same movement. If you are serving but find you’ve started paying attention to how people look at you, lower your head today. If you’ve been hurt because you weren’t noticed, take your eyes off people today. Revival doesn’t begin with a bigger event; revival begins with a company of people willing to bow their heads. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. See no one but Jesus.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we bow down before you. Forgive us: so often, while you are using us, we quietly lift our heads. Make us honest vessels, standing in the right place; don’t let us block your light, but let us reflect it. We are willing to be the colt, the bridge, the clay jar. Have first place in our lives, in our homes and in our church. Brothers and sisters, let’s declare together: Lord, I am not the star. Be exalted, and may all people come to see you because of me! In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re reading Lesson 13 of Morning Devotion 321 together: Lift Up No One — Lift Up Only Jesus. Our theme verse is Matthew 17:8: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” Please say it with me: no one, except Jesus alone. Today’s lesson has a subtitle, and it is the most important picture in the whole lesson: I am the donkey’s colt; he is the King. May the Lord engrave this picture on our hearts this morning, and may he use this lesson to adjust the posture of our service.

Brothers and sisters, let me begin with something that happens in the sky. The sun is roughly four hundred times the size of the moon; yet the sun is also roughly four hundred times further from the earth than the moon is. Four hundred times the size, four hundred times the distance, and so to our eyes they look exactly the same size. So as long as the moon stands on that line in between, a small moon can cover the whole sun completely.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to what this is telling us. The moon gives off no light of its own; every bit of its light is borrowed. A rock like that — giving no light, not burning — can nonetheless hide the sun. Not because it is big, but because it is standing in the wrong place. Let me tell you something closer to our everyday lives. A brother led worship for the first time. That day the presence of the Holy Spirit was unmistakable, and after the service everyone gathered round him and said: You sang so beautifully today! Your voice really carries an anointing! The second week, he started paying attention to whether he was in tune; the fourth week, he found that when he prayed, what came to mind was not the face of the Lord but the applause of the congregation. Later, with tears in his eyes, he said: I didn’t fall. I just slowly moved myself into the middle.

Now we come to the Mount of Transfiguration. Matthew’s Gospel was written sometime between AD 50 and 70 for Jewish believers, to prove that Jesus is the Messiah, the King. What happened six days before the transfiguration? Peter had just recognised Jesus as the Christ, and in the blink of an eye he was trying to stop the Lord going to the cross, and was rebuked: you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men. Then the Lord said: if anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself. Brothers and sisters, “deny himself” is exactly what the 321 vision means: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Six days later, Jesus was transfigured, and Moses and Elijah appeared. Peter blurted out: Lord, let me make three tents, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah. He meant no harm; he spoke out of eagerness; but he set the Creator alongside the created. The Father interrupted him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” Then the cloud lifted, and they saw only Jesus.

Key point one: people are not the focus; Jesus is the focus. The lesson says that however gifted we are, we are ultimately vessels in the hands of Jesus. Paul says, “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” 2 Corinthians 4:7. The word for “clay vessel” originally meant the cheapest earthenware; every household had them, and nobody grieved when one broke. Brothers and sisters, why did God put the treasure in clay vessels? Paul gives the answer himself: so that the power may be shown to be of God. If the treasure were put in a golden vessel, people’s eyes would stop at the gold; put it in a clay jar, and people can see the treasure.

The lesson puts it very precisely: a vessel has no worth in itself; it is who uses it that determines its glory and its function. Think of an ordinary wooden staff — it’s worth next to nothing; but in Moses’ hand, stretched out over the Red Sea, the waters parted, and from then on that staff was called God’s rod. Did the staff change? No — what changed was who was holding it. But brothers and sisters, the Bible has one example that is truly alarming. The bronze serpent in the wilderness was made by Moses at God’s command, and everyone bitten by a serpent looked at it and lived; but more than seven hundred years later King Hezekiah broke it in pieces, because in those days the children of Israel burned incense to it. The bronze serpent that had once saved lives ended up as an idol. A vessel that is exalted will sooner or later be broken.

Psychology offers us a piece of supporting evidence. Around 1999 and 2000, Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky at Cornell University in the United States described the “spotlight effect”. They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room, then asked them to estimate how many people had noticed; their estimates came out at roughly twice the actual number. Brothers and sisters, there are two reminders here. First, we are not as important as we imagine. Second, since we are naturally inclined to turn the spotlight on ourselves, not exalting ourselves will never happen automatically — it has to be a deliberate, daily choice made by relying on the Holy Spirit. The 321 vision says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Key point two: the lesson of the donkey’s colt — being used is no reason to be exalted. On Palm Sunday, the Lord sent his disciples to fetch a donkey’s colt. Mark records: you will find a young donkey tied, on which no one has sat. If anyone asks, say: the Lord needs him. Brothers and sisters, remember those four words: the Lord needs him. That colt was no thoroughbred, no warhorse; it had no training and no track record at all. Its only credentials in all its life were those four words. And some five hundred years earlier, Zechariah had prophesied it: behold, your King comes to you, lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

What a fervent scene it was that day. A very great multitude spread their clothes on the road; others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road; and the crowds in front and behind kept shouting: Hosanna to the son of David! Brothers and sisters, let me ask the lesson’s piercing question: whom were the people welcoming? The colt, or Jesus? The answer is obvious: Jesus. The colt walked right in the middle of it all — cloaks on its back, branches under its hooves, cheering in its ears; it was present for all the pageantry, and not one bit of the glory was its own. That is exactly the situation of everyone who serves.

The lesson goes on to say something sobering: if the colt had lifted up its head amid the crowd’s cheers, Jesus would have fallen off its back, and the focus would have changed. Brothers and sisters, what a vivid picture that is. The colt’s job is to keep its head down, to carry the load, to keep walking forward; if its head comes up, its back tilts, and the one riding on it can’t sit steady. When our heads are down, the Lord sits steady and people see the King; when our heads come up, the Lord sways and people see the donkey. And the most dangerous thing is this: when the colt lifts its head, it feels as though it is being affirmed, being effective, being used by God. The 321 vision says: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

Key point three: the right attitude in service is head down, not head up. The lesson says that being used by the Lord is an immense honour, but that honour is not to add points to our name; it is so that Jesus is glorified. Paul says, “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord.” 2 Corinthians 4:5. We don’t preach ourselves. Brothers and sisters, ask yourself three questions. First, when I talk about this, who is the subject of the sentence? Second, where are my listeners being led — to the Lord, or to me? Third, if my name were removed from this, would I still be willing to do it? That third question cuts the deepest.

But brothers and sisters, the lesson reminds us: true humility is not denying what God has done; it is knowing clearly that it is Jesus who is doing the work through me. What does Paul say? “I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” 1 Corinthians 15:10. Acknowledge the facts, give back the glory — that is the standard sentence pattern of humility. The management scholar Jim Collins, in Good to Great, recorded a five-year research project. He found that the leaders of the greatest companies looked out of the window to give the credit to others when things went well, and looked in the mirror to take the responsibility themselves when things went badly. If even research in the world can see this, how much more the kingdom of God! James 4:6 says, God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.

Key point four: what happens when the church starts exalting people? The lesson has a sense of proportion: celebrity speakers and eye-catching events aren’t wrong in themselves, but if we’re not watchful, we may, without even noticing, put people in the place of focus. The clearest case in the New Testament is in Corinth. One said, I follow Paul; another, I follow Apollos. How did Paul answer? Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants? I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. The word “servant” originally meant one who waits at table. Brothers and sisters, at a banquet no guest remembers who carried the dishes in. Exalting people never leads to unity; it leads to factions.

The book of Acts contains two scenes in sharp contrast. In Lystra, the crowds wanted to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods, and the two apostles tore their clothes, sprang into the crowd and cried out: Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you. In Caesarea, King Herod put on his royal robes, and the people shouted: the voice of a god, and not of a man! Herod didn’t give God the glory, so an angel of the Lord immediately struck him, and he was eaten by worms and died. Brothers and sisters, notice: Herod’s sin was not seizing the glory but not giving the glory. Silence can sometimes be consent. The church exists not to promote people but to exalt Christ, so that in all things he might have the preeminence.

Key point five: what draws people is not us but Jesus lifted up. The Lord says, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” John 12:32. The very next verse explains: he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die. Brothers and sisters, see this clearly: the first meaning of the Lord’s “lifted up” is being lifted up on the cross. That is a tremendous reversal — the world’s exaltation is being put up high and looked up to; the Lord’s being lifted up is being nailed to wood and laying down his life for people. The word “draw” originally means to pull or drag, like hauling a boat up onto the shore with a rope. What truly draws people’s hearts is the cross. In the wilderness, those bitten by serpents only had to look at the bronze serpent, and they lived.

The lesson says: if a church relies only on events to draw people, it will wear itself out; but if it relies on the glory of Jesus to draw people, the result is a revival that is real, lasting and transforms hearts. There’s a very practical logic here: people drawn by events are loyal to the events; people drawn by a speaker are loyal to the speaker; all of these pass, so you have to keep putting on another one, bigger than the last. Only people drawn by Jesus are loyal to Jesus. History bears this out: the Welsh Revival of 1904 and the Great Pyongyang Revival of 1907 had features in common, and none of them was innovation in method; they were deep confession and worship. Brothers and sisters, remember the total eclipse? When the moon blocks the sun’s photosphere, people can see the corona. When our self grows quiet, people see the Lord’s glory.

Now let’s practise. Practice one: give the glory to Jesus straight after you serve. Whether it’s preaching, praying, sharing, counselling or visiting, within ten minutes go back to your inner room and say to the Lord: Lord, you did all this, not me; the glory is yours. Put down roots through the eight stages — Information: the glory was never mine to begin with; Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you see that faint longing in your heart to be praised; Conviction: giving back the glory isn’t losing out; it’s returning to your originally intended position; Implementation: don’t leave it past that evening. Practice two: after a meeting, ask yourself — do I love Jesus more? Or do I only remember the speaker and the atmosphere? Write two lines: what did this meeting show me about Jesus? What am I going to change this week because of it?

Practice three: each week meditate on one sentence — I am the colt. The lesson gives three questions to ask yourself: were there times this week when I lifted my head? Did I block the glory of Jesus? Am I willing to become his vessel more humbly? Information: read Mark 11 and remember those four words, “The Lord needs him.” Evaluation: after a month, see whether your list of head-lifting moments has a pattern — is it when you’re praised? When you’re comparing yourself? Or when you’re overlooked? Correction: prepare a one-line prayer: Lord, this is yours, not mine; I am the colt, and you are the King. Repetition: let that sentence become your silent prayer before you step up to the pulpit, before you speak. Multiplication: teach it to your spiritual children. One sentence can protect a person for a lifetime.

Brothers and sisters, let’s set this lesson within the framework of the 321 vision. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — though he existed in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; the Bible is my standard — God says, I will not give my glory to another; the Holy Spirit is my guide — the Lord says, he will glorify me. Notice: even the Holy Spirit does not exalt himself. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — the King is on the colt’s back, so the colt must keep its head down; let Jesus receive all the glory — even one per cent of the credit has to be handed over. The Goal: establish God’s system, a system that sees no one but Jesus. And the lesson reminds us: you are not the star; you are a bridge. A bridge is there to be walked across; a bridge sits low; and the Lord Jesus himself is that bridge.

Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s closing words are beautiful: God has never looked for famous people; he looks for people willing to make Jesus famous. Through the ages, the people God has used most mightily have often been those who disappeared. John the Baptist said, I must decrease, and then went down into prison; Paul said, I am nothing to speak of, and then wrote letters from a cell in Rome; the colt completed its task, and the Bible never so much as mentions where it went afterwards. They all disappeared — yet the One they pointed to is still praised by hundreds of millions two thousand years later. If you are serving but find you’ve started paying attention to how people look at you, lower your head today. Revival doesn’t begin with a bigger event; it begins with a company of people willing to bow their heads.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we bow down before you. You are the Lord who was transfigured on the mountain; you are the King who rode into Jerusalem on a donkey’s colt; you are the Saviour who was lifted up from the earth for us. Forgive us: so often, while you are using us, we quietly lift our heads; sometimes it isn’t that we snatch your glory — we simply forget to turn it back to you. Make us honest vessels, standing in the right place; don’t let us block your light, but let us reflect it. Have first place in our lives, in our homes and in our church. Brothers and sisters, let’s declare together: Lord, I am not the star. Be exalted, and may all people come to see you because of me! No one else — only Jesus. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: A Mountain That Can Fall, a Pillar That Can Run
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a picture all of us have seen.

In Italy there stands a world-famous bell tower: the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Construction began in 1173, and by the time the builders reached the third storey it had already started to lean, because the ground beneath it was soft alluvial soil. The workmen stopped, started again, stopped again; all told, the building took nearly two hundred years. Later craftsmen made the columns on the upper storeys taller on one side than the other, trying to “bend” the tower back into line, and the result was a tower shaped like a banana. By the end of the twentieth century the top had drifted more than four metres from the vertical, at an angle of about 5.5 degrees. In 1990 the Italian government closed the tower and brought in an international panel of experts. It took eleven years, drawing soil out from beneath the foundations on the north side, to pull it back to about 3.99 degrees.

Brothers and sisters, the surface of that tower is marble — finely carved and dazzling to behold. The problem was never the surface. The problem was the foundation.

Our elders have a little rhyme: “Lean on a mountain, the mountain may fall; lean on a man, the man may run; lean on the Lord Jesus — best of all.” It sounds like a folk saying, yet it touches the deepest truth of the human heart.

All our lives we are looking for something to lean on. As children we lean on our parents; as we grow up we lean on our qualifications; once we enter the working world we lean on our connections; in middle age we lean on our savings; in old age we lean on our children. We lean on systems, on positions, on a clean health-check report, on an insurance policy, on someone with a big name. These are not bad things, and God often provides for us through them. But brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: anything that can change cannot be a foundation.

You think “lean on a mountain, the mountain may fall” is an exaggeration? Mountains really do move. On 25 April 2015 a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck Nepal, and nearly nine thousand people lost their lives. That earthquake even rewrote the terrain of the Himalayas. In December 2020 the governments of China and Nepal jointly announced a new official height for Mount Everest: 8,848.86 metres. Even the highest mountain on earth has to be measured again. Mountains move, mountains collapse, mountains have to be re-surveyed.

You think “lean on a man, the man may run” is too harsh? No. People don’t run away out of malice; people are simply limited. The one who loves you most will grow old; the one who backs you most will grow tired; the most faithful person you know will one day come to the end of their life. During his second imprisonment in Rome, Paul wrote to Timothy: “At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me. May it not be held against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (2 Timothy 4:16–17). Paul didn’t blame them. He simply stated a fact: people will leave, and the Lord will stand by you.

So is there anything at all that doesn’t change?

Scientists, in fact, understand this problem better than anyone. Humanity once measured length by a metal bar. In 1889 the International Bureau of Weights and Measures cast the “International Prototype of the Metre” in platinum-iridium and stored it just outside Paris; every “metre” in the world was measured against it. But metal expands with heat and contracts with cold; it oxidises; it wears away. So in 1983 the General Conference on Weights and Measures decided to stop relying on that bar and to define the metre by the speed of light instead. Time is the same: since 1967, one second has been defined by the transition frequency of the caesium-133 atom.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Even science admits that a standard cannot be built on something that changes. In the end, humanity had no choice but to anchor its standards to the most unchanging constants in the universe.

And what about our lives? Our families, our service, our churches? Where are we going to lay our foundation?

The Bible gives only one answer, and he is a Person: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Hebrews 13:8).

The title of today’s lesson is very direct: Rely on No One but Jesus. This is not about becoming solitary, refusing friends or refusing help. It is about moving the foundation back to where it belongs. People can be companions; they cannot be the foundation. Methods can be tools; they cannot be what we rely on. This morning, let’s move the whole weight of our lives off the mountain that can fall and the people who can run, and back onto the Rock that never changes.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Multiple-Choice Question on the Eve of a Nation’s Fall
sections.html:
Our key passage today comes from Jeremiah chapter 17.

Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, from a priestly family in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin. He was called in the thirteenth year of Josiah king of Judah, and he served right through to the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon and the exile of the people — more than forty years in all. He is known as “the weeping prophet”, because the message he preached was exactly what his nation least wanted to hear.

What was Judah’s situation at the time? The Assyrian Empire was in decline, and two great powers, Egypt and the new Babylon, were locked in a tug-of-war up and down the corridor of Canaan. Little Judah was caught in the middle, and the royal court was split into two factions: one wanted to lean on Egypt, the other on Babylon. The hottest question in the whole nation was not “What does God say?” but “Whom should we rely on?” Long before Jeremiah, Isaiah had already warned: “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, and rely on horses, and trust in chariots because they are many, and in horsemen because they are very strong, but they don’t look to the Holy One of Israel, and they don’t seek Yahweh!” (Isaiah 31:1).

Jeremiah 17 opens by naming the root of the problem: “The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond. It is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of your altars” (Jeremiah 17:1). The sin is not carved in stone; it is carved on the tablet of the heart. This is a problem of the heart, not a problem of strategy.

Then, in verses 5 to 8, God sets out a multiple-choice question. There are only two options. There is no third.

The first option: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh” (Jeremiah 17:5). The word for “flesh” here is the Hebrew basar: the body that perishes and wastes away. The Chinese Bible renders the phrase “an arm of flesh and blood”, and the arm stands for strength. Put together, it means strength that decays. God is not saying people have no strength; he is saying that human strength decays.

Notice the second half of verse 5: “whose heart departs from Yahweh.” That is the key. The real problem with relying on people is not that we “asked someone for help”; it is that our heart has left God. It is a question of order, a question of the throne — who sits on the throne of my heart.

And the result? “For he will be like a bush in the desert, and will not see when good comes, but will inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, an uninhabited salt land” (Jeremiah 17:6). The “bush in the desert” is a small, stunted shrub of the wilderness. It isn’t dead; it is alive — but it can do no more than stay alive. Even if rain falls right beside it, it cannot feel it, because it stands in salt land, brackish ground where water won’t stay and roots can’t go deep.

The second option: “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh” (Jeremiah 17:7). The Hebrew root behind “trust” here is batach: to put your whole weight down on something, to lean on it securely, to entrust yourself without a trace of wariness. The word does not describe intellectual agreement; it describes handing over the full weight of who you are.

And the result? “For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit” (Jeremiah 17:8).

Brothers and sisters, please notice: God did not say that those who trust in Yahweh will never meet the heat. The text says they “will not fear when heat comes.” Nor did he say there will be no year of drought; he said they “will not be concerned in the year of drought.” The same sun beats down on the desert bush and on the tree by the water. The difference is not the environment. The difference is where the roots go down.

Then verse 9 is the key verse of the whole chapter: “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9). Why is it so easy for us to rely on people? Because the human heart is deceitful; it even deceives itself. With our lips we say “I trust the Lord”, while in our hearts we are working out a different plan. That is why in verse 10 God says: “I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.”

That is the background to this lesson: a nation on the eve of its fall, facing a multiple-choice question. And every morning when we wake up, we have to answer the same question all over again.

sections.heading: 1. Everything in the World Changes; Only Jesus Does Not
sections.html:
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.” (Hebrews 13:8)

“For I, Yahweh, don’t change; therefore you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed.” (Malachi 3:6)

“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.” (James 1:17)

Brothers and sisters, in this fast-shifting world, no person, no system and no circumstance is truly reliable. Economies collapse, affections change, workplaces restructure, friendships drift apart; even the religious systems we know so well can fail us. That isn’t pessimism. That’s honesty.

James 1:17 uses a beautiful image from the sky. “The Father of lights” means the God who made the stars. “Turning shadow” in the Greek is literally “the shadow cast by turning”. Every light on earth shifts: the sun rises and sets, and shadows move from east to west; the moon waxes and wanes; the stars rise and set. But the One who made the light does not shift. There is not a trace of shadow on him, not a single degree of deviation.

We tend to think we are standing still. Yet as you sit there right now, the earth is carrying you round on its axis at about 1,670 kilometres an hour (near the equator), while orbiting the sun at about 29.8 kilometres a second. We have not stopped for a single second. Life is the same: we think everything is just as it was, when in fact everything is moving.

Psychology measured the weight of “change” long ago. In 1967 two psychiatrists at the University of Washington, Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe, published the Social Readjustment Rating Scale, which turned life events into stress scores: the death of a spouse, 100 points; divorce, 73; being fired, 47; changing jobs, 36. Even “good things” like marriage, promotion and moving house add to the stress score. What wears us out is not only bad things; it is “change” itself. The human heart is made to long for a fixed point to stand on.

The classic study published in 1958 in the journal American Psychologist by Harry Harlow, a psychologist at the University of Wisconsin, is more direct still. He let infant monkeys choose between two surrogate mothers: one made of wire, with a feeding bottle attached; the other made of soft cloth, with no milk. The infant monkeys went to the wire mother only when hungry, for a few sips of milk; the vast majority of their time they spent clinging tightly to the cloth mother. When frightened, every one of them rushed to the cloth mother. Harlow’s conclusion: a creature’s need for something to “lean on” is not only about getting supplies; even more, it is about finding security.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly how God made us. We are created beings, made to live “leaning on” someone. The question was never “Should I lean on anything?” The question is “Whom do I lean on?”

At the opening of his Confessions, Augustine prayed to God: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” In sixteen hundred years that sentence has never gone out of date, because the make-up of the human heart has not changed.

And what about Jesus? In the original of Hebrews 13:8, the three times — “yesterday, today, and forever” — are laid side by side with no verb at all — just one phrase, “the same” (ho autos), holding them together. The Jesus of the past, the Jesus of the present and the Jesus of eternity are one and the same. The power with which he turned water into wine at Cana has not faded. The compassion with which he touched the coffin at Nain has not cooled. The love with which he wept for you in Gethsemane has not lessened one bit.

The 321 vision speaks of the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Brothers and sisters, a foundation is called a foundation precisely because it does not move. However beautiful the marble of the Leaning Tower of Pisa, once the foundation gives way, everything is lost. If we lay the foundation of our lives on “people”, we are building our house on shifting sand. Only when we lay the foundation on Jesus — the One who does not move — can we stand firm.

So the first mindset that must change is this: not “the world is too chaotic for me to feel secure”, but “I have put my security in the wrong place.” Change the mindset and you change the life.

sections.heading: 2. Are You Looking for a Method, or for Jesus?
sections.html:
“Jesus said to him, ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.’” (John 14:6)

“God, you are my God. I will earnestly seek you. My soul thirsts for you. My flesh longs for you, in a dry and weary land, where there is no water.” (Psalm 63:1)

Brothers and sisters, when we face difficulties and problems, the first thing we usually look for is a “solution”: Who can help me? What should I do? Is there a success story I can copy?

That is human instinct. But what Jesus wants us to look for is not a method. It is himself.

Notice the grammar of John 14:6. Jesus did not say, “I point out the way”; he said, “I am the way.” He did not say, “I teach the truth”; he said, “I am the truth.” He did not say, “I give people life”; he said, “I am the life.” The Greek here uses the definite article three times over: the way, the truth, the life. Jesus is not the one who brings the answer. He is the answer itself.

The setting of these words is more moving still. It was the Last Supper, and the Lord had just told them he was going away. Thomas grew anxious and said, “Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?” (John 14:5). Thomas wanted a “route map”; the Lord gave him himself. Brothers and sisters, our prayers are often just like that: Lord, give me a method. And the Lord says: Child, I give you myself.

When David wrote Psalm 63, he was in the wilderness of Judah. That was real drought, a real lack of water, a real flight for his life. Yet look at what he says. He doesn’t say, “I thirst for water.” He says, “My soul thirsts for you.” What he sought in a land without water was not water but the source of life. That is the mark of spiritual maturity: in a dry land, the first thing you turn to is God, not a water supply.

Jeremiah puts it even more sharply: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at the order of those two evils. The first: forsaking the spring of living water. The second: cutting out cisterns for themselves. Cutting cisterns is hard work; you hack away at the rock one blow at a time. People aren’t lazy. People work very hard — in the wrong direction. And however skilfully a cistern is cut, it will crack, because a cistern can only store water; it cannot produce it. Methods are the cistern. Jesus is the spring.

Second Chronicles records a heartbreaking example. As a young man, Asa king of Judah relied greatly on God. With five hundred and eighty thousand men he went out against an army of a million Cushites, and he prayed: “Yahweh, there is no one besides you to help, between the mighty and him who has no strength. Help us, Yahweh our God; for we rely on you, and in your name are we come against this multitude” (2 Chronicles 14:11). And God struck the Cushites down. But in his later years, when the northern kingdom of Israel came against him, he no longer sought God. Instead, he sent the silver and gold of the temple and the palace to Ben-Hadad king of Aram, borrowing outside power to break the siege. The prophet Hanani came to rebuke him: “For Yahweh’s eyes run back and forth throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. You have done foolishly in this; for from now on you will have wars” (2 Chronicles 16:9). Sadder still is the sentence that follows: “In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa was diseased in his feet. His disease was exceedingly great: yet in his disease he didn’t seek Yahweh, but just the physicians” (2 Chronicles 16:12).

Please note: the Bible is not saying it is a sin to see a doctor. What it points out is that he “didn’t seek Yahweh, but just the physicians.” The problem lies in that word “just” — and in that “didn’t”. Methods are not sin. Putting a method in God’s place is.

The 321 vision teaches the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Our trouble today is often that we turn the whole order upside down — we deal with the task first, then look for people, and pray last of all. The result is that we rely on the brain and ourselves, and the more we think, the more we worry. The Bible says: “for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you find joy; rely on the brain and yourself, and you find worry.

So the second mindset that must change is this: not “I need an answer”, but “I need the One who is the Answer.”

sections.heading: 3. Revival Comes Not from Methods but from Jesus
sections.html:
“Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies. (Zechariah 4:6)

“Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)

Brothers and sisters, when many churches today pursue revival, they often imitate the models of successful churches, borrow the anointing language of whatever wave is current, and copy other people’s experiences and structures. These things are not necessarily wrong in themselves, but we can easily overlook a spiritual fact: what truly brings breakthrough and revival is not a model, not a strategy, not an event — it is Jesus.

The setting of Zechariah 4 fits this exactly. It was after the return from exile, and Zerubbabel was leading a weary people to rebuild the temple. They were few, they had little money, enemies harassed them, and the work had stalled for years. The angel showed the prophet a vision: a lampstand of pure gold, with two olive trees beside it, and oil flowing from the trees into the lampstand of its own accord. The meaning of the vision is plain: the lamp shines not because people keep carrying oil in, but because God himself supplies it without ceasing.

And so God spoke those famous words: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). “Might” in Hebrew is chayil — armies, wealth, the strength of a group. “Power” is koach — an individual’s physical strength, ability, skill. One is the resources of a team; the other is the ability of a person. In one stroke, God rules out both of the great categories people rely on.

Brothers and sisters, there is an important distinction here. The Lord is not saying “methods are sin”; he is saying “methods are not the source of power.” It is like an electric light. The switch matters, but the switch does not generate electricity. You could fill an entire wall with the most beautiful switches in the world, and the room would still be dark, because the electricity doesn’t come from the switch.

What’s more, someone else’s method is not necessarily the path God has prepared for us. The Bible has a fine example. When David was about to fight Goliath, Saul dressed him in his own armour, put a bronze helmet on his head and clothed him in a coat of mail. It was the best equipment of the day, fit for a king. But David said, “I can’t go with these; for I have not tested them” (1 Samuel 17:39). So he took them off, picked up his staff, five smooth stones and his sling, and went out in the name of Yahweh of Armies. Saul’s armour might have worked for Saul; for David it was a straitjacket.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly today’s temptation: we often put on someone else’s armour and walk someone else’s road, and in the end we look neither like ourselves nor like what God wants us to become. Every church’s road to revival should be the fruit of walking intimately with Jesus, receiving from him specifically, and responding to him genuinely.

Church history confirms this again and again. On 13 August 1727, at Herrnhut in Germany, the Moravian Brethren experienced an outpouring of the Holy Spirit during a communion service. Before that, this group of refugees from many different backgrounds had been quarrelling and splitting into factions. They did not rely on some new programme. Under the leadership of Count Zinzendorf, they confessed their sins, were reconciled and prayed with one heart. After the revival, they began a prayer watch in shifts; according to the Moravians’ own records, this round-the-clock prayer continued without a break for more than a hundred years and sent out hundreds of missionaries. The starting point of revival was not a strategy meeting. It was a group of people coming back before Jesus.

The 321 vision speaks of the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Brothers and sisters, when our eyes turn to “how to do it”, we drift, without noticing, away from “whom we rely on”. If revival is the credit of our methods, then the glory goes to the methods. If revival is Jesus’ own work, then the glory goes to Jesus. Which kind of revival do we want?

So the third mindset that must change is this: not “find the right model and revival will come”, but “return to the right Head, and only then will revival come.”

sections.heading: 4. Joshua’s Way to Victory in Battle: Relying Wholly on God
sections.html:
“When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man stood in front of him with his sword drawn in his hand. Joshua went to him and said to him, ‘Are you for us, or for our enemies?’ He said, ‘No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.’ Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and worshiped, and asked him, ‘What does my lord say to his servant?’” (Joshua 5:13–14)

Brothers and sisters, when the Israelites entered Canaan, they faced the combined armies of many nations, fortified cities and battles whose outcome no one could know. Yet they won one victory after another. Why? Their victories did not come from training and equipment; they came from relying wholly on God’s leading.

Look at this scene in Joshua chapter 5. Joshua had just led the people across the Jordan; they had been circumcised, they had kept the Passover, and the manna had stopped. Ahead of them lay Jericho — the first stronghold of Canaan. He went up close to the city alone, probably surveying the ground and thinking through his tactics. Suddenly a man with a drawn sword was standing in front of him.

Joshua asked a very “human” question: “Are you for us, or for our enemies?” That is the way of thinking we know best — divide people into two sides and see who is on mine.

The answer turned the whole question on its head: “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.”

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to that “No.” What the Lord means is: I have not come to join your side; I have come to take command. The question was never “Is God on my side?” The question is “Am I on God’s side?” It isn’t God coming to help me fight my battle; it is me joining God’s army to fight God’s battle.

Joshua’s response is beautiful. He didn’t argue; he didn’t explain. “Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and worshiped, and asked him, ‘What does my lord say to his servant?’” (Joshua 5:14).

Notice what he calls himself: servant. Who was he? He was Moses’ successor, the supreme commander of the whole army of Israel, the very man to whom God had personally promised, “Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9). He had every right to call himself commander. Yet he fell face down, gave up the commander’s place, and stepped back into the position of a servant.

The 321 vision puts it well: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. That is exactly what Joshua did outside Jericho. He laid down “I am the commander” and returned to “I am the servant.” The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is yielding up our limited self so that the infinite Commander can come in.

Then the commander said: “Take off your sandals, for the place on which you stand is holy” (Joshua 5:15). These are the very words God had spoken to Moses at Horeb forty years earlier (Exodus 3:5). Taking off your sandals means dropping your own defences and your own stance; in the ancient Near East, removing your sandals also symbolised giving up your rights. The first step to victory is not putting on your battle boots. It is taking off your sandals.

And then, right at the opening of chapter 6, comes this: “Yahweh said to Joshua, ‘Behold, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and the mighty men of valor’” (Joshua 6:2).

Brothers and sisters, notice the tense. God did not say, “I will give it to you.” God said, “I have given … into your hand.” The battle hadn’t been fought, yet the outcome was already settled — because the one fighting was not Joshua; it was Yahweh. And the battle plan that followed was even more outlandish: march round the city once a day for six days; on the seventh day, march round seven times, the priests blow the trumpets, and the people shout. That is not military tactics. It is a “training in obedience.” What God wanted his people to learn was this: the walls fall not because you shout loudly, but because God has spoken.

But if you keep reading, you will see a very important contrast.

Chapter 7: Ai. Ai was small. The spies came back and said: “Don’t let all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and strike Ai. Don’t make all the people to toil there, for there are only a few of them” (Joshua 7:3). So three thousand went up, and “they fled before the men of Ai” (Joshua 7:4). They won at Jericho, big as it was, yet lost at Ai, small as it was. Why? Apart from Achan’s sin, you will find this: before attacking Jericho they inquired of God; before attacking Ai they assessed the people.

Chapter 9: the Gibeonites. The Gibeonites put on worn-out clothes, brought dry, hard bread and came pretending to surrender. The text names Israel’s failure in a single sentence: “The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth” (Joshua 9:14). Without inquiring of God, they signed a treaty — and once signed, it was a permanent treaty, leaving trouble behind it for hundreds of years.

Brothers and sisters, put these three events side by side and the message is clear: inquire of God and you win; don’t inquire of God and you lose out. The difference is not the size of the matter. The difference is whether you have handed the commander’s place over to God.

In his 2001 book Good to Great, the leadership researcher Jim Collins studied eleven companies that went from mediocre to excellent, and found that the leaders at the very top level shared one trait: when things went well, they looked out of the window and gave the credit to others; when things went badly, they looked in the mirror and took the responsibility on themselves. Brothers and sisters, what the business world took decades of research to discover, Joshua acted out face down on the ground more than three thousand years ago.

In the same way, the Head of the church is Jesus — not the pastor, not the leaders, not the system.

sections.heading: 5. The Key to the Church: Who Is in Charge? Who Is Leading?
sections.html:
“For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the assembly, being himself the savior of the body.” (Ephesians 5:23)

“He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.” (Ephesians 1:22–23)

“He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18)

Brothers and sisters, the Bible says that Christ is the head of the church. The Greek word for “head” is kephalē: it means the head of a body, but also the source, the chief, the seat of authority. It is an image from the body, and it is also a declaration about how the church is ordered.

Think about it: what would happen if a body had two heads? The left foot heads east, the right foot heads west; the hand wants to grab, the mouth wants to let go. That isn’t richness; that’s a seizure. Much of the quarrelling, exhaustion and tearing apart in churches, traced back to its root, comes not from a lack of love but from too many heads.

The human body has a wonderful design. Your heartbeat, your breathing, your body temperature — none of them needs your willpower to direct it; the brainstem takes care of them for you. That is the function of the “head”: as long as the head is alive, the body has order. Conversely, the most terrible thing that can happen to a body is not an injured finger; it is a broken neck, with the signals cut off. That is called paralysis.

So the church’s greatest crisis is not a shortage of people, money or space. It is when the signal is cut — when we are no longer connected to the Head.

If a church is not led by Jesus but runs on human experience, ability or enthusiasm, then behind what looks like revival lies a crisis. Rely on human experience, and experience goes out of date; rely on human ability, and ability runs dry; rely on human enthusiasm, and enthusiasm cools. More dangerous still, when a whole group leans on one person, the moment that person falls, the whole system falls with them.

Jesus put it with complete clarity: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Notice that the Lord did not say, “Apart from me you will do a little less.” He said, “You can do nothing.” Not half the efficiency — zero.

What did the early church do? Before the Lord ascended, he commanded them: “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father” (Acts 1:4). Those hundred and twenty people were short on nothing so much as time, and nothing was more urgent to them than preaching the gospel. Yet the Lord told them to wait. So in the upper room they devoted themselves with one accord to prayer. They waited ten days; the Holy Spirit came; and in a single day three thousand people were baptised and turned to the Lord.

Later, when a great dispute broke out in the church over whether Gentiles must be circumcised, how did the letter recording the conclusion of the Jerusalem Council put it? “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things” (Acts 15:28). Look at the order: the Holy Spirit, and us. Not “we passed a resolution and then asked the Holy Spirit to bless it”, but “the Holy Spirit, and us.”

Brothers and sisters, what we truly need is not more resources or more talent, but more “relying on Jesus”: seeking him in our meetings, relying on him in our decisions, looking to him in our difficulties. As long as Jesus is in charge, the church will walk the road of victory.

Revelation chapter 3 paints a startling picture. The Lord says to the church in Laodicea: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). These are words the Lord speaks to a church.
