script: Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Our elders have a little rhyme: “Lean on a mountain, the mountain may fall; lean on a man, the man may run; lean on the Lord Jesus — best of all.”
This morning let’s look at this together: rely on no one but Jesus. That doesn’t mean we give up our friends or refuse help; it means we move the foundation of our lives back to where it belongs.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa in Italy began to lean by the time the builders reached the third storey, because the ground beneath it was soft. The surface is marble, but the problem was the foundation.

Is “lean on a mountain, the mountain may fall” an exaggeration? In 2020 China and Nepal jointly announced a new height for Mount Everest. Even the highest mountain in the world has to be measured again.

Is “lean on a man, the man may run” too harsh? No. People don’t run away out of malice; people are simply limited. The one who loves you most will grow old; the one who backs you most will grow tired. Paul says, “But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (2 Timothy 4:17).
Brothers and sisters, remember this: anything that can change cannot be a foundation.
Our theme passage today is in Jeremiah chapter 17.

In Jeremiah’s day, Judah was on the brink of collapse. The royal court was split into two factions: one said lean on Egypt, the other said lean on Babylon. The hottest question in the whole nation was not “What does God say?” but “Whom should we rely on?” So God set out a multiple-choice question, with only two options.
The first: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh.” Like a bush in the desert — alive, but only just alive.
The second: “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh.” Like a tree planted by the waters, spreading out its roots by the river.

Brothers and sisters, God did not say that those who trust in him will never meet the heat; the text says they “will not fear when heat comes.” The same sun beats down on the desert bush and on the tree by the water. The difference is not the environment; it is where the roots go down.
Key point one: everything in the world changes; only Jesus does not.

Brothers and sisters, humanity used to measure a metre by a metal bar that expanded with heat and contracted with cold; in 1983 the metre was redefined by the speed of light. Even science admits that a standard cannot be built on something that changes.
The scale Holmes and Rahe published in 1967 found that even good things like marriage, promotion and moving house add to our stress. What wears us out is not only bad things; it is change itself.
So is there anything that doesn’t change? Yes. “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Hebrews 13:8).
The 321 vision speaks of the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. A foundation is called a foundation precisely because it does not move.
Key point two: are you looking for a method, or for Jesus?

When we meet difficulties, our first thought is usually: who can help me? But the Lord says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He didn’t say, “I point out the way”; he said, “I am the way.” He is the answer itself.
Jeremiah says God’s people committed two evils: “they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

Brothers and sisters, people aren’t lazy; people work very hard — in the wrong direction. Methods are the cistern; Jesus is the spring. In his later years King Asa of Judah “in his disease didn’t seek Yahweh, but just the physicians” (2 Chronicles 16:12). The problem lies in that word “just”.
Key point three: revival comes not from methods but from Jesus.
God said to Zerubbabel, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6).

The Lord isn’t saying methods are sin; he is saying methods are not the source of power. It’s like a light switch: the switch matters, but the switch doesn’t generate electricity. Fill a whole wall with switches, and the room is still dark.

What’s more, someone else’s method isn’t necessarily the path God has given us. Saul gave David his best armour, and David said, “I can’t go with these; for I have not tested them” (1 Samuel 17:39). Saul’s armour was a straitjacket for David.
Key point four: Joshua’s way to victory was relying wholly on God.
Outside Jericho, Joshua asked the man with the drawn sword, “Are you for us, or for our enemies?” He answered, “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army” (Joshua 5:14).
Brothers and sisters, did you hear that “No”? The question was never “Is God on my side?” The question is “Am I on God’s side?”
And Joshua fell face down and called himself a servant. The 321 vision says: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.
But at Gibeon, “the men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth” (Joshua 9:14), and they were deceived. Inquire of God and you win; don’t inquire of God and you lose out.
Key point five: the key to the church is who is in charge and who is leading.

The Bible says Christ is the head of the church (Ephesians 5:23). What would happen if a body had two heads? The left foot heads east, the right foot heads west. That isn’t richness; that’s a seizure.
The Lord says, “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Not half the efficiency — zero.
Revelation paints a startling picture: the Lord standing outside the church door, knocking. The church was meeting as usual, serving as usual — and the Lord was outside.
This morning let’s honestly ask ourselves: in my family, in my service, is Jesus sitting on the throne, or standing outside the door?
A gentle reminder: methods are tools; Jesus is the one we rely on.

Brothers and sisters, I’m not against planning. The question is which seat our methods occupy. Moses said, “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here” (Exodus 33:15). He would rather go without Canaan than have a Canaan without the presence of God.
When you walk relying on Jesus, even a cup of water or a single prayer will bring God’s presence and bear fruit.
Next come three practices.
First, declare every morning: “Lord Jesus, today I will not rely on myself or on people; I will rely on you alone!” Speak before your feet even touch the floor.
Second, when you need help, pray first, then ask. Praying first and then asking for help, versus asking for help and then praying — only minutes apart, yet a whole throne apart.
Third, before you serve, be still and ask, “Lord, how do you see this?” Proficiency is a grace and also a temptation, because proficiency lets us keep going without needing to rely on God.
Walk these three practices all the way through the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Brothers and sisters, every person and thing in this world will change, but Jesus never fails.
He is your ever-present help in trouble. He is the commander of Yahweh’s army. He is the anchor of your soul.
An anchor isn’t dropped onto the ship; it is thrown overboard. If your anchor is cast onto your own abilities or onto some person, it is still on the ship.
Let Jesus come in from outside the door, from the last resort to the first one we turn to. Revival is not an event; revival is Jesus reigning once again as King among his people.
Let’s declare together: Lord Jesus, I do not rely on people; I rely on you alone!
Let’s pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that we so often lean on mountains, on people, on ourselves. Please forgive us. This morning, like Joshua, we fall face down and hand the commander’s place back to you.
Make us like a tree planted by the waters, spreading out its roots by the river; not afraid when heat comes; not anxious in the year of drought; never ceasing to bear fruit.
Reign as King in our families; reign as King in our church. May all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Our elders have a little rhyme: “Lean on a mountain, the mountain may fall; lean on a man, the man may run; lean on the Lord Jesus — best of all.”
This morning we’re going to face this together: rely on no one but Jesus.

Let me be clear first. This lesson isn’t asking us to become solitary or give up our friends. God often provides for us through people. What this lesson does is move the foundation of our lives back to where it belongs: people can be companions, but they cannot be the foundation; methods can be tools, but they cannot be what we rely on.

In Italy there stands the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Construction began in 1173, and by the third storey it had already started to lean, because the ground beneath it was soft alluvial soil. By the end of the twentieth century the top had drifted more than four metres from the vertical. In 1990 the Italian government closed the tower, and it took eleven years, drawing soil out bit by bit from beneath the foundations on the north side, to pull it back to about 3.99 degrees.
Brothers and sisters, the surface of that tower is marble, finely carved. But the problem was never the surface. The problem was the foundation.
Remember this: anything that can change cannot be a foundation.

Some say “lean on a mountain, the mountain may fall” is an exaggeration. It isn’t. In December 2020 China and Nepal jointly announced a new official height for Mount Everest. Even the highest mountain on earth has to be measured again.

Then is “lean on a man, the man may run” too harsh? It isn’t harsh either. People don’t run away out of malice; people are simply limited: the one who loves you most will grow old; the one who backs you most will grow tired.

During his second imprisonment, Paul wrote to Timothy: “All left me … But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (2 Timothy 4:16–17). He didn’t blame anyone; he simply stated a fact: people will leave, and the Lord will stand by you.
Our theme passage today is in Jeremiah chapter 17.

Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, a priest of Anathoth. He was called in the thirteenth year of King Josiah and served for more than forty years; he is known as the weeping prophet. Judah was caught between Egypt and the new Babylon, and the royal court was split into a pro-Egypt and a pro-Babylon faction. The hottest topic in the whole nation was not “What does God say?” but “Whom should we rely on?” So God set out a multiple-choice question, with only two options.

The first: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh.” Notice the second half — whose heart departs from Yahweh. The problem with relying on people isn’t that we asked someone for help; it’s that our heart has left God.
The second: “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh.” The Hebrew root here is batach, meaning to put your whole weight down on something.

One is like a bush in the desert — alive, but only just alive; the other is like a tree planted by the waters, spreading out its roots by the river. Brothers and sisters, God did not say that those who trust in him will never meet the heat; the text says they “will not fear when heat comes.” The difference is not the environment; it is where the roots go down.
Key point one: everything in the world changes; only Jesus does not.
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Hebrews 13:8).

Brothers and sisters, this verse lays three times side by side, held together by one phrase, “the same”. The power with which he turned water into wine at Cana has not faded; the love with which he wept for you has not lessened one bit. James also says, with him there “can be no variation, nor turning shadow” (James 1:17). Every light on earth shifts; the One who made the light does not.
In fact, scientists understand better than anyone how hard it is to find something that doesn’t change.

Humanity used to measure length by a metal bar. In 1889 the International Bureau of Weights and Measures cast the International Prototype of the Metre, but metal expands with heat, contracts with cold and wears away; so in 1983 the metre was redefined by the speed of light. Brothers and sisters, even science admits that a standard cannot be built on something that changes.

Psychology is the same. In 1967 Holmes and Rahe published the Social Readjustment Rating Scale and found that even good things like marriage, promotion and moving house add to the stress score. What wears us out is not only bad things; it is change itself.

In 1958 Harlow at the University of Wisconsin also found that infant monkeys went to the wire mother only when hungry, for milk, but the moment they were frightened, every one of them rushed to the cloth mother. We are created beings, made to live leaning on someone; the question is not whether we lean, but whom we lean on.
The 321 vision speaks of the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. A foundation is called a foundation precisely because it does not move.
Key point two: are you looking for a method, or for Jesus?

When we meet difficulties, our first thought is usually: who can help me? But the Lord says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He didn’t say, “I point out the way”; he said, “I am the way.” Jesus is not the one who brings the answer; he is the answer itself. It was the night of the Last Supper; Thomas wanted a route map, and the Lord gave him himself.

When David wrote Psalm 63, he was fleeing for his life in the wilderness. He didn’t say, “I thirst for water”; he said, “My soul thirsts for you.” In a land without water, what he sought was not water but the source of life.

Jeremiah puts it even more sharply: God’s people committed two evils — “they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

Look at the order: first they forsook the spring, then they cut their own cisterns. Brothers and sisters, people aren’t lazy; people work very hard — in the wrong direction. And however skilfully a cistern is cut, it will crack, because a cistern can only store water; it cannot produce it. Methods are the cistern; Jesus is the spring.

As a young man King Asa of Judah relied greatly on God, yet of his later years the Bible records: “in his disease he didn’t seek Yahweh, but just the physicians” (2 Chronicles 16:12). The Bible isn’t saying it is a sin to see a doctor; the problem lies in that word “just”.
The 321 vision teaches the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.
Key point three: revival comes not from methods but from Jesus.

When many churches today pursue revival, they often imitate successful models and copy other people’s structures. That isn’t necessarily wrong, but it is easy to overlook a spiritual fact: what brings revival is not a model or a strategy — it is Jesus.

After the return from exile, Zerubbabel was leading a weary people to rebuild the temple; they were few, they had little money, and the work had stalled. God showed Zechariah a vision: a lampstand of pure gold with two olive trees beside it, and oil flowing into the lampstand of its own accord. The lamp shines not because people keep carrying oil in, but because God supplies it.

And so God said, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). “Might” means the resources of a group; “power” means an individual’s ability. In one stroke God rules out both kinds of reliance.

Brothers and sisters, the Lord isn’t saying methods are sin; he is saying methods are not the source of power. It’s like a light switch: the switch matters, but the switch doesn’t generate electricity. Fill a whole wall with switches, and the room is still dark.
What’s more, someone else’s method isn’t necessarily the path God has prepared for us.

When David was about to fight Goliath, Saul dressed him in his own best armour. David said, “I can’t go with these; for I have not tested them” (1 Samuel 17:39). Saul’s armour worked for Saul, but for David it was a straitjacket.

Church history confirms this again and again. On 13 August 1727, at Herrnhut in Germany, the Moravian Brethren experienced an outpouring of the Holy Spirit during a communion service. Before that they had been quarrelling and splitting into factions; they didn’t rely on some new programme — they confessed their sins, were reconciled and prayed with one heart. After the revival they began a prayer watch in shifts which, according to their records, continued for more than a hundred years.

The starting point of revival was not a strategy meeting; it was a group of people coming back before Jesus. The 321 vision speaks of the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.
Key point four: Joshua’s way to victory in battle was relying wholly on God.

When the Israelites entered Canaan, they faced allied armies and fortified cities, yet they won one victory after another. Their victories did not come from training and equipment; they came from relying wholly on God.

Outside Jericho, Joshua went up close to the city to survey the ground, and suddenly he saw a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword. He asked a very “human” question: “Are you for us, or for our enemies?”
The man answered, “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army” (Joshua 5:14).
Brothers and sisters, did you hear that “No”? The Lord hasn’t come to join your side; he has come to take command. The question was never “Is God on my side?” The question is “Am I on God’s side?”

Joshua didn’t argue; he fell face down on the ground, worshipped, and called himself a servant. He was the supreme commander of the whole army, yet he gave up the commander’s place. The 321 vision says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Then the commander told him to take off his sandals, because the place where he stood was holy. Brothers and sisters, the first step to victory is not putting on your battle boots; it is taking off your sandals.
And then, in chapter 6, comes Yahweh’s first word: “Behold, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and the mighty men of valor” (Joshua 6:2).

Notice the tense. God did not say, “I will give it to you”; God said, “I have given it into your hand.” The battle hadn’t been fought, yet the outcome was already settled — because the one fighting was not Joshua; it was Yahweh.

The battle plan that followed was even more outlandish: march round the city for six days; on the seventh day march round seven times, blow the trumpets and shout. That is not military tactics; it is training in obedience. And a battle fought that way left no commander any credit to claim afterwards.

But if you keep reading, you’ll see a vitally important contrast. In chapter 7, Ai was small; the spies said two or three thousand men would be enough to take it, and the three thousand who went up fled before the men of Ai. Why? Before attacking Jericho they inquired of God; before attacking Ai they assessed the people.

In chapter 9, the Gibeonites put on worn-out clothes, brought dry, hard bread and came pretending to surrender. The text names the cause in a single sentence: “The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth” (Joshua 9:14).

Brothers and sisters, the message is clear: inquire of God and you win; don’t inquire of God and you lose out. The difference is not the size of the matter; it is whether you have handed the commander’s place over to God.
Key point five: the key to the church is who is in charge and who is leading.
The Bible says, “Christ also is the head of the assembly” (Ephesians 5:23). The Greek word for “head” is kephalē; it means the head of a body, but also the source and the seat of authority.

Brothers and sisters, what would happen if a body had two heads? The left foot heads east, the right foot heads west. That isn’t richness; that’s a seizure. Much of the tearing apart in churches comes not from a lack of love but from too many heads.

Your heartbeat and your breathing don’t need your willpower to direct them; the brainstem takes care of them for you. The most terrible thing for a body is not an injured finger but a broken neck, with the signals cut off. So the church’s greatest crisis is not a shortage of people or money; it is when the signal is cut. The Lord says, “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Not half the efficiency — zero.

Revelation chapter 3 paints a startling picture. The Lord says to the church in Laodicea, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Revelation 3:20). The church was meeting as usual, giving as usual — and the Lord was standing outside the door.

The early church was not like that. Before he ascended, the Lord commanded his disciples, “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father” (Acts 1:4). Time was the thing they were shortest of, yet the Lord told them to wait. They waited ten days; the Holy Spirit came; and in a single day three thousand people turned to the Lord. Later the letter from the Jerusalem Council said, “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us” (Acts 15:28).

Brothers and sisters, what we need is not more resources but more relying on Jesus: seeking him in our meetings, relying on him in our decisions. The 321 vision speaks of the Goal: establish God’s system. A human system is a pyramid; God’s system is a set of concentric circles, with Jesus at the centre.
A gentle reminder: methods are tools; Jesus is the one we rely on.

Let me keep this balanced. We are not against planning; God is a God of order. The question is not whether we have methods but which seat our methods occupy. Methods are like the oars of a boat; if you row in the desert, you can row till your hands bleed and you will never reach the shore. God gives the water.

At the foot of Mount Sinai, Moses said something I love: “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here” (Exodus 33:15). He would rather go without Canaan than have a Canaan without the presence of God.
Brothers and sisters, when you walk relying on Jesus, even a cup of water or a single prayer will bring God’s presence and bear fruit.
Next come three practices.

Practice one: declare every morning — “Lord Jesus, today I will not rely on myself or on people; I will rely on you alone!” When you wake up, don’t start fretting over your to-do list; before your feet even touch the floor, hand over the throne. This sentence isn’t just an attitude; it is a spiritual switch.

Practice two: when you need help, pray first, then ask. When you hit a problem, don’t reach for your phone straight away; be still for one minute first. Brothers and sisters, this isn’t telling us not to ask people for help; what changes is the order. Praying first and then asking for help, versus asking for help and then praying — only minutes apart, but in reality a whole throne apart.

Practice three: before any church ministry, quietly seek the heart of Jesus. Whether you’re leading worship, preaching, holding a meeting or making pastoral visits, ask first, “Lord, how do you see this?” Proficiency is a grace, and it is also a temptation; what is frightening about proficiency is that it lets us keep going without needing to rely on God. The day the Gibeonites came, the Israelites were simply too proficient.

Walk these three practices all the way through the eight stages of changing our mindset: first take in the Information; ask the Holy Spirit for Revelation; move from knowing to Conviction, then to Implementation; take three minutes of Evaluation each evening, and make Correction on the spot when you drift; through Repetition let it become a habit; and finally Multiplication — bring one person into the practice and let them bring another. Brothers and sisters, what you teach others is what truly becomes your own.
Let’s look at this lesson once more within the framework of 321. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal all point to the same thing: rely on no one but Jesus.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. When the self-centred meet a difficulty, their first thought is “What am I going to do?” or “Whom do I know?”; the selfless person’s first thought is “Lord, how do you see this?” Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan; pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.
Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering the limitless. Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. What this lesson must change is the link furthest upstream — the mindset. Someone may ask: if we’re not to rely on people, why build 235 relationships? Brothers and sisters, 235 is not about leaning on one another; it is about holding one another up as together we rely on Jesus. A true spiritual companion doesn’t make you more dependent on them; they bring you closer to the Lord.
Brothers and sisters, every person, every thing and every circumstance in this world may change, but Jesus never fails.
He is your ever-present help — “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psalm 46:1).
He is the Commander who leads you to victory — “I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army” (Joshua 5:14).
He is the anchor of your soul — “This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast” (Hebrews 6:19).
A ship’s anchor isn’t dropped onto the ship; it is thrown overboard. If your anchor is cast onto your own abilities or onto some person, it is still on the ship.
Let us practise every day laying down our dependence on people and relying on Jesus alone; let Jesus come in from outside the door, from the last resort to the first one we turn to.
Revival is not an event; revival is Jesus reigning once again as King among his people. Let’s declare together with one heart: Lord Jesus, I do not rely on people; I rely on you alone!
Let’s pray together.

Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that we so often lean on mountains, on people, on ourselves; we wear ourselves out cutting our own cisterns, and we have forsaken you, the spring of living water. Lord, forgive us. This morning, like Joshua, we fall face down before you and hand the commander’s place back to you.

Teach us to make our declaration to you first thing each morning, to turn to you first when we meet difficulties, and to wait quietly on you before we serve. Make us like a tree planted by the waters, spreading out its roots by the river; not afraid when heat comes; not anxious in the year of drought; never ceasing to bear fruit.
Reign as King in our families; reign as King in our church. May all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Hardest Face to Let Go Of
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today let’s begin with a very ordinary scene.

A group of people have just taken a group photo, and someone posts it to the group chat. The moment each person opens the picture, where do their eyes land first? Not on the mountain in the background, not on the flowers to one side, not on the guest of honour standing in the middle — but on “my face”. Were my eyes shut? Was my hair a mess? Did I stand somewhere flattering? If I came out badly, then even if everyone else is beaming, a voice inside me will still say: don’t post this one.

It is a tiny reflex, yet it gives away a very deep secret: in the whole world we see, there is one image that always stands at the very front — and that is “self”.

Social media has magnified this secret. The invention of the front-facing phone camera allowed human beings, for the first time, to see themselves anytime and anywhere. How many times a day do we look at ourselves? In the mirror, in photos, in our stories, checking under our posts for likes. We live in an unprecedented age of “looking at ourselves without end”.

And two thousand years ago, the Bible had already set exactly the opposite picture before us. Matthew 17:8 says: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).

This sentence comes right after the Transfiguration. The disciples lift their heads from the ground. The mountain is still the same mountain, the cloud still the same cloud, but in their eyes only one remains — Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, the “one” in this sentence that is hardest to let go of is not really Moses, nor Elijah, nor Peter, James or John. The “one” that is hardest to let go of is ourselves.

On the road of pursuing spiritual life, our greatest obstacle is often not our circumstances, nor other people, but “self”. However hard our circumstances, God can change them; however hard other people are, God can soften them. But the “self” standing right before my eyes and blocking my view of Jesus — only when I myself am willing to step aside can God be seen.

When we fix our eyes on ourselves and make much of ourselves; when “I” becomes the centre of our words, the motive of our service, the core of our faith, our gaze shifts away from Jesus. Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: this is not simply a matter of pride; it is a misaligned focus of faith. When the focus shifts, the direction shifts; when the direction shifts, a whole life shifts.

And this is exactly Satan’s favourite move. He doesn’t need to get you to commit adultery, commit murder or worship idols. All he has to do is gently turn your camera a few degrees — away from Jesus and towards yourself — so that you start looking at yourself, emphasising yourself, satisfying yourself. After that, he doesn’t need to do anything more, because the fall will happen on its own.

Let me use an astronomical phenomenon to show how frightening this is. The diameter of the sun is about 1.39 million kilometres, roughly four hundred times the diameter of the moon; yet the sun is also roughly four hundred times farther from us than the moon is. So, seen from the earth, the sun and the moon look almost exactly the same size. And that produces an astonishing phenomenon: that small moon, which gives off no light of its own, need only move into the right position to cover the entire sun completely — a total solar eclipse.

Brothers and sisters, “self” is like that moon. In itself it isn’t large at all, and it gives no light whatsoever. But when it comes too close to our eyes and happens to stand right in front of Jesus, it can blot out the glorious Christ entirely and plunge our world into darkness in an instant.

The darkness of a total eclipse lasts only a few minutes. But if a Christian lets “self” stand in front of Jesus year after year, that darkness can last a lifetime.

The title of this lesson is “Seeing Self Brings the Fall”. Together we will look at four things: first, our greatest enemy is often “self”; second, Satan’s first scheme is to get people to look at themselves; third, looking at ourselves means walking in Satan’s footsteps; fourth, Jesus’ example is to see not himself but only the Father. Finally we will practise together turning from “looking at ourselves” to “seeing Jesus alone”.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Transfiguration and the Words “Jesus Alone”
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of the words “they saw no one, except Jesus alone”, we must go back to their context.

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is the apostle Matthew, the tax collector whom Jesus called as he sat at the tax office (Matthew 9:9). This Gospel is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish believers. That is why the whole book quotes the Old Testament again and again and sets out to prove one thing over and over: Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the son of David, the offspring of Abraham.

The Transfiguration is recorded in Matthew 17:1–8, with parallel accounts in Mark 9:2–8 and Luke 9:28–36. It happened at a crucial turning point.

Just six days earlier, on the road at Caesarea Philippi, Jesus had asked his disciples, “Who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). That was a high point. But immediately afterwards, Jesus said plainly for the first time that he must go up to Jerusalem to suffer, be killed and rise on the third day. Peter at once took him aside and rebuked him: “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.” Jesus turned and said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men” (Matthew 16:23).

Brothers and sisters, notice the sequence. Peter had only just been praised, and the next moment he was called Satan. Why? Because he had turned from “setting his mind on the things of God” to “setting his mind on the things of men”. The moment the focus shifted, his spiritual standing changed. That is precisely the theme of this lesson: seeing self brings the fall.

Then Jesus spoke words that set the tone for the whole passage: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

Six days later, Jesus took Peter, James and John and brought them up a high mountain by themselves. The text says: “He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light” (Matthew 17:2). Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with Jesus. Moses represents the Law, Elijah the Prophets; the whole Old Testament stood there, speaking with this One.

Peter’s reaction is fascinating. He said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew 17:4). Luke 9:33 honestly adds a comment: “not knowing what he said.”

Three tents — this is a “seeing self” proposal. Peter wanted to hold on to the experience, to arrange the scene, to play a part in it. He put Jesus on the same level as Moses and Elijah: one tent each. And he would be the one putting up the tents.

How did God respond? “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him’” (Matthew 17:5).

God didn’t answer Peter’s question. God corrected Peter’s focus directly. Not three tents, but one beloved Son. Not three men, but one voice — “Listen to him.”

When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces and were very afraid. “Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid.’ Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:7–8).

The action of “lifting up their eyes” is in the original ἐπαίρω τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς, literally “to raise the eyes”. They had been lying face down, heads bowed, seeing nothing but the ground and themselves. Only when Jesus came, touched them and told them to get up did they raise their eyes.

And “Jesus alone” in Greek is εἰ μὴ αὐτὸν Ἰησοῦν μόνον, literally “no one except Jesus himself only”. The word μόνον means “only, solely, alone”. This is not to say that Moses and Elijah are unimportant. It is to say that when the glory is revealed, every supporting actor must leave the stage, and only One may remain on it.

Brothers and sisters, this is the rule of heaven. Revelation chapter 5 describes worship in heaven: myriads upon myriads of angels, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders cry out with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who has been killed to receive the power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing!” (Revelation 5:12). Heaven has countless worshippers, yet only one focus of worship.

If we hope one day to join the worship team of heaven, then today, here on earth, we must begin learning the same thing: to see not ourselves, but Jesus alone.

sections.heading: 3. Key Point 1: Our Greatest Enemy Is Often “Self”
sections.html:
We often think that what holds back our spiritual growth is something outside us. Work is too busy; our family doesn’t believe; someone at church is hard to get along with; our health is poor; money is tight. These are all real difficulties, but they are usually not the greatest enemy.

The Bible speaks very directly about this. Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

Notice the order: first deny yourself, then take up the cross, and only then follow. Denying of self is the first step. If the first step is never taken, the next two are only religious motions.

“Deny himself” in Greek is ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai), meaning “to disown utterly, to refuse to acknowledge, to cut all ties with”. In Matthew’s Gospel this word appears on another famous occasion as well: when Jesus foretold that Peter would deny him three times, he used exactly the same word (Matthew 26:34, 75).

Brothers and sisters, do you hear the contrast? When Peter applied that “denial” to Jesus, it was the greatest failure of his life; yet when Jesus asks us to apply the very same “denial” to ourselves, it becomes the greatest success of ours. Denying of self means that when “self” walks up and demands sovereignty, we point at him and say: I do not know this man.

Paul puts it even more searchingly: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

In this verse there is a death, and there is a life. “It is no longer I” is the death; “Christ lives in me” is the life. The 321 vision puts it very clearly: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness does not mean annihilating ourselves into nothing; selflessness means letting the infinite Lord fill all my space. We are emptied in order to be filled; we step aside so that the Lord may be revealed.

Modern psychology has in fact brushed against the edges of this phenomenon. In 1972 the psychologists Shelley Duval and Robert Wicklund proposed Objective Self-Awareness Theory. They found that when a person is placed in front of a mirror or a camera, their attention turns from the outside world to themselves; and once attention turns to the self, people immediately compare themselves with the standards in their minds, and what follows is often unease, anxiety and self-criticism.

In other words, scientific experiments observed something the Bible had long since spelled out: when people keep staring at themselves, what comes is not peace but unrest.

In 1970 the psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr. published his famous “mirror self-recognition test” in the journal Science, showing that chimpanzees can recognise themselves in a mirror. Human infants gain this ability at around eighteen to twenty-four months. Interestingly, as soon as self-awareness appears, emotions such as shame, jealousy and showing off appear along with it. Seeing ourselves has never come cheap.

I want to point out one thing in particular. In 2003 the psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues (Jennifer Campbell, Joachim Krueger and Kathleen Vohs) published a large-scale review of the research in the journal Psychological Science in the Public Interest, and its conclusion shook the education world of the day: raising self-esteem does not cause better academic results or job performance; rather, good performance raises self-esteem. In other words, the decades-old assumption that “the more you look at yourself and affirm yourself, the better you’ll do” could not stand up to rigorous testing.

Brothers and sisters, the world spent decades and untold sums of money only to arrive, barely, at the Bible’s front door. And the Bible said from the outset: “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think” (Romans 12:3).

Let me give an example from everyday life. A sister sings beautifully and is invited to sing a solo at church. The first time she stands up, there is only one prayer in her heart: Lord, please use this song to comfort the people out there. When she finishes, she is in tears herself, and many in the congregation are touched by the Lord. The second time, someone praises her voice as truly anointed. The third time, she starts paying attention to whether the pianist is drowning her out, starts noticing the camera angle, and after singing, starts checking online whether anyone has shared the video.

The song hasn’t changed; the voice hasn’t changed; even the spot where she stands hasn’t changed. What has changed is the focus. The first time she was looking at Jesus; later she was looking at herself. From the outside, nothing is different; from heaven, these are two completely different things.

That is why we say our greatest enemy is often ourselves. This enemy doesn’t attack you from outside; he adjusts your camera from within. He doesn’t change what you do; he only changes why you do it.

The 321 vision reminds us: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When the focus is on myself, I live in comparison; when the focus is on others, I live in my emotions; when the focus is on my circumstances, I live in fear. Only when the focus is on Jesus do I live in faith.

sections.heading: 4. Key Point 2: Satan’s First Scheme — Getting People to Look at Themselves
sections.html:
The first spiritual battle in human history was not fought on a battlefield. It took place in a conversation in front of a tree.

In the Garden of Eden, the serpent said to the woman: “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5).

Brothers and sisters, notice how clever Satan’s words are. He didn’t tell Eve to hate God; he didn’t tell her to worship another god; he didn’t say a single vulgar word. What he said was a word of “advancement”: you will be like God. It sounds like helping people move upwards, but in reality it pulls them away from God’s presence.

The heart of this move was to shift Eve’s attention from “what God has said” to “what I could become”. The moment the focus shifted, the result followed: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate” (Genesis 3:6).

“Good for food” is the need of the flesh; “a delight to the eyes” is the lust of the eyes; “to be desired to make one wise” is the pride of life. The apostle John later summed up these three in exactly the same way: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s” (1 John 2:16).

From that moment on, human eyes have been fixed on ourselves. Look at their first reaction after they sinned: “Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves” (Genesis 3:7). Their eyes were opened, yet what they saw was not God but themselves; not glory but shame. Satan promised “like God”; what he actually delivered was “naked”.

When people see themselves, they want to satisfy themselves; when people set their minds on the flesh, they drift away from God’s will. Paul puts it with absolute finality: “because the mind of the flesh is hostile toward God; for it is not subject to God’s law, neither indeed can it be” (Romans 8:7).

The word “mind” here is the Greek φρόνημα (phronēma). It refers not to a passing thought, but to “the bent of the mind, a pattern of thinking, the direction the whole heart is facing”. So Paul is not talking about an occasional moment of weakness, but about which way your heart is heading as a whole. Romans 8:6 says: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.”

Brothers and sisters, there is a question here we must face honestly: why is it so easy for people to look at themselves?

Modern neuroscience offers an interesting piece of corroboration. In 2001 Marcus Raichle and his colleagues at Washington University in St. Louis published research in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showing that the human brain has a set of regions that are actually most active when we are “doing nothing”. They called it the Default Mode Network. A great deal of later research found that the activity of this network is closely tied to self-referential thinking — in other words, the moment a person is idle, the brain’s default channel switches automatically to “thinking about me”.

Brothers and sisters, this shows exactly why looking at Jesus takes practice, while looking at ourselves doesn’t. Looking at ourselves is the default setting; looking at Jesus is a choice. Drifting downstream takes no effort; only going against the current needs the oars.

So what can truly satisfy us? Not self-fulfilment, but God himself. Psalm 37:4 says: “Also delight yourself in Yahweh, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Psalm 37:4).

Notice the order in this verse: first delight in Yahweh, and only then are the desires of your heart given. Many people reverse the order: let me first get what I want, and then I’ll be happy. The result? They get it, and the happiness lasts three days. So they want something bigger — and the happiness still lasts only three days. That is the mathematics of self-satisfaction: the denominator always runs faster than the numerator.

At the opening of his Confessions, Augustine wrote a prayer that has been repeated down the ages: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Those words sum up the whole human condition: the hole in our hearts was dug in the shape of God, and anything else we pour into it leaks away.

I often use an illustration. A small child stands in front of a waterfall holding a plastic cup. He keeps checking how full his cup is, but he never once looks up at the water pouring down. His cup can only ever hold so much, yet the waterfall has never stopped. Looking at ourselves is staring at the cup; looking at Jesus is lifting our eyes to the living water that never stops flowing.

This is what 321 calls the shift in perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the Worldly system to God’s. Satan’s first scheme is to stop you making that shift; all he wants is for you to keep your head down, looking at your own cup.

sections.heading: 5. Key Point 3: Looking at Ourselves Means Walking in Satan’s Footsteps
sections.html:
Why did Satan fall from heaven? We tend to assume it was because he did something horribly evil. In fact, the reason the Bible records for his fall comes down to two words, said five times over: I will, I will, I will, I will, I will.

Isaiah 14:12–15 says: “How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’ Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit” (Isaiah 14:12–15).

Five times “I will”, and in return one “you shall be brought down”. Brothers and sisters, this is the shortest and most terrifying chain of cause and effect in the whole Bible.

Ezekiel 28:17 adds another angle: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor.” Notice: the reason for his fall was not that he was ugly but that he was beautiful; not that he lacked splendour but that he had splendour and looked at his own splendour. The root of Satan’s fall was not that he lacked power, but that he “looked at himself and wanted for himself” far too much.

The Hebrew root for “pride”, גָּאָה (ga’ah), originally means “to rise, to swell up”, like water rising. Pride is not a sudden movement; it is a slowly rising water level. By the time you notice, the water is already over the roof. That is why Proverbs 16:18 says: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

The 321 vision puts this very plainly: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Satan refused to be a creature; he wanted to be the Creator. He left his originally intended position, and he lost everything.

And this spirit of “I will” was not locked away in Sheol along with Satan. It has seeped into today’s society, and into today’s church as well:

I want to be seen. I want to be famous. I want to succeed. I want people’s approval.

Brothers and sisters, is any one of these an obvious sin? No. They even sound perfectly normal, ambitious, healthy. That is exactly what makes them dangerous.

Even if what we are doing is “spiritual work”, if the motive is “I want”, the end is still hostility towards God. That is a strong statement, but Jesus himself said something stronger still: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity’” (Matthew 7:21–23).

Notice what these people are holding in their hands: prophesying, casting out demons, doing mighty works. What a dazzling ministry CV! Yet the Lord’s reply is: “I never knew you.”

Why? Listen closely to their words: “Didn’t we prophesy in your name?” The subject of the sentence is “we”. All through their speech, “we” comes up again and again, while Jesus is used merely as a name to invoke. They used the Lord’s name to do their own work and make their own name.

In Matthew chapter 6 Jesus had already warned against this pattern: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:1). Three times he speaks of giving, praying and fasting, and three times he closes with the same sentence: “Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2, 5, 16).

“Have received” in Greek is ἀπέχω (apechō), a technical term from the business documents of the day meaning “payment received in full; account settled”. In other words, the moment human applause breaks out, the account in heaven is settled; there is no balance left.

Brothers and sisters, if we make a name on earth but have our name struck off in heaven, how tragic that would be!

Let me give an everyday example. There is a way of spending called “buy now, pay in instalments”: easy right now, with the cost pushed into the future. Chasing human praise is spiritual buy-now-pay-later: it feels great now, and the bill comes afterwards. Denying of self is like paying in cash: it hurts a little at the time, but you owe nobody anything.

Here I also want to mention a fascinating finding from psychology. In 2000 the psychologists Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky published a series of experiments on the “Spotlight Effect” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room, then asked them to estimate how many people had noticed. On average the participants estimated that about half the people had noticed; in fact only about a quarter remembered.

Brothers and sisters, this research shows a fact that is both funny and freeing: the spotlight you thought was always shining on you doesn’t actually exist. We spend most of our lives managing an image that hardly anyone is looking at.

So the pursuit of “I want to be seen” is, at heart, performing in front of empty seats. Meanwhile, the One who truly is watching is looking not at your performance but at your heart. First Samuel 16:7 says: “I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

The 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. When one “I want” meets another “I want”, tension arises in the church; when two “I want”s refuse to give way, ministry grinds to a halt, relationships break down, and in the end both sides lose. But when one person steps aside first, humility starts to spread. Brothers and sisters, will you be the one who steps aside first?

sections.heading: 6. Key Point 4: Jesus’ Example — Seeing Not Himself but Only the Father
sections.html:
Having spent three key points on the problem, we now turn to the perfect answer.

The first of the Three Foundations is “Jesus is my role model”. And Jesus’ ministry on earth is the clearest demonstration of “seeing not himself but only the Father”.

Jesus said: “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me” (John 5:30).

In this verse there are two negatives and two positives. “Can … do nothing” and “don’t seek my own will” are the negatives; “as I hear, I judge” and “but the will of my Father who sent me” are the positives. This is the Son of God, who has all power, and yet he says, “I can of myself do nothing.”

Verse 19 of the same chapter says it more fully: “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19).

Brothers and sisters, notice the spiritual order here: first see, then do. Jesus’ actions did not start from his own plans; they started from what he saw the Father doing.

Nor did he ever contend for his own glory. John 8:50 records him saying: “But I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges” (John 8:50). And in his final prayer, he said to the Father: “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do” (John 17:4).

Jesus did not perform miracles to make a name for himself, nor teach the truth to build a reputation. His focus was always “the Father’s will”; his actions were “doing only what he saw the Father doing”; his joy was “letting the Father be glorified”.

Paul turned this example into the greatest hymn in the history of the church: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

“Emptied himself” in Greek is κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to empty, to make void”. Brothers and sisters, set Philippians 2 side by side with Isaiah 14 and you will see two completely opposite paths in the universe:

Satan said, “I will ascend into heaven,” and ended up brought down to Sheol. Jesus said, “I don’t seek my own will,” and emptied himself, going down to the very lowest place — and God raised him to the very highest. Philippians 2:9 goes on: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

One path is wanting to be high, and ending up brought low; the other is going low, and being raised up by God. Brothers and sisters, which path will you take?

Today Jesus has been lifted up onto the throne. In heaven, all worship has only one focus — Jesus Christ. The scene in Revelation chapter 5 shows plainly that heaven allows only one focus: the Lamb of God. The apostle John says: “I heard every created thing which is in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, on the sea, and everything in them, saying, ‘To him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb be the blessing, the honor, the glory, and the dominion, forever and ever! Amen!’” (Revelation 5:13).

Heaven has no second pulpit, no second spotlight, no second name being cheered.

John the Baptist is another beautiful example in the New Testament. His disciples came running to tell him: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him” (John 3:26). This was an obvious attempt to stir him up: your people are being stolen. John’s reply became the motto of everyone who serves: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

“Increase” and “decrease” in the original are αὐξάνω and ἐλαττόω, a pair of contrasting verbs: one growing, one diminishing. John was not forced off the stage; he gladly turned the spotlight away from himself. He said he was only the friend of the bridegroom, who rejoices greatly at hearing the bridegroom’s voice (John 3:29).

Brothers and sisters, our greatest temptation in serving is to mistake the friend of the bridegroom for the bridegroom.

Let me use an illustration. The moon at night is beautiful, but the moon has not a glimmer of light of its own. It shines only because it reflects the light of the sun. The best moon is the one that blocks the least light and reflects the most. Yet, as we said earlier, that same moon, if it moves into the wrong position, can cover the entire sun.

The same moon, in the right position, reflects glory; in the wrong position, it hides glory. Brothers and sisters, what decides it is not your size but your position.

Paul uses another lovely image: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

When psychologists put a mirror in front of people, they see themselves, and the result is anxiety. Paul says that when we behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, we ourselves become that mirror, reflecting the Lord’s image, and the result is “from glory to glory”.

The same mirror: look at yourself and you are trapped in it; look at the Lord and you are transformed. This is what 321 calls the fivefold change, which begins with the mindset — change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. And the first step of all this is simply to lift your eyes off yourself.

If we long one day to join the worship team of heaven, then we must start learning now: to see not ourselves, but Jesus alone.

sections.heading: 7. An Important Reminder: Not Suppressing Ourselves, but Lifting Up Jesus
sections.html:
At this point some brothers and sisters may be struggling inside: Does that mean I’m not allowed any thoughts of my own? Is even looking after myself a sin? Do I have to keep putting myself down and disliking myself?

No. We need to be clear about this.

The trouble with looking at ourselves is not that self-knowledge is wrong. At the very opening of his Institutes of the Christian Religion, Calvin says that nearly all our wisdom consists of two parts: the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves — and the two are bound together. Knowing yourself is not wrong; on the contrary, it is part of godliness.

So where does the problem lie? It lies in the moment when “I” becomes the focus, becomes the motive, becomes the one in charge. That is when faith goes off course.

The difference here is a matter of position, not of existence. God has never wanted to erase you; God wants you to return to your originally intended position. 321 puts it superbly: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

In the Bible, the reactions of those who truly saw God are worth noticing. Isaiah saw the Lord seated on a high and lofty throne in the temple, and he said: “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). After God questioned Job out of the whirlwind, Job said: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. Therefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:5–6).

Notice: they did not first loathe themselves and then see God. They first saw God, and only then came to a true assessment of themselves. The order matters enormously. If a person simply stares at themselves, digging out their faults, that is not humility; it is just another form of self-centredness — negative self-centredness, but self-centredness all the same. True humility is having your eyes so filled by a far greater Presence that there is simply no room left to keep fussing over yourself.

And look at what happened next. After Isaiah was cleansed by a live coal from the altar, God asked, “Whom shall I send?” Isaiah said: “Here I am. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8). And Job? “Yahweh turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends. Yahweh gave Job twice as much as he had before” (Job 42:10).

Brothers and sisters, those who see God are not wiped out; instead they are sent, restored and given double.

God does not want you to suppress yourself or deny your worth. He wants you to find your true self in Jesus — and that “self” exists to glorify him.

Jesus himself once spoke words that hold both losing and finding: “For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 16:25).

The 321 vision says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus — entering the limitless and living out the limitless; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Put a drop of water on the palm of your hand, and in less than half a day it has evaporated; pour the same drop into the ocean, and it will never dry up. Selflessness is not disappearing; it is entering the limitless.

sections.heading: 8. Integrating the 321 Vision: Selflessness Overcomes Satan
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the message of this lesson is in fact the very heart of the 321 vision.

Each of the Three Foundations moves the focus away from ourselves.

Jesus is my role model — he said, “I can of myself do nothing” (John 5:30). If even the Son of God did not act on his own, what grounds do I have for acting on my own?

The Bible is my standard — when “I want” rises up in my heart, I don’t ask what I want; I ask what the Bible says. If the standard lies within me, I have become my own god; only if the standard lies in the Bible is God God.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. Out of the heart is the wellspring of life (Proverbs 4:23).

The Two Core Values are the very conclusion of this lesson.

Let Jesus be King — a kingdom can have only one king. When I sit on the throne, Jesus can only be an adviser; and an adviser can be consulted — or ignored. Letting Jesus be King means handing that chair back to him.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — notice: “all”. Not ninety per cent to the Lord and ten per cent kept for myself. The person who keeps back ten per cent will sooner or later end up quarrelling with someone over that ten per cent.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. A human system is a pyramid: the higher up you are, the more you are seen. God’s system is a body, in which each member does its own part, and there is only one Head — Christ (Ephesians 4:15–16).

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Satan fell because of “I will”; Adam and Eve fell because of “you will be like God”. The title of this lesson hits the mark exactly: seeing self brings the fall.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Brothers and sisters, remember this: you don’t need pride to defeat Satan’s pride. Just use humility, and he has nothing to push against. Satan can attack someone standing on a high place, but he cannot drag down someone who is already lying face down at the Lord’s feet.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. What this lesson must change first is the mindset — so the greatest enemy is not my circumstances but myself; so “I want” is not ambition but danger; so not seeing myself is not a loss but freedom. When the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, the way I speak, the way I spend money and the way I set priorities all change; then the relationships at home change, and only last of all does ministry change.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people reverse the order and charge into ministry first, and the result is that the bigger their ministry grows, the emptier their life and the worse their relationships. Brothers and sisters, people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

The shift in perspective: from the human to the divine, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the Worldly system to God’s. “Famous on earth, struck off in heaven” — that phrase is exactly the showdown between “temporary” and “eternal”. Earthly fame lasts at most for one generation’s memory; heaven’s remembrance endures forever and ever.

The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2”, we practise living a selfless (0) life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, notice this: not one of these nine graces is borne for ourselves. A fruit tree never eats its own fruit. If you are still looking at yourself, the fruit you bear will never get any further than you.

The 235 relationships: become a “2” with selfless people, spiritual companions to each other, reminding one another where the focus belongs; build the “3”, becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing “see not yourself, but Jesus alone” on to the next generation; become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, serving together with no one fighting for the place in the middle.

The Path of Serving is Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit guides me, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, I let him be King, and in the end all glory goes to him. On this path, with every step, there is a little less of “self” and a little more of Christ.

sections.heading: 9. Putting It into Practice: From “Looking at Myself” to “Looking at Jesus”
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very practical exercises. We will keep all three, and use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep into our lives.

Practice 1: Every morning, say to the Lord: “Lord, today I don’t want to look at myself; I only want to look at you.”

After you get up, while you wash, or before you head out, close your eyes and say honestly to Jesus: “Lord, today I don’t want to fix my eyes on my own weaknesses, cravings, needs or performance. I only want to fix my eyes on you.”

This is a spiritual vaccination. A vaccine works by preparing the body’s defences before the virus invades in force. In the same way, if we set our focus right before the day’s pressures, comparisons and criticisms arrive, we won’t be dragged around by our emotions all day.

Brothers and sisters, notice the timing: after you get up, not before you go to sleep. The first thought of the day often sets the direction of the whole day. Psalm 5:3 says: “Yahweh, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly” (Psalm 5:3).

Practice 2: Whenever you think “I want …”, stop at once and ask, “What does Jesus want?”

When thoughts like “I want to succeed”, “I want to be famous” or “I want to be in control” start up in your life or service, pause immediately and ask in your heart: “Lord Jesus, what do you want in this?”

It is a very short question, but it is a steering wheel. If a plane flying from Taipei to Tokyo is off course by a single degree, it will miss its destination by tens of kilometres. Life is the same. This small question will help you break out of self-centredness and turn towards God’s will.

The Lord Jesus himself modelled this turn in the Garden of Gethsemane: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). Brothers and sisters, if even the Lord had to say these words, how much more do we need to say them every day.

Practice 3: Every evening, reflect: “Where did I see myself today? Where did I see Jesus?”

At the end of the day, take a few quiet minutes and honestly ask yourself three questions:

First, at what moment today was I making myself stand out?

Second, was there anything I did to satisfy my own “I want”?

Third, at what moments today did I fix my eyes on Jesus, obey him and let him be glorified?

Brothers and sisters, don’t let this reflection turn into self-accusation. Psalm 139:23–24 gives us the right attitude: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24). Notice the last line: it doesn’t stop at “any wicked way”; it moves on to “lead me in the everlasting way”.

Deepening the three practices with the eight stages of changing our mindset

Stage 1, Information. Today’s lesson is the information. Now you know: seeing self brings the fall; see no one else but Jesus.

Stage 2, Revelation. If information stays only in the head, it is just knowledge. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn these words into your own seeing, so that in some specific situation you suddenly recognise: so that moment, I was looking at myself.

Stage 3, Conviction. True conviction is admitting that this applies to you, not just to other people. The sign of conviction is that you stop defending yourself.

Stage 4, Implementation. Starting tomorrow morning, do Practice 1. Don’t wait until you feel like it; do it first, and the feelings will catch up.

Stage 5, Evaluation. The evening reflection of Practice 3 is your evaluation. A few minutes each day — it needn’t be long, but it must be honest.

Stage 6, Correction. Evaluation without correction is only regret. If you find that in some matter today you looked at yourself, then tomorrow, in that same matter, deliberately step aside once.

Stage 7, Repetition. One time of practice won’t change a person; a year of practice will. Brothers and sisters, spiritual muscle is like physical muscle: it grows through the number of repetitions.

Stage 8, Multiplication. Find a brother or sister to be your “2”. Practise together, and once a week ask each other: “This week, where did you see yourself? Where did you see Jesus?” If the practice stops with you, it still circles back to self; only when it is passed on to others have you truly stepped out of yourself.

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call: Unseen on Earth, Remembered in Heaven
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we have come to the end of this lesson.

Jesus said: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

These words come from a banquet scene. Jesus noticed how the invited guests were jostling for the places of honour, and he told them a parable: don’t go and sit in the place of honour yourself, in case a guest more distinguished than you has been invited and the host comes and says to you, “Give this person your place,” and then, red-faced, you have to move down to the lowest place. Better to go and sit in the lowest place, so that when the host comes he says to you, “Friend, move up higher,” and then you will be honoured in front of everyone at the table.

Notice that Jesus did not say, “Don’t have any honour.” He said that honour should be received from the host’s hand, not grabbed for yourself.

“Exalt” and “humble” in Greek are ὑψόω (hypsoō) and ταπεινόω (tapeinoō), and both words appear together in Philippians 2 as well: Christ “humbled himself” (tapeinoō), and God “highly exalted him” (hyperypsoō). Brothers and sisters, this is not a motivational slogan. It is a law by which the universe runs — a law God himself demonstrated in his own Son.

First Peter 5:5–6 says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:5–6).

“In due time” — those three words are for every anxious heart. You don’t have to arrange the timetable yourself, fight for a position yourself, or argue your own innocence. God has his time.

When we are willing not to put ourselves forward or exalt ourselves on earth, the Father himself will remember us and lift us up into the right place.

Brothers and sisters, this morning let us make three decisions together.

First, step aside. Move the shadow that stands in front of Jesus out of the way. You don’t have to destroy it; you only have to step aside.

Second, look up. Like the disciples on the Mount of Transfiguration, lift your eyes from where you lie face down. Jesus will touch you and say to you: “Get up, and don’t be afraid” (Matthew 17:7).

Third, let him be King. Hand the chair on the throne back to him; let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Let us learn to be like Jesus, living not for ourselves but only for the glory of God. Let us practise every day seeing not ourselves but Jesus alone, until the day we stand with him in glory.

keyVerses: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
practices: Every morning, say to the Lord
Whenever you think “I want …”, stop at once and ask
Reflect every evening
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you for setting this mirror before us this morning. We confess that for years, what has stood between us and you has often been not our circumstances, not other people, but ourselves.

Lord, forgive the “I want” in our hearts. Forgive us for doing things in your name while quietly building our own name. Forgive us for fussing over position in our service, over who is right in our relationships, and over our image in front of others.
Touch us, as you once touched those three disciples lying face down on the ground, and say to us: “Get up, and don’t be afraid.” When we lift up our eyes, let us see no one, except you alone.

Lord, we are willing to step aside, willing to look up, willing to let you be King. May the Holy Spirit remind us every day that whenever an “I want” rises in our hearts, we turn to you at once and ask: Lord, what do you want?
May we be unseen on earth and remembered by you in heaven. To him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb, be the blessing, the honour, the glory and the dominion, forever and ever.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8). In your life or service over the past week, was there a moment when you realised you were actually “looking at yourself”? What was the situation? What do you think Jesus wanted from you in that moment?

“He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). When his disciples were all turning to follow Jesus, John the Baptist still gladly stepped aside. In your family, workplace or ministry right now, what is one matter in which the Holy Spirit is reminding you to “step aside first”? What concrete step are you willing to take on it this week?
