blog.title: The Little Moon That Hides the Sun

blocks.x: Why “seeing self” brings the fall
A group photo lands in the group chat. Whose face do your eyes look for first?
Your own, right? Were my eyes shut? Was my hair a mess? Did I stand somewhere flattering? If I came out badly, then even if everyone else is beaming, I’ll still say: don’t post this one.
It is a tiny reflex, yet it gives away a very deep secret: in the whole world we see, there is one image that always stands at the very front — and that is “self”.
And two thousand years ago, the Bible had already set exactly the opposite picture before us:
“Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
1. The “one” hardest to let go of is me
This sentence comes from the Transfiguration. The disciples lift their heads from the ground. The mountain is still the same mountain, but in their eyes only one remains — Jesus.

On the road of pursuing spiritual life, our greatest obstacle is often not our circumstances, nor other people, but “self”. However hard our circumstances, God can change them; however hard other people are, God can soften them. But the “self” standing right before my eyes — only when I myself am willing to step aside can God be seen.

Let me share an astronomical fact. The diameter of the sun is about 1.39 million kilometres, roughly four hundred times that of the moon; and the sun is also roughly four hundred times farther from us than the moon is. So, seen from the earth, the two look the same size. And that produces an astonishing phenomenon: that small moon, which gives off no light of its own, need only move into the right position to cover the entire sun completely — a total solar eclipse.

“Self” is like that moon. It isn’t large at all, and it gives no light whatsoever. But when it comes too close to our eyes and happens to stand right in front of Jesus, it can blot out the glorious Christ entirely.
The darkness of a total eclipse lasts only a few minutes. But if someone lets “self” stand in front of Jesus year after year, that darkness can last a lifetime.
2. Satan’s first move is not to get you to commit a great sin
In the Garden of Eden, the serpent said to the woman: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)

Satan didn’t tell Eve to hate God; he didn’t tell her to worship another god; he didn’t say a single vulgar word. What he said sounded like “advancement”. He simply shifted her attention from “what God has said” to “what I could become”.
The moment the focus shifted, the fall began.

Interestingly, modern research has left clues pointing the same way. In 1972 the psychologists Duval and Wicklund proposed Objective Self-Awareness Theory: the moment a person faces a mirror or a camera, attention turns to the self; and once attention turns to the self, what follows is often unease, anxiety and self-criticism. In 2001 Raichle and his colleagues at Washington University in St. Louis found that the human brain has a set of regions that are actually most active when we are “doing nothing”, and later research showed it is closely tied to self-referential thinking.
In other words: looking at ourselves is the default setting; looking at Jesus is a choice. Drifting downstream takes no effort; only going against the current needs the oars.

And Satan himself was the very first traveller on this road. Isaiah records him saying “I will” five times — I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of assembly, I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, I will make myself like the Most High; and what he received in return was one sentence: “you shall be brought down to Sheol”.

This spirit of “I will” is still alive today: I want to be seen, I want to be famous, I want to succeed, I want people’s approval. Not one of these is an obvious sin — and that is exactly what makes them dangerous.
3. Jesus’ way: emptying himself, then being highly exalted
Jesus said: “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge.” (John 5:30)
He did not perform miracles to make a name for himself, nor teach the truth to build a reputation. Paul says he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”, and God highly exalted him.
Satan wanted to be high, and fell; Jesus went low, and was raised up by God. What decides it is not your size but your position.
The moon has not a glimmer of light of its own; it shines only because it reflects the sun. The best moon is the one that blocks the least light.

This is not telling you to suppress yourself. God doesn’t want to erase you; God wants you to return to your originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Those in the Bible who truly saw God all saw God first, and only then saw themselves clearly; and they were not wiped out, but sent and restored. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering the limitless. Put a drop of water on the palm of your hand, and in half a day it has dried up; pour it into the ocean, and it will never dry up.
Three small things you can do today
First, every morning say to the Lord: “Lord, today I don’t want to look at myself; I only want to look at you.”
Second, whenever an “I want” rises in your heart, stop at once and ask: “Lord Jesus, what do you want in this?”
Third, every evening ask yourself: where did I see myself today? Where did I see Jesus?
Jesus said: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11)
Unseen on earth, and one day remembered in heaven.
Reflection question: This week, was there a moment when you were really “looking at yourself”? If you could do it again, how would you turn your focus back to Jesus?

Read the key verse, Matthew 17:8 (read the full verse), stressing “they saw no one, except Jesus alone”.
Name the thread of the lesson: seeing self brings the fall; seeing Jesus alone brings freedom.
Preview the four points: our greatest enemy is self, Satan’s first scheme, Satan’s footsteps, Jesus’ example.

Open with the group-photo scene: the moment a photo opens, our eyes always look for our own face first.
Note that in the age of the front-facing camera, we are the generation in history that sees itself the most.

Astronomy illustration: the sun’s diameter is about 1.39 million km, about 400 times the moon’s, and it is about 400 times farther away — so the little moon can cover the whole sun in a total solar eclipse.
Application: self is not big and gives no light, yet because it is too close to our eyes it hides the glorious Christ.

God says: This is my beloved Son. Listen to him
Moses and Elijah leave; only One remains
Matthew 17:1–8
Background: Matthew’s Gospel was written by the apostle Matthew, between AD 50 and 70, for Jewish believers.
Context: Peter had just confessed “You are the Christ”, then the next moment was called Satan for “setting his mind on the things of men” (Matthew 16:23).
Jesus immediately said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16:24), setting the tone for the passage.
Peter’s three tents were an attempt to arrange the scene and play a part; Luke 9:33 says he was “not knowing what he said”.
In the original, “Jesus alone” literally reads “no one except Jesus himself only”; μόνον means only, solely, alone.
Point 1: Our greatest enemy is “self”
“If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself”
Matthew 16:24
“Deny” in the original: disown utterly, cut all ties
No longer I, but Christ lives in me
“Deny himself” is the Greek ἀπαρνέομαι, the same word used for Peter’s threefold denial of the Lord (Matthew 26:34, 75).
Peter applying “denial” to Jesus was his greatest failure; our applying “denial” to ourselves is our greatest success.
Quote Galatians 2:20: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”
Psychology: Duval & Wicklund’s (1972) Objective Self-Awareness Theory shows that facing a mirror or camera turns attention to the self, followed by anxiety and self-criticism.
321: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, others or circumstances.
Point 2: Satan gets people looking at themselves
“You will be like God, knowing good and evil”
Genesis 3:5
Eyes opened — yet what they saw was nakedness
The mind of the flesh is hostile toward God
Satan didn’t tell Eve to hate God; he spoke a word of “advancement”: you will be like God.
The focus shifted from “what God has said” to “what I could become”, and the fall happened.
The three things in Genesis 3:6 — good for food, a delight to the eyes, desired to make one wise — match 1 John 2:16: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, the pride of life.
Satan promised “like God”; what he delivered was “naked” (Genesis 3:7).
“Mind” in Romans 8:7 is φρόνημα: the bent of the whole heart, not a passing thought.
True satisfaction is not self-fulfilment
“Delight yourself in Yahweh”
Psalm 37:4
Delight in the Lord first; then desires are given
The brain’s default channel: thinking about me
The order in Psalm 37:4: first delight in Yahweh, then the desires of your heart are given.
The mathematics of self-satisfaction: the denominator always runs faster than the numerator; the happiness lasts three days.
Augustine, Confessions: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
Science: Raichle et al. (2001, PNAS) found the brain’s Default Mode Network is most active when we are idle, closely tied to self-referential thinking.
Illustration: a child staring at how full his plastic cup is, never looking up at the waterfall that never stops.
Point 3: Looking at ourselves walks in Satan’s footsteps
Five “I will”s, one “you shall be brought down”
Isaiah 14:13–15
I want to be seen, famous, successful, approved
Famous on earth, struck off in heaven — how tragic
Isaiah 14:13–15: five “I will”s, in return for “you shall be brought down to Sheol”.
Ezekiel 28:17: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty” — the cause of the fall was not ugliness but beauty.
The Hebrew root for “pride”, גָּאָה, means to rise, to swell up; pride is a slowly rising water level (Proverbs 16:18).
Matthew 7:22–23: prophesying, casting out demons, mighty works — yet the Lord says, “I never knew you.”
Matthew 6:2, “they have received their reward”: ἀπέχω is a business term, “payment received in full”; once human applause breaks out, heaven’s account is settled.
Point 4: Seeing not himself, only the Father
“I can of myself do nothing”
John 5:30
He emptied and humbled himself; God highly exalted him
Heaven has one focus: the Lamb of God
John 5:19, 30: first see what the Father is doing, then act; don’t seek your own will.
Philippians 2:5–9: “emptied himself” is κενόω, to empty; he humbled himself, and God highly exalted him.
Contrast with Isaiah 14: Satan wanted to rise and fell; Jesus went low and was highly exalted.
Revelation 5:13: heaven has no second spotlight; the only focus of worship is the Lamb.
John the Baptist: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30); our greatest temptation is to mistake the friend of the bridegroom for the bridegroom.
Reminder: not suppressing self, but lifting up Jesus
God doesn’t erase you; he restores your intended position
See God first, then see yourself clearly
Isaiah: Here I am. Send me!
Selflessness is not nothing; it is entering the limitless
Calvin, opening of the Institutes: wisdom consists of two parts — the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves.
Isaiah 6:5, 8: first he saw the Lord’s glory and said “Woe is me”, then “Here I am. Send me!”
Job 42:5–6, 10: first he saw God with his own eyes, then he was restored and given double.
The order matters: staring at yourself and digging out faults is not humility but negative self-centredness.
Illustration: a drop of water on your palm dries in half a day; poured into the ocean, it never dries; selflessness is entering the limitless.

The Lord modelled it in Gethsemane: “not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39).
The evening reflection of Practice 3 takes the attitude of Psalm 139:23–24, not self-accusation.

From “Looking at Myself” to “Seeing Only Jesus”
“They saw no one, except Jesus alone”
Matthew 17:8
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 15
Greet the brothers and sisters and state today’s theme: what blocks our view of Jesus is often ourselves.
Read the key verse, Matthew 17:8 (read the full verse), stressing “they saw no one, except Jesus alone”.
Lay out the roadmap: four key points and three practices.
Set the tone: seeing self brings the fall; seeing Jesus alone brings freedom.
Introduction 1: The “one” hardest to let go of
A group photo arrives — we look for ourselves first
We are the generation that sees itself the most
The greatest obstacle: not circumstances, not others
but the “self” standing in front
Everyday scene: the moment a group photo opens, our eyes look for our own face first.
With the front-facing camera, human beings can for the first time see themselves anytime, anywhere.
God can change circumstances and soften other people; only “self” requires us to step aside ourselves.
Point out that this is not simply a matter of pride, but a misaligned focus of faith.
Introduction 2: A little moon hides the sun
The sun’s diameter: about 400 times the moon’s
And about 400 times farther away
So the little moon can cover the sun
“Self” is not big — just too close to our eyes
Astronomical fact: the sun’s diameter is about 1.39 million km, about 400 times the moon’s; it is also about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.
Hence a total solar eclipse: the moon, which gives no light, covers the entire sun.
Application: self is not big at all and gives no light, yet being too close to our eyes it hides Christ.
A total eclipse lasts a few minutes; “self” blocking Jesus can mean a lifetime of darkness.
Satan doesn’t need you to commit a great sin; he only needs to turn your camera a few degrees.
Key verse and background: the Transfiguration
Peter wants three tents, one place each
God says: This is my beloved Son. Listen to him
Moses and Elijah leave; only One remains
Matthew 17:1–8
The author is the apostle Matthew, writing between AD 50 and 70 for Jewish believers; the whole book proves that Jesus is the Messiah.
Context: Peter had just confessed “You are the Christ”, then the next moment was called Satan for “setting his mind on the things of men” (Matthew 16:23).
Jesus immediately said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16:24).
Peter’s three tents were a “seeing self” proposal; Luke 9:33 says he was “not knowing what he said”.
In the original, “lifting up their eyes” means raising the eyes; “Jesus alone” literally reads “no one except Jesus himself only”.
Point 1a: Denying self is the first step
“If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself”
Matthew 16:24
Deny self, then take up the cross, then follow
Skip the first step, and the rest is religious motion
Note the order: deny self, take up the cross, follow — the three steps cannot be reversed.
What holds us back is usually not work, family, health or money, but ourselves.
However hard our circumstances, God can change them; however hard others are, God can soften them; but self, we must move aside ourselves.
321: life first, then relationships, then ministry; denying self is a lesson of life.
Point 1b: The weight of “deny” in the original
“Deny himself”: ἀπαρνέομαι
Meaning: disown utterly, cut all ties
The same word as Peter’s denial of Jesus
Matthew 26:34, 75
ἀπαρνέομαι means “to disown utterly, to refuse to acknowledge”.
The same word is used of Peter’s threefold denial of the Lord (Matthew 26:34, 75).
Peter applying “denial” to Jesus was his greatest failure; our applying “denial” to ourselves is our greatest success.
Denying self means that when “self” walks up demanding sovereignty, we point at him and say: I do not know this man.
Point 1c: No longer I, but Christ
“It is no longer I who live,
but Christ lives in me”
Galatians 2:20
The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless
In Galatians 2:20 there is a death, and there is a life.
Selflessness is not annihilating ourselves, but letting the infinite Lord fill all my space; we are emptied in order to be filled.
Psychology: Duval & Wicklund’s (1972) Objective Self-Awareness Theory — attention turned to the self brings anxiety and self-criticism.
Baumeister et al.’s (2003) large-scale review found that raising self-esteem does not cause better performance.
Romans 12:3 said it long ago: “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think.”
Point 2a: Satan’s first scheme
“You will be like God, knowing good and evil”
Genesis 3:5
Not “hate God” — just “look at yourself”
The focus shifts, and the fall begins
The first spiritual battle took place in a conversation in front of a tree.
Satan spoke a word of “advancement”; it sounds like helping people upwards, but it actually pulls them away.
The focus shifted from “what God has said” to “what I could become”.
321: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place.
Point 2b: Eyes opened, yet seeing nakedness
Good for food, a delight to the eyes,
desired to make one wise (Genesis 3:6)
Lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, pride of life
1 John 2:16
The three things in Genesis 3:6 correspond exactly to 1 John 2:16.
Genesis 3:7: their eyes were opened, and what they saw was not glory but shame.
Satan promised “like God”; what he delivered was “naked”.
“Mind” in Romans 8:7 is φρόνημα, the bent of the whole heart; 8:6 says the mind of the flesh is death.
Point 2c: True satisfaction is in God himself
“Delight yourself in Yahweh”
Psalm 37:4
Delight in the Lord first; then desires are given
The brain’s default channel: thinking about me
Note the order: first delight in Yahweh, then the desires are given.
The mathematics of self-satisfaction: the denominator always runs faster than the numerator; the happiness lasts three days.
Augustine, Confessions: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
Science: Raichle et al.’s (2001, PNAS) Default Mode Network — the moment we are idle, we automatically think about ourselves.
Illustration: staring at your own plastic cup, or looking up at the waterfall that never stops?
Point 3a: Five “I will”s
“I will ascend into heaven …
I will make myself like the Most High”
Isaiah 14:13–14
The result: brought down to Sheol
Satan fell not because he lacked power, but because he “looked at himself and wanted for himself” far too much.
Isaiah 14:13–15: five “I will”s, in return for one “you shall be brought down”.
Ezekiel 28:17: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty” — not ugliness, but beauty.
The Hebrew root for “pride”, גָּאָה, means to rise; pride is a slowly rising water level (Proverbs 16:18).
Point 3b: Today’s four “I want”s
I want to be seen, I want to be famous
I want to succeed, I want people’s approval
If the motive is “I want”, it is still hostility to God
Famous on earth, struck off in heaven — how tragic
These four sound perfectly normal, even ambitious — that is exactly what makes them dangerous.
Matthew 7:22–23: prophesying, casting out demons, mighty works — yet the Lord says, “I never knew you.”
Notice the subject of their sentences is always “we”; Jesus is merely a name to invoke.
Matthew 6:1–2: good deeds done to be seen by others — “they have received their reward”.
ἀπέχω is a business term, “payment received in full”; once the applause breaks out, heaven’s account is settled.
Point 3c: That spotlight doesn’t exist
Spotlight Effect: we guess half will notice
In fact only about a quarter remember
“Yahweh looks at the heart”
1 Samuel 16:7
The Spotlight Effect experiments of Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky (2000).
Participants wearing an embarrassing T-shirt estimated about half would notice; in fact only about a quarter remembered.
We spend most of our lives managing an image that hardly anyone is looking at.
The One who truly is watching looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).
321: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.
Point 4a: Jesus did nothing of himself
“I can of myself do nothing.
As I hear, I judge”
John 5:30
First see the Father, then act
John 5:30 has two negatives and two positives.
5:19: “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.”
The spiritual order: first see, then do.
John 8:50: “I don’t seek my own glory”; 17:4: “I glorified you on the earth.”
321: Jesus is my role model — if even the Son of God did not act on his own, what grounds do I have for acting on my own?
Point 4b: The way of emptying, the way of exaltation
“He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”
Philippians 2:7
He humbled himself; God highly exalted him
Heaven has one focus: the Lamb of God
“Emptied himself” is κενόω: to empty, to make void.
Set Philippians 2 beside Isaiah 14: Satan wanted to rise and fell; Jesus went low and was highly exalted.
Philippians 2:9: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name.”
Revelation 5:13: heaven has no second spotlight.

John the Baptist: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30); don’t mistake the friend of the bridegroom for the bridegroom. The moon has no light of its own; the best moon reflects the most and blocks the least; the same moon in the right position reflects glory, and in the wrong position hides it.
Reminder: not suppressing self, but lifting up Jesus
God doesn’t erase you; he restores your intended position
See God first, then see yourself clearly
Isaiah: Here I am. Send me!
Selflessness is not nothing; it is entering the limitless
Calvin, opening of the Institutes: wisdom consists of the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves.
Isaiah 6:5, 8; Job 42:5–6, 10 — first seeing God, then a true assessment of self.
Staring at yourself and digging out faults is not humility but negative self-centredness.
Matthew 16:25: whoever loses his life for the Lord’s sake will find it.

Practice 1: Morning and in the moment
Morning: Lord, today I don’t want to look at myself
I only want to fix my eyes on you
