4. Blessing: may the brothers and sisters, when they lift their eyes, see no one except Jesus alone.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin with a question: over this past week, what picture has filled your heart most often — Jesus, or yourself? The title of today’s lesson is “Seeing Self Brings Fear”. The key verse is very short, just one line: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

In 1912 the Titanic struck an iceberg. But what tore open the hull was not the part floating above the water. Only about one-ninth of an iceberg shows above the surface; the rest lies hidden beneath. Brothers and sisters, our faith is just the same. What sinks a Christian is seldom the great wind and waves everyone can see. It is the mass beneath the surface that we don’t want to face — our gaze fixed on ourselves. The circumstances outside are only the impact; the “looking at self” inside is the breach. Fear doesn’t knock at the door; it seeps in under it.

Our key verse comes from the Transfiguration. Just six days earlier, Peter had confessed, “You are the Christ,” and was then immediately rebuked by the Lord for “setting his mind on the things of men”. So the Lord took them up the mountain and let them see his glory. The Father spoke from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” (Matthew 17:5) The disciples fell on their faces and were very afraid. And then? They lifted their heads, and saw no one, except Jesus alone.

Brothers and sisters, where does the word “afraid” first appear in the Bible? Not at the Flood, not on a battlefield, but the first time a human being looked carefully at himself. Adam said: “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.” (Genesis 3:10) The serpent said their eyes would be opened, and their eyes were indeed opened — but the first thing they saw was not God; it was themselves. And so human beings began to cover, to hide and to shift the blame. We still do all three today. We cover ourselves with qualifications, with job titles, with busyness, even with ministry. God called out in the garden, “Where are you?” Not because he couldn’t find Adam; God was asking: Adam, what position are you living in now?

When we see our own lack, we cannot believe in Jesus’ abundance; when we see our own smallness, we cannot rely on Jesus’ greatness; when we see our own weakness, we can hardly experience Jesus’ almighty power. Brothers and sisters, if our focus is on ourselves, we sink into self-pity, self-blame, anxiety and fear. But if our focus turns to Jesus, even in the middle of the storm we can still walk on the water.

Peter is the best reminder of all. Of the twelve disciples, only he got out of the boat, and he really did walk on the water. So why did he sink? The text says: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid.” (Matthew 14:30) Brothers and sisters, notice that the wind had been there the whole time. The wind didn’t get stronger; Peter’s eyes changed. Hebrews tells us to be “looking to” Jesus, and that word means taking your eyes off everything else. Robert Murray M’Cheyne is generally credited with saying: for every look at yourself, take ten looks at Christ.

Third, faith and fear: you can walk by only one. Ten of the spies came back from Canaan and said: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.” (Numbers 13:33) But they had never even asked the other side! Forty years later Rahab revealed the truth: the people in the city had long since lost heart in terror. It wasn’t that they didn’t know God; it was that they no longer kept their eyes on God. The same walls, the same sons of Anak, yet Caleb and Joshua said: “Yahweh is with us. Don’t fear them.” (Numbers 14:9) The difference wasn’t in the intelligence; it was in the focus. That is why God said to Joshua: “Don’t be afraid. Don’t be dismayed, for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.” (Joshua 1:9)

Brothers and sisters, when do you notice a single drop of water? When it is on its own, separated. When people lose their unity with one another, we easily see one person — and that person is ourselves. And often we are not isolated by others; we choose to separate ourselves. A single drop of water soon evaporates, but joined into a river, it can bring life. When we are willing to lay ourselves down and enter into unity, we will no longer see ourselves, but see only Jesus.

These four points really say only one thing: focus. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person covers, hides, sinks and sees himself as a grasshopper; the selfless person lifts up his eyes and sees no one except Jesus alone. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. All three times Satan tempted the Lord he said, “If you are the Son of God” — what he wanted was to shift the focus from the Father to self. Brothers and sisters, he still uses the same trick today. He won’t tell you not to believe in God; he will just keep you looking at yourself. And the person he fears most is the one who sees no one except Jesus alone.

So we have three practices. First, notice when you start looking at yourself. When you hear your heart say “I just can’t”, “What if it doesn’t work out?” or “What will people think of me?”, say straight away: “Lord Jesus, I turn to you.” Second, replace the language of fear with the language of faith: though I am weak, the Lord is my strength; though the storm rages, the Lord is still with me; what is impossible for me is possible for God. Third, reach out and connect with others; refuse isolation. This week, greet a member of the body and share your struggle with a companion. And one small reminder: feelings change, but God’s word does not. Let truth be greater than feelings; let Jesus be greater than self.

Brothers and sisters, “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” (2 Timothy 1:7) Paul, who wrote these words, was in a Roman prison at the time. Fear should not become our habit; faith is our calling. Look at what the Lord does: he comes, he touches them, and he says, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.” You don’t have to become strong first before you can lift your head; you lift your head first, and then you become strong.

Let us pray together. Lord Jesus, we confess that so often, the moment we see ourselves we hide, and the moment we see the wind and the waves we sink. Forgive us for putting our focus in the wrong place. Reach out and touch us, and say to us: Get up, and don’t be afraid. Holy Spirit, help us this week to turn to you, and to turn to our brothers and sisters. When we lift up our eyes, may we see no one, except you alone. Reign as King, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin with a question that cuts deep: over this past week, what picture has filled your heart most often — Jesus, or yourself? The title of today’s lesson is “Seeing Self Brings Fear”, and the subtitle is: when our focus turns to ourselves, fear swallows up faith. The key verse is just one short line: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8) Over the next half hour we will walk four stretches of road together: from the Garden of Eden to the Sea of Galilee, from the wilderness of Kadesh to the Lord Jesus’ prayer for his disciples’ unity. We will see one thing: where your focus is, there your life is.

In April 1912, the Titanic struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. But what tore open the hull was not the part floating above the water. Only about one-ninth of an iceberg’s volume shows above the surface; the rest lies hidden beneath. Brothers and sisters, our life of faith is just the same. What really sinks a Christian is seldom the great wind and waves everyone can see. It is the mass beneath the surface that we don’t want to face — our gaze fixed on ourselves. The circumstances outside are only the impact; the “looking at self” inside is the breach.

Fear doesn’t knock at the door; it seeps in under it. You won’t hear a sound. You’ll simply find, one day, that prayer has grown heavy, that going to fellowship has become a chore, that you rehearse every sentence three times in your head before you say it. How does it start? Very often with a glance. A glance at your own weakness, a glance at your own failure, a glance at the gap between you and others. When Adam and Eve had sinned, the first thing they felt was not repentance but fear. Seeing self brings fear, shame, flight and separation.

Our key verse comes from Matthew chapter 17. The author, Matthew, was Levi the tax collector; the book is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, mainly for Jewish believers. Chapter 17 records the Transfiguration. Just six days earlier, Peter had confessed, “You are the Christ,” and was then rebuked by the Lord: “you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” (Matthew 16:23) So the Lord took them up the mountain. Peter wanted to make three tents, and at once the Father spoke from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” (Matthew 17:5) There is only one focus.

Brothers and sisters, where does the word “afraid” first appear in the whole Bible? Not at the Flood, not on a battlefield, not in the face of death. It appears the first time a human being looked carefully at himself. Adam said: “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.” (Genesis 3:10) The same man, the same garden, the same God — and he had never been afraid before. What changed was not the surroundings but the way of seeing. The serpent’s original promise was, “your eyes will be opened” (Genesis 3:5). Their eyes were indeed opened, but the first thing they saw was not God; it was themselves. This is the truest picture of the human fall: not a loss of sight, but a change to the wrong focus.

The Hebrew hides a profound play on words here. Genesis 2:25 says the man and his wife were “naked”, and that word is arummim; 3:1 says the serpent was more “subtle”, and that word is arum — they sound almost exactly alike. Human nakedness was originally free of fear; once the serpent came in, the very same nakedness turned into shame. Nothing about the thing itself changed; what changed was the way of seeing. And here is one more word to remember: the Hebrew for “afraid”, yare’, can also be translated “to fear” in the sense of reverence. So fear turns out to be reverence pointed at the wrong object.

Under fear, people do three things, and Adam did all three. Cover: he sewed fig leaves together. Hide: he hid among the trees of the garden, away from the presence of Yahweh God. Shift the blame: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” We are the same today; we cover ourselves with busyness, even with ministry. Psychology offers corroboration too: Nolen-Hoeksema at Yale studied “rumination” and found that repeatedly staring at ourselves only prolongs and deepens depression. When God asks, “Where are you?”, it is not because he can’t find us; he is asking: what position are you living in?

The second key point: when we see ourselves, we cannot see Jesus. Brothers and sisters, let’s read slowly: when we see our own lack, we cannot believe in Jesus’ abundance; when we see our own smallness, we cannot rely on Jesus’ greatness; when we see our own weakness, we can hardly experience Jesus’ almighty power. If our focus is on ourselves, we sink into self-pity, self-blame, anxiety and fear. And let me be fair to Peter: of the twelve disciples, only he got out of the boat, and he really did walk on the water. That was no illusion; it was a miracle. The other eleven stayed in the boat the whole time, just watching. So the problem was not that he lacked courage; the problem was his focus.

So why did he sink? The text says: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink.” (Matthew 14:30) The Greek word for “saw” describes a continuing gaze, not a passing glance. Notice: the wind had been there the whole time; it was already strong when he got out of the boat. The wind didn’t get stronger; Peter’s eyes changed. Hebrews tells us to be “looking to” Jesus, and that word literally means taking your eyes away from everything else. You cannot stare at the wind and look to the Lord at the same time. And the tenderest part is the next line: Jesus immediately stretched out his hand and took hold of him. The Lord’s hand is faster than our failure.

In 1999 Simons and Chabris of Harvard carried out an experiment, published in the journal Perception. They asked participants to watch a video and count the passes. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the frame, beat his chest right in the centre and stayed there for about nine seconds. Around half the participants never saw it at all. This is called “inattentional blindness”. Brothers and sisters, when you spend all day counting up your own weaknesses and inadequacies, you become blind to Jesus standing right in front of you. It isn’t that Jesus isn’t there; it’s that we aren’t looking. Robert Murray M’Cheyne is generally credited with saying: for every look at yourself, take ten looks at Christ.

The third key point: faith and fear — you can walk by only one. Twelve spies explored the land of Canaan and came back forty days later. Their first sentence was accurate: surely it flows with milk and honey. But the next sentence turned: the people who dwell in the land are strong. In the end they said: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.” (Numbers 13:33) Notice the second half: had they asked a single one of the sons of Anak? Not one. Forty years later Rahab revealed the truth: “As soon as we had heard it, our hearts melted.” (Joshua 2:11) The other side had been scared to death all along.

Yet on the very same journey, two men brought back a completely different report. “Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, ‘Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!’” (Numbers 13:30) He and Joshua said: “Yahweh is with us. Don’t fear them.” (Numbers 14:9) Brothers and sisters, the same walls, two opposite conclusions. The difference wasn’t in the intelligence; it was in the focus. The ten spies looked first at the giants and then at themselves, and God disappeared from view; Caleb looked first at God, and the giants became bread. It wasn’t that they didn’t know God; it was that they no longer kept their eyes on God. And so a whole generation wandered the wilderness for forty years until they died — not because the enemy was too strong, but because their focus was in the wrong place.

Why does bad news always sound louder than good news? In 1979 Kahneman and Tversky published their “Prospect Theory” in the journal Econometrica, finding that the pain people feel at a loss is roughly twice the pleasure they feel at an equal gain. Kahneman was later awarded the 2002 Nobel Prize in Economics for it. So with milk and honey right before their eyes, all they could hear was the echo of the city walls. That is why God said to Joshua: “Don’t be afraid. Don’t be dismayed, for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.” (Joshua 1:9) God’s assurance was not that the enemy had grown weaker, but that “I am with you.”

The fourth key point is a beautiful one. Brothers and sisters, when do you notice a single drop of water? Standing on the beach looking out over the whole Pacific, you don’t notice any single drop. When do you notice one? When it is on its own, separated, cut off from the other drops. In the same way, when people lose their unity with one another, we easily “see one person” — and that person is ourselves. Often we are not isolated by others; we choose to separate ourselves. The more isolated we are, the more fragile we become; the more fragile, the more afraid. That is exactly how Adam ended up hiding among the trees.

There is a real scientific fact here. Whether water evaporates quickly or slowly depends on the ratio of surface area to volume. The smaller the drop, the larger its surface area relative to its volume, and the faster it evaporates. Spread a quantity of water into a thin mist, and in a few minutes it’s gone; gather it into a reservoir, and it can supply a whole city. This is a spiritual sign the Creator placed in the material world: isolation exposes us; gathering preserves us. Solomon said: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Ecclesiastes 4:12) The Lord Jesus said: “from within him will flow rivers of living water.” (John 7:38) A river has never been the work of one drop.

In 2010 Professor Holt-Lunstad of Brigham Young University in the United States published a meta-analysis pooling 148 studies and more than three hundred thousand people. The conclusion: people with stronger social connections had about a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival. Even our bodies protest: human beings were not designed to survive alone. God said before human beings had ever sinned: “It is not good for the man to be alone.” (Genesis 2:18) And the Lord prayed: “that they may be one, even as we are one.” (John 17:22) This is the 321 “235 relationship”: 2 is spiritual companions, 3 is spiritual parents and children, 5 is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Next come the practices for daily life. Practice 1: notice when you start “looking at yourself”. When you find your heart saying “I’m so weak; I just can’t”, “What if it doesn’t work out?” or “What will people think of me?” — those three look at your own ability, your own results and your own image. The moment they appear, say straight away: “Lord Jesus, I turn to you.” Martin Luther is generally credited with saying: you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair. Practice 2: replace the language of fear with the language of faith. Though I am weak, the Lord is my strength; though the storm rages, the Lord is still with me; what is impossible for me is possible for God.

Practice 3: reach out and connect with others; refuse “isolation”. This week, please deliberately do one thing: greet a member of the church body, share your struggle with a brother or sister you trust, or join a small group or a ministry team. James says: “Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed.” (James 5:16) The condition for healing is “to one another” and “for one another”. And one small reminder: our feelings change, but God’s word does not. Feelings are excellent servants but terrible masters. Let truth be greater than feelings; let Jesus be greater than self.

Let’s place today’s content within the 321 framework. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless; selflessness is not having nothing, but entering the limitless. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. The order matters too: life first, then relationships, then ministry; and the order of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. And there is the 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we live out the selfless “0”, and the ninefold fruit of the Spirit grows within the relationship. And there is the shift in perspective: from the human to the divine, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

Brothers and sisters, we have come to the close. “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” (2 Timothy 1:7) Fear paralyses us, so God gives power; fear makes us look out only for ourselves, so God gives love; fear throws our thoughts into confusion, so God gives self-control. Paul, who wrote these words, was in a Roman prison at the time. In the place where he had every reason to be afraid, he wrote the least fearful sentence of all. Look once more at the scene: “Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid.’” (Matthew 17:7) You don’t have to become strong first before you can lift your head; you lift your head first, and then you become strong.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that we are so often like Adam, hiding the moment we see ourselves; like Peter, sinking the moment we see the wind and the waves; like those ten spies, seeing ourselves as grasshoppers. Lord, forgive us for putting our focus in the wrong place. Reach out and touch us, and say to us: Get up, and don’t be afraid. Holy Spirit, help us: the moment the language of fear appears, may we turn to you; whenever we want to hide, may we reach out and connect with our brothers and sisters. When we lift up our eyes, may we see no one, except you alone. Reign as King, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Greatest Distance Is the Silence Under One Roof
sections.html:
A couple who had been married for more than twenty years came to see their pastor. They hadn’t been fighting or throwing things; they sat at either end of the sofa with an empty seat between them. The wife said, “We haven’t had a proper conversation in three months.” The husband, head bowed, added, “Actually, we see each other every day. It’s just that we stopped living in the same house a long time ago.”

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that the greatest distance between two people is not high mountains and long rivers, not the ends of the earth, but two people sitting right next to each other while their hearts draw back, inch by inch?

The Bible has a name for this drawing back. It is called “separation”.

Separation makes no sound. It isn’t fierce like an argument or glaring like a betrayal. It is quiet, slow and perfectly polite. It simply makes you reply to one message fewer, go to one meeting fewer, speak one honest word fewer, take one step fewer towards someone. But by the time you come to your senses, that invisible wall has already been built high and thick.

Today we are going to face a very important question together: why does separation happen?

Right at the start, the lesson uncovers the first layer of the answer — separation is not neutral; it is Satan’s weapon. Then the lesson helps us see Jesus: he came to restore relationships. And then the lesson names the first cause of separation in a single word: comparison.

The theme verse for this lesson is just one short sentence, yet it is the key to the whole lesson: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order in this sentence. First “no one”, then “Jesus alone”. When our eyes move off people and our focus turns to Christ, comparison stops; when comparison stops, fear fades; when fear fades, the wall of separation comes down.

This is the core practice of Kingdom 321: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

This morning, let’s lift up our eyes together. May the Holy Spirit help us take down, one by one, the walls that have long fallen into disrepair yet still stand between us and other people.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: “Jesus Alone” on the Mount of Transfiguration
sections.html:
Our theme verse is Matthew 17:8. To really grasp the weight of this sentence, we have to go back up that mountain.

(1) Author, date and audience

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is the apostle Matthew, also called Levi, formerly a tax collector in Capernaum (Matthew 9:9). A man his own people regarded as a traitor and the religious world regarded as a sinner was called by Jesus to be a disciple. That fact is itself a footnote to this lesson: from the very beginning, Jesus was tearing down the walls between people.

Evangelical scholars generally hold that Matthew’s Gospel was written between AD 50 and 70, mainly for Jewish Christians. The book quotes the Old Testament more than sixty times, and everywhere it sets out to prove one thing: Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the son of David, the son of Abraham (Matthew 1:1).

But Matthew is also the only one of the four Gospels to use the word “church” explicitly (Matthew 16:18; 18:17). In other words, Matthew wants people not only to know the King, but to enter the King’s community. Knowing Jesus is life; entering the community is relationships — this is exactly what 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry.”

(2) The context

The Transfiguration in chapter 17 follows straight on from chapter 16. In the region of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:15–16) Immediately afterwards, the Lord said plainly for the first time that he must go up to Jerusalem, suffer many things, be killed and rise on the third day. But Peter took him aside and tried to talk him out of it, and the Lord turned and rebuked him: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” (Matthew 16:23)

Brothers and sisters, notice: it was just when the disciples were at their most confused, most prone to comparing themselves with each other, most eager to argue about who was the greatest, that Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain.

“After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light.” (Matthew 17:1–2)

Moses and Elijah appeared and talked with Jesus. The moment Peter saw them, he said, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (Matthew 17:4)

Brothers and sisters, what lies hidden in Peter’s words? The most natural and the most deadly of human habits — ranking, comparing, grading. Three tents means three positions; three positions means a league table. Once people start a league table, their eyes fill with “who is greater than whom”, and cracks begin to appear in relationships.

How did God respond? “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’” (Matthew 17:5) The disciples fell on their faces, terribly afraid. Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.”

And then comes our theme verse for today: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

(3) The threefold message of this verse

First, the three tents were never built. The league table people wanted, God blew away with a single sentence.

Second, Moses stood for the Law and Elijah for the Prophets; both Old Testament giants withdrew, and only Jesus remained. Hebrews says, “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son.” (Hebrews 1:1–2) There is only one focus.

Third, the tone of “no one” in the original is that they raised their eyes and looked all around, and apart from Jesus they could see no one else. It doesn’t mean that people vanished; it means that when Christ is lifted up, other people are no longer the ruler we measure ourselves by.

Brothers and sisters, this is the key to the lesson. Comparison is “lifting up our eyes and seeing only people”; faith is “lifting up our eyes and seeing only Jesus”. Today’s lesson is learning to move our eyes off people and back onto the Lord.

sections.heading: 3. Key Point 1: Separation Is Not Neutral — It Is Satan’s Weapon
sections.html:
The lesson comes straight to the point: Satan doesn’t only want people to drift away from God; he wants them separated from one another.

(1) The first scene of separation: the Garden of Eden

The first human separation happened at the moment of the Fall. “They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.” (Genesis 3:8)

Notice the order: the moment humans sinned, their first reaction was to hide from God. That is separation from God. Then God came and questioned him, and Adam said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” (Genesis 3:12) In one sentence he shifted the blame onto his wife — and onto God. That is separation from people.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? When sin comes in, separation follows right behind. Satan has never changed his methods: first he cuts you off from God, then he cuts you off from people, and finally he sets you at odds even with yourself.

This is exactly what 321 says: the root sickness of the old self is the self-centred life. Self-centred people make themselves the centre of everything, and people who make themselves the centre inevitably push others away. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; and every time we leave our originally intended position, it leaves a crack in our relationships.

(2) The thief comes to steal, kill and destroy

The lesson quotes the words of the Lord Jesus. In full they read: “The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

This verse sets out two very clear lines. Satan’s line is stealing, killing and destroying; Jesus’ line is life, and life more abundant.

What does Satan steal? Our unity. What does Satan kill? Our relationships. What does Satan destroy? God’s purpose that we should “all be one”.

In his high-priestly prayer before his Passion, the Lord Jesus said: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the last phrase — “that the world may believe”. Unity isn’t just a slightly nicer atmosphere; unity is the evidence for the gospel. And so that evidence is precisely what Satan attacks.

In Life Together, Bonhoeffer gives a weighty warning: the person who loves his dream of community more than the actual community becomes a destroyer of community. Brothers and sisters, we seldom leave a group because we hate it; we usually leave because that group “doesn’t quite match the picture in my head”. This is the most respectable kind of separation, and Satan’s favourite.

(3) Once a member is cut off, the result is death

The lesson uses a very powerful image: we are members of the body of Christ. Paul says, “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.” (1 Corinthians 12:27) And again: “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” (1 Corinthians 12:21)

A finger separated from the hand doesn’t become freer; within minutes it begins to die. Because life isn’t in the finger; life is in the body.

This is not just an image; it is a measurable fact. In 2010, Julianne Holt-Lunstad, a psychologist at Brigham Young University in the United States, and her colleagues published a meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine combining 148 studies and more than three hundred thousand participants. The results showed that people with strong social connections had about a 50 per cent higher likelihood of survival than those who lacked them. In further research in 2015 she found that loneliness raises the risk of death by about 26 per cent, and social isolation by about 29 per cent. In 2023 the US Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy, issued an advisory on “Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation”, stating that the harm of social disconnection to health is comparable to smoking fifteen cigarettes a day.

Brothers and sisters, science is only saying again, with data, what the Bible said long ago: a member cut off from the body dies.

So the lesson draws a conclusion, and I ask you to keep it in your heart: the final result of separation is not independence; it is death.

People who leave the church slowly dry up spiritually; people who cut themselves off from others grow harder and lonelier at heart; couples who choose a cold war at home lose the warmth of their relationship drop by drop. A cold war sheds no blood, but it lets love slowly lose its heat — and losing heat is also a way to die.

(4) Applying 321

321 says the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Satan attacks every single link in that chain. So we must be very clear-headed: when you notice yourself starting to want to avoid people, to leave the group chat, to be “fine on my own”, most of the time that is not maturity; that is a battlefield.

Lord, give us eyes to discern: separation is not neutral. It is never simply a matter of personality, or simply of being busy. It is a weapon, and the one holding it is the evil one.

sections.heading: 4. Key Point 2: Jesus Came to Restore Relationships
sections.html:
How warmly the lesson puts it: thank the Lord, Jesus didn’t come to rebuke us, but to restore our relationship with God and with others.

(1) He came to break down the dividing wall

Paul says of Christ: “For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation,” (Ephesians 2:14)

In those days “the middle wall of separation” was a physical thing. Between the outer and inner courts of the Second Temple stood a stone barrier, engraved with warnings in Greek and Latin: any Gentile who crosses this boundary does so at his own risk, and the penalty is death. One wall divided people into two kinds: those who may come near, and those who may not.

Paul says that Christ tore down this wall on the cross. He goes on: “and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it.” (Ephesians 2:16)

Brothers and sisters, the cross has a vertical beam and a horizontal one. The vertical beam restores our relationship with God; the horizontal beam restores our relationship with others. Take away either one, and it is no longer a cross.

(2) He chose not a palace but a manger

The lesson reminds us: he could have chosen to be born in a palace, but he chose a manger, because he would not be separated from people.

“She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in bands of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn.” (Luke 2:7)

A palace has guards, gates and ranks; a manger has no door. So that night the wise men from the east could come, and the shepherds keeping watch over their flocks in the fields could come too. Scholars and shepherds, rich and poor, knelt for the first time before the same baby. Brothers and sisters, the very first scene of salvation is a scene without walls.

The place where he grew up was the same. The people of Nazareth said, “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?” (Matthew 13:55) He chose to grow up in a carpenter’s family, planing wood day after day, mending roofs, paying the rent, because he wanted to live among people. The Word became flesh and lived among us (John 1:14) — and the word “lived” in the original carries the sense of “pitching a tent”. He doesn’t shout to us from behind the clouds; he pitches his tent right next door to ours.

(3) He drew near to sinners, embraced children and touched the sick

The lesson says: in Jesus’ ministry we see him drawing near to sinners, embracing children and touching the sick, paying no attention to the world’s opinion, all to close the distance between himself and people.

He drew near to sinners. “The Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, ‘This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.’” (Luke 15:2) In that culture, eating at the same table meant identifying with someone, accepting them. They meant this as an accusation, without realising that it is the very definition of the gospel.

He embraced children. The disciples rebuked those who brought children to him, but the Lord was indignant and said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.” “He took them in his arms, and blessed them, laying his hands on them.” (Mark 10:14, 16)

He touched the sick. A man with leprosy came and pleaded with him. Under the law of Moses, this man was not to be touched, and Jesus could perfectly well have healed him with a single word. But the Bible says: “Jesus stretched out his hand, and touched him, saying, ‘I want to. Be made clean.’ Immediately his leprosy was cleansed.” (Matthew 8:3) Brothers and sisters, that man may not have been touched by anyone for years. The Lord knew that sickness can be healed with a word, but loneliness has to be healed with a touch.

(4) An example from life, and a piece of research

A brother once told me that while he was in hospital, the messages he received most were “Hang in there!” But what really made him cry was a pastor’s wife who said nothing at all — she just sat by his bed and held his hand for fifteen minutes.

In 2003 the social neuroscientist Naomi Eisenberger of the University of California, Los Angeles, and her colleagues published a study in the journal Science. They found that when people were excluded by a group in an experiment, the brain region activated (the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex) overlapped heavily with the region activated by physical pain. In plain words: being left out really does hurt — and the brain counts it as that kind of pain.

Brothers and sisters, this is why Jesus “touched”. He wasn’t only dealing with disease; he was dealing with the pain of being shut out.

(5) Applying 321

321 says: Jesus is my role model. So when it comes to “relationships”, what is Jesus’ role model for us? Taking the initiative, humbling himself, drawing near, setting no threshold.

321 also says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Notice that “relationships” comes before “ministry”. We often work very hard while our relationships run up debt all the way. That is not the Lord’s order. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The lesson concludes: unity is his mission; separation is Satan’s scheme. If you and I want to live in the likeness of Jesus, we must break free from the snare of separation and learn to connect with people and be one with God.

sections.heading: 5. Key Point 3: Why Does Separation Happen? The First Cause — Comparison
sections.html:
The lesson goes to the heart of it: why does separation happen? The first cause is comparison.

(1) Comparison defined, and the Scripture

Paul puts it very strongly: “For we are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.” (2 Corinthians 10:12)

“Without understanding” in the original means having no insight, being unwise. Paul’s point is that using people as a ruler is foolish in itself, because the ruler keeps changing. Today you beat this person; tomorrow you meet that one. You come out ahead in this, and fall behind in something else. Measure yourself with a moving ruler, and you can measure for a lifetime without ever arriving at peace.

Ecclesiastes saw through this long ago: “Then I saw all the labor and achievement that is the envy of a man’s neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.” (Ecclesiastes 4:4) So the motive behind all our striving, much of the time, isn’t love; it’s not wanting to lose.

Proverbs says, “The life of the body is a heart at peace, but envy rots the bones.” (Proverbs 14:30) Rot starts from the inside: the outside still looks fine while the bones are already hollow. Comparison is that kind of disease: it doesn’t shout or make a scene; it just slowly eats away the joy inside you.

(2) Comparison → fear → separation: Satan’s favourite strategy

The lesson gives us a very clear chain: comparison makes us anxious, envious and afraid, and in the end it makes us separate. Comparison → fear → separation.

Why does comparison breed fear? Because the moment I compare, my worth is placed somewhere others can overtake it at any time. Since I could be overtaken at any time, I have to be on my guard; since I have to be on my guard, I can’t get too close; since I can’t get too close, separation is born.

The apostle John gives us the antidote: “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love.” (1 John 4:18)

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: what deals with fear is not trying harder to win, but experiencing love more deeply. You don’t have to beat anyone to deserve to be loved; in Christ you are already loved.

(3) Confirmation from psychology

In 1954 the social psychologist Leon Festinger put forward “social comparison theory” in the journal Human Relations. He argued that people have a basic drive to evaluate their abilities and worth by comparing themselves with others. When an objective standard is lacking, people automatically take those around them as the standard.

Festinger was describing, not promising. He described a human tendency; the Bible sets out to change that tendency. Paul says, “But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.” (Galatians 6:4) God gives each person a different measure; he asks only whether you have been faithful, not whether you have won.

Today this tendency has been magnified countless times over. In 2012 Hui-Tzu Grace Chou and Nicholas Edge published a study in the journal Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking whose very title was “They Are Happier and Having Better Lives than I Am”. They found that the more often people browsed social media, the more likely they were to believe that other people’s lives were happier than their own. Brothers and sisters, what we scroll past on our phones every day is usually other people’s carefully chosen highlights, and what we compare them with is our own unedited everyday life. That contest is unfair from the very start.

(4) A parable

A piano teacher once said something very wise: if a student keeps his attention on the practice room next door, his fingers will never play well, because his ears aren’t on his own piano.

Comparison is putting your ears in someone else’s practice room. Your hands are still on your own keys, but your heart left long ago. No wonder there’s no music.

In Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis says that pride is essentially competitive — people are proud not of having something, but of having more of it than others. That goes straight to the heart of it: the root of comparison is pride.

(5) Applying 321

321 says: pride is the root of the problem; humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Comparison is the classic symptom of the self-centred life. Self-centred people have to keep confirming where they stand, so they have to keep measuring and comparing. Selfless people don’t. Because selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20).

In The Freedom of Self-Forgetfulness, Pastor Timothy Keller wrote a line that is often quoted: gospel humility is not thinking more of myself or thinking less of myself; it is thinking of myself less. Brothers and sisters, that is “selflessness” — not putting yourself down, but no longer needing to think about yourself all the time.

That is why our theme verse is so precious: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8) Comparison looks at people; faith looks at Jesus.

sections.heading: 6. Key Point 4: An Example from Scripture — Saul and David
sections.html:
The lesson gives a heartbreaking example, one that acts out every step of “comparison → fear → separation” before our eyes.

(1) It began with affection

King Saul was fond of David at first. Because David was skilled at playing the lyre, he was summoned to serve at the palace. The Bible says, “David came to Saul, and stood before him. He loved him greatly; and he became his armor bearer.” (1 Samuel 16:21)

Brothers and sisters, remember this verse. Their relationship wasn’t bad from the start. Many broken relationships were beautiful at the beginning. The problem isn’t how they began, but what happened along the way.

(2) A song that stirred up comparison

After David killed Goliath, the Israelites came home victorious. “The women sang to one another as they played, and said, ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.’” (1 Samuel 18:7)

To be fair, this song was praising Saul. “Saul has slain his thousands” was very high praise. But Saul didn’t take in a word of it. He heard only one thing: David’s number is bigger than mine.

“Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, ‘They have credited David with ten thousands, and they have only credited me with thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?’ Saul watched David from that day and forward.” (1 Samuel 18:8–9)

Brothers and sisters, this is how terrible comparison is. Comparison makes you hear a compliment as a threat. Comparison makes you hear your own death knell in someone else’s good news. The original says Saul “watched” David — eyed him — and the word carries the sense of a continual, unrelenting stare. From that day on, Saul could never take his eyes off David. His focus had changed — no longer God, no longer the nation, but that man.

(3) Comparison breeds fear

The Bible goes on: “Saul was afraid of David, because Yahweh was with him, and had departed from Saul.” (1 Samuel 18:12)

Notice the order: first anger, then the hostile stare, then fear. On the surface it was anger; underneath it was all fear. The voice in Saul’s heart was just what the lesson describes: “Will he replace me? Will he take my place?”

Brothers and sisters, let me be honest: nine times out of ten, when we lose our temper it isn’t because we are strong, but because we are afraid. Afraid of being replaced, afraid of being looked down on, afraid of being outshone.

(4) Fear breeds separation

And then separation came. “Therefore Saul removed him from his presence, and made him his captain over a thousand; and he went out and came in before the people.” (1 Samuel 18:13)

See how cleverly this was done. Saul didn’t drive David away; he promoted him. On the surface it was a vote of confidence; in reality it was a transfer. The title “captain over a thousand” bought the words “removed him from his presence”.

Brothers and sisters, in the church, at work, in the family, how much separation is accomplished in this respectable way? I haven’t fallen out with you; I just don’t consult you any more. I haven’t kicked you out; I’ve just moved you to another group. I haven’t said I don’t want you; I’m just “giving you more room to grow”.

The words of separation are often very polite, but the results of separation never are.

(5) How separation ends

The lesson is right: separation doesn’t solve the problem; it ends in broken relationships, a divided kingdom and one’s own ruin.

From then on Saul threw his spear at David, sent men to lie in wait for him, hunted him into the wilderness, slaughtered eighty-five priests of the city of Nob (1 Samuel 22:18), and finally died by his own hand on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:4). And the very thing he feared — David taking the throne — was not delayed by a single day because of his separation.

This is exactly what 321 says: pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose. Saul wanted to hold on to his throne, and he lost it; he wanted to get rid of a threat, and he got rid of his most loyal servant.

By contrast, how different David’s response was. When Saul was asleep in the cave, David’s men said his chance had come, but David only cut off the corner of his robe, and afterwards his heart struck him, and he said: “Yahweh forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, Yahweh’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is Yahweh’s anointed.” (1 Samuel 24:6)

Brothers and sisters, why was David able not to take revenge? Because David’s focus wasn’t on Saul; it was on God. He didn’t need to knock someone else down to keep himself safe, because the one who had set him up was God, not himself.

This is humility drawing out humility, so that both sides win. Saul lifted his eyes and saw only David, and so he lost everything; David lifted his eyes and saw only Yahweh, and so he gained everything.

(6) A reminder

Saul’s tragedy didn’t begin with killing; it began with listening to a song. A song, a remark, a number, a post — the seeds of comparison are often too small to mention. But if a seed isn’t dealt with, it grows into a tree, the tree bears the fruit of fear, and when the fruit falls, it is separation.

So we have to deal with it at the seed stage. And that is exactly what the lesson’s first practice asks us to do.

sections.heading: 7. Key Point 5: Today’s Church Often Falls into the Trap of Comparison Too
sections.html:
The lesson very honestly turns the mirror on us. It lists three common situations.

(1) Small churches fear that big churches will steal their people

They worry that their members will be lured away by a big church’s programmes, venue and choir. So now and then things are said from the pulpit that sound like reminders but are really defence.

(2) Big churches fear that small churches will be a burden

They worry about too many needs, resources being divided, being tied down by responsibilities. So they politely keep their distance, and cooperation never gets past “let’s wait and see”.

(3) Denominations separate from one another

Over differences in speaking in tongues, worship style, views of the end times, church government and how often to take Communion, they separate from one another, refuse to cooperate, and even attack each other.

The lesson puts its finger right on it: behind these actions that look like “standing for pure faith” lies, in fact, the fear and insecurity brought on by “comparison” that has never been dealt with.

Brothers and sisters, please don’t misunderstand me. Pure faith must be held fast, the boundaries of truth must be clear, and heresy must be discerned. For the truth of the gospel, the apostle Paul once opposed Cephas to his face (Galatians 2:11). But we must honestly ask ourselves one question: is my insistence this time really for the truth, or for saving face? Is it to guard God’s glory, or to guard my position?

Telling the difference isn’t actually hard. Someone who separates for the sake of truth feels sorrow in their heart; someone who separates because of comparison feels a thrill. When we hear that another church has run into trouble, if a flicker of relief crosses our heart, that is a warning sign.

Paul says, “Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.” (Romans 12:15) This verse is the best thermometer for testing separation. When others are honoured, can I be genuinely glad? When others fall, can my heart genuinely ache?

“When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.” (1 Corinthians 12:26)

(4) An example from nature

California’s redwoods are the tallest trees on earth, growing to more than a hundred metres. You’d expect trees that tall to have very deep taproots, but the truth is quite the opposite: redwood roots are shallow, usually only two or three metres deep, yet they spread out sideways for tens of metres, tightly intertwined with the roots of the redwoods beside them. A redwood standing alone would fall in a strong wind; a redwood forest, holding hands, stands even against a hurricane.

Brothers and sisters, the church is a redwood forest. We can stand tall not because each of us has rooted deeply on our own, but because we are tightly bound to one another.

Geese are the same. In 1970, Lissaman and Shollenberger published an aerodynamic analysis in the journal Science showing that birds flying in V formation, by using the upwash from the wingtips of the companion ahead, can increase the flock’s range by as much as 71 per cent compared with flying alone. The lead goose works hardest, so they take turns; the geese behind keep honking to encourage those in front.

God has already written his purpose into his creatures: fly together, and you fly far.

(5) Applying 321

321 says the Goal is to establish God’s system. A system is not an institution; it is a network of relationships. Satan has his system too, and it runs on comparison, competition and fear; God’s system runs on humility, connection and love.

Every time we choose not to compare, choose to draw near, choose to bless, we are dismantling Satan’s system and establishing God’s system.

The psalm says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1) The psalm goes on to say that it is like the precious oil on the head, like the dew of Hermon, “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (Psalm 133:3)

Brothers and sisters, the place where the blessing is commanded is “there” — where brothers live together in unity. If you leave that place, the blessing won’t run after you.

sections.heading: 8. Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness, from Comparison to Unity
sections.html:
(1) The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

Jesus is my role model. In relationships, Jesus’ role model is to set up no walls, set no limits and take the initiative to draw near. He chose not the palace but the manger, not the throne but the cross.

The Bible is my standard. When the voice of comparison speaks up, we don’t take our feelings as the standard; we take God’s word as the standard: “But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.” (2 Corinthians 10:12)

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Unity isn’t something people squeeze out by effort. Paul says, “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” (Ephesians 4:3) Notice that it is the unity “of the Spirit” — given by the Spirit; our responsibility is not to manufacture unity but to “keep” it.

Let Jesus be King. Saul’s problem, in the end, was that he would not let God be King; he wanted to be king himself. Everyone who makes himself king sees other people as rivals.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. When all the glory goes to him, we don’t have to scramble for the few crumbs that could never go round anyway. If the glory goes to me, there’s never enough to share; if the glory goes to the Lord, there’s always enough.

Establish God’s system. God’s system is a system without separation, a family where people care for one another and build one another up.

(2) The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

Comparison is the self-centred life’s most honest confession. Someone who is still comparing is saying: my worth needs other people falling behind to prove it.

But the new self in Christ doesn’t have to live like that. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Brothers and sisters, if the “I” has already been crucified, who is left who needs to win?

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. When you no longer need to prove yourself, you are truly free for the first time.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Saul wanted to take God’s place in deciding who would be king, and so he destroyed himself; David let God be God, and so God lifted him up.

(3) The fivefold change

Change the mindset, and the life changes; change the life, and daily living changes; change daily living, and relationships change; change relationships, and ministry changes.

You can’t deal with comparison by starting with behaviour; you have to start with mindset. If deep down you still believe “my worth depends on my ranking”, however hard you suppress envy, it will still break out through some other crack. The mindset must change first: my worth has been set by Jesus with his precious blood, not by other people’s results.

(4) A shift of perspective

From the human perspective to God’s: what Saul heard was a league table; what God saw was a servant after his own heart.

From the earthly perspective to the heavenly: on earth there is only one seat at the top; in heaven a seat is prepared for every overcomer.

From the temporary perspective to the eternal: thousands and tens of thousands of battle honours will be forgotten in thirty years; but the step you take today towards someone you feel distant from will remain in eternity.

From the worldly perspective to the godly: the world says you only have worth if you beat others; God says that in Christ you are already loved.

(5) The 920 practice and the 235 relationship

The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. This week, whoever God places beside you is your “2”. And the way to practise is to live out the selfless “0” — laying yourself down and letting the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice: not one of these nine graces grows in separation. Patience needs someone to be patient with; kindness needs someone to be kind to; peace needs someone to be at peace with. God has placed that person who makes you uncomfortable beside you not to torment you, but to bear fruit in you.

The 235 relationship: become a “2” with someone who is selfless, as spiritual companions; establish a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Ecclesiastes says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10)

Comparison turns us into one person on our own; connection makes us two, three, a fivefold team. Satan wants you on your own, because someone on their own is the easiest to deal with.

sections.heading: 9. Putting It into Practice: Training a Mindset That Removes Separation
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very concrete practices. Let’s work them through thoroughly using 321’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Notice the seeds of comparison

This week, watch whether you are comparing yourself with others without realising it: comparing work, gifts, service, achievements, families, churches.

Whenever you catch yourself thinking this way, say to the Lord: “Lord, I won’t look at people, and I won’t look at myself; I will see only you!”

Information: first accept a fact — comparison is a human instinct, not a sign that you are especially bad. Festinger’s 1954 social comparison theory has already shown that people naturally use those around them as a ruler.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light so you can see where you are most prone to compare. Usually that is the area where you feel least secure.

Conviction: believe God’s word over your feelings — “But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.” (2 Corinthians 10:12)

Implementation: this week, carry a small card or open a page in your phone’s notes; every time a comparing thought arises, make a mark and immediately say that declaration.

Evaluation: at the weekend, look at that page. What do you compare most — ability, appearance, achievement, or other people’s praise?

Correction: for the item that comes up most, find a verse of God’s word and memorise it; tomorrow morning, read that verse before you switch on your phone.

Repetition: not for a week, but for a lifetime. Lifting your eyes is a single movement, yet you have to keep doing it all your life.

Multiplication: tell a spiritual companion about this practice, and do it together, checking in with each other.

Practice 2: Stop spreading words of comparison

When we keep repeating things like “Such-and-such church is amazing,” “Look, he’s better than you,” or “Why can’t we measure up to others?”, these words not only trap us in comparison but also push others into fear and competition.

This week, practise turning words like these into: “God has a different plan and a different grace for every person and every church.”

Information: words have power. “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21)

Revelation: listen to your own mouth. When you praise one child, do you casually put down another? When you praise one church, do you casually take a swipe at your own?

Conviction: believe that one sentence from me can plant fear in someone’s heart — or plant a blessing there.

Implementation: this week, make a rule — never give praise that compares two people. If you praise, praise someone on their own; if you correct, correct someone on their own.

Evaluation: every night before bed, ask one question: did the words I spoke today draw people closer or push them away?

Correction: if you got it wrong, go back the next day and add a sincere word of blessing.

Repetition: keep it up for thirty days in a row, until the new way of speaking becomes a habit.

Multiplication: share it in your small group and invite everyone to make this commitment together.

Practice 3: Take the initiative to connect with someone you feel “distant” from

This week, choose someone you have drifted away from because of a misunderstanding, a difference of opinion or comparison, and take one step towards reconciliation: send a message to say hello, invite them for a coffee, or pray for them and bless them.

The lesson says: being one with others is the greatest weapon for defeating Satan’s scheme of separation.

Information: the Lord says, “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” (Matthew 5:23–24) The Lord didn’t say to wait until you feel like it; he said go first.

Revelation: be still for three minutes and let the Holy Spirit place a name on your heart. The first name that comes to mind is usually the one.

Conviction: believe that the one who takes the initiative is not the loser but the overcomer.

Implementation: send that message today. Don’t explain the past; just say hello to the present. A simple “How are you doing these days? I thought of you and prayed for you” is enough.

Evaluation: the other person may respond warmly, or coolly, or not at all. Either way, you have taken down the wall on your side.

Correction: if the first step is too big, make it smaller; if the timing isn’t right, pray first and try again in a month.

Repetition: reach out to one person every month, and in a year twelve walls will have come down.

Multiplication: when you have tasted the joy of reconciliation, tell others about it, so they too find the courage to take that step.

A Gentle Reminder: Comparison looks at people; faith looks at Jesus

The lesson ends with this reminder: when we take our eyes off people and turn from competition to Christ, we discover that in Christ we have long since received grace, been loved and been accepted, and we don’t need comparison to prove ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, this is our theme verse: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call: Choose Unity, and You Are Walking the Road of Revival
sections.html:
The lesson’s conclusion is weighty, and it is right: the church is not an arena; it is God’s family.

The rule of the arena is: if someone wins, someone has to lose. The rule of the family is: when one does well, the whole family does well.

If we separate because of comparison, we give Satan an opening and rob God’s family of its power. A divided army is defeated before the enemy lifts a finger.

So the lesson calls us: let us learn to be like Jesus, willing to take the initiative to draw near to anyone at all, regardless of status, setting up no barriers. Let us accept one another, build one another up, and become vessels of unity in God’s hands.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to give you three calls.

First, let Jesus be King. No longer let comparison be king, no longer let fear be king, no longer let “I have to win” be king. Hand the throne back to the Lord who alone is worthy of it.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. When someone else is lifted up and you can say in your heart, “Amen, may the glory go to the Lord,” in that moment you have already overcome.

Third, lift up your eyes. Today, right now, take your eyes off the person who unsettles you and raise your head — see no one, except Jesus alone.

Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, running continuously since 1938, has followed several hundred men throughout their lives, tracking their health and happiness. Its director, Professor Robert Waldinger, has distilled more than eighty years of findings into one sentence: good relationships keep us happier and healthier. Not wealth, not fame, not rankings.

God wrote this truth into Genesis long ago: “Yahweh God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone.’” (Genesis 2:18)

Brothers and sisters, it is not good to be alone. Unity is good.

Let us make the lesson’s declaration of faith together: Lord Jesus, I will not let comparison separate me; I choose unity, to bear witness to your love and your glory!

keyVerses: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
practices: Notice the seeds of comparison
Stop spreading words of comparison
Reach out to someone you feel “distant” from
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You came not to rebuke us, but to restore our relationship with God and with others. You broke down the dividing wall; you chose the manger rather than the palace; you reached out and touched the one no one else dared to touch. Lord, you are our role model.

Lord, we confess that there is comparison in us. We compare our work, our gifts, our service, our achievements, our families, our churches. Comparison makes us anxious, anxiety makes us afraid, and fear makes us draw back step by step, building one invisible wall after another. Please forgive us.
Take Saul’s eyes away from us and give us David’s heart — not looking at people, not looking at ourselves, but looking to you alone.
Holy Spirit, shine your light on us, and show us the name of the one we have drawn away from; and give us courage to take a step towards reconciliation today.

Lord, we hand the throne to you. Reign as King, and receive all the glory. Use us in our families, our churches and our workplaces as vessels of unity, as people who tear down walls, to establish God’s system.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: “For we are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.” (2 Corinthians 10:12) Please share honestly: what was the most recent comparison that left you feeling uneasy? Underneath that unease, what was the real fear?

Question 2: “Therefore Saul removed him from his presence, and made him his captain over a thousand; and he went out and came in before the people.” (1 Samuel 18:13) Saul accomplished separation by “promotion”. In your own life, is there a relationship where you are keeping your distance in some respectable way? What concrete action are you willing to take this week to make the first step towards reconciliation?
l017.title: Comparison Brings Separation
l017.subtitle: Why Separation Happens (Part 1)
l017.partTitle: Unit 2 · Jesus — The Focus of Revival

blog.title: The Wall That Began with One Comparison

blocks.x: Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 17 · Blog Post

A couple who had been married for more than twenty years came to see their pastor. They hadn’t been fighting or throwing things; they sat at either end of the sofa with an empty seat between them. The wife said, “We haven’t had a proper conversation in three months.” The husband, head bowed, added, “Actually, we see each other every day. It’s just that we stopped living in the same house a long time ago.”
The greatest distance between two people has never been the ends of the earth; it is two people sitting right next to each other while their hearts draw back, inch by inch.
The Bible has a name for this drawing back. It is called “separation”.
Separation is not neutral

Separation is quiet. It isn’t fierce like an argument or glaring like a betrayal. It simply makes you reply to one message fewer, go to one meeting fewer, speak one honest word fewer. By the time you come to your senses, that invisible wall has already been built high and thick.

The Lord Jesus said: “The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10) What Satan steals is our unity; what he kills is our relationships; what he destroys is God’s purpose that we should “all be one”.

Paul says: “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.” (1 Corinthians 12:27) A finger separated from the hand doesn’t become freer; within minutes it begins to die. Because life isn’t in the finger; life is in the body.

In 2010 the psychologist Julianne Holt-Lunstad combined 148 studies and more than three hundred thousand participants, and found that people with strong social connections had about a 50 per cent higher likelihood of survival than those who lacked them. Science is only saying again, with data, what the Bible said long ago: the final result of separation is not independence; it is death.
The first cause is comparison
So how does separation begin?
Usually with comparison. Comparison makes us anxious, anxiety makes us afraid, and fear makes us draw back. Comparison, fear, separation — this is Satan’s favourite three-step routine.

King Saul was fond of David at first. Until the day the women sang: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” (1 Samuel 18:7) To be fair, this song was praising Saul. But he didn’t take in a word of it. He heard only one thing: David’s number is bigger than mine.

The Bible goes on to say that Saul watched David with a hostile eye, that Saul was afraid of David, and “therefore Saul removed him from his presence, and made him his captain over a thousand”. He didn’t drive David away; he promoted him. On the surface it was a vote of confidence; in reality it was a transfer.

How much separation is accomplished in this respectable way? I haven’t fallen out with you; I just don’t consult you any more. I haven’t kicked you out; I’ve just moved you to another group. The words of separation are often very polite, but the results of separation never are.

The church is the same. Small churches fear that big churches will steal their people; big churches fear that small churches will be a burden; denominations separate from one another over worship styles and differences of belief. Behind these actions that look like “standing for pure faith” often lies the fear and insecurity brought on by comparison that has never been dealt with.
Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one
This lesson’s theme verse is just one sentence: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

On the Mount of Transfiguration, Peter was eager to make three tents. Three tents means three positions; three positions means a league table. God blew the league table away with a single sentence: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” When the disciples raised their heads again, only Jesus remained.

Comparison looks at people; faith looks at Jesus. When we take our eyes off people and turn to Christ, we discover that in Christ we have long since received grace, been loved and been accepted, and we don’t need comparison to prove ourselves at all.

This week, why not try three small things? First, notice the seeds of comparison: whenever a comparing thought arises, say to the Lord, “I won’t look at people, and I won’t look at myself; I will see only you.” Second, stop spreading words of comparison, and say instead, “God has a different plan and a different grace for every person.” Third, choose someone you feel distant from, and send them a greeting, invite them for a coffee, or quietly pray for them and bless them.
The church is not an arena; it is God’s family. The rule of the arena is: if someone wins, someone has to lose. The rule of the family is: when one does well, the whole family does well.
Choose unity, and you are walking the road of revival.
Reflection question: If you were still for three minutes right now, whose name would the Holy Spirit place on your heart? This week, what one concrete thing will you do for that person?
