blog.title: The Wall Came Down — Is the One in Your Heart Still Standing?

blocks.x: Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 19 · Tearing Down the Wall of Self-Centredness

In the small hours of 13 August 1961, the people of Berlin went to sleep as usual. When day broke, there was a barbed-wire fence running down the middle of their streets. The same city, the same people — cut in two overnight. Later the barbed wire became concrete, a wall 3.6 metres high and 155 kilometres long, and it stood for twenty-eight years.

On 9 November 1989 the wall fell, and the whole world cheered in front of their television sets. But the Germans coined a phrase of their own: “the wall in the head.” Concrete can be knocked down in a few months; the wall in people’s hearts is one no bulldozer can shift.
Every separation you can see on the outside was first built on the inside.
Three bricks, one word
Lesson 19 of Morning Devotion 321 continues our look at why separation happens. We have already seen comparison, suspicion and unforgiveness; this lesson looks at three more.

The first is self-interest. The world says, “In business there are no permanent friends, only permanent interests.” The saying moved from diplomacy into business, and from business it has quietly moved into the family and the church. Siblings fall out over a plot of land, marriages grow cold through self-protection, small groups quarrel over position. The root isn’t in our circumstances. James puts it bluntly: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1). The word “war” in the original means to encamp, to draw up in battle array — the battlefield isn’t the meeting room; it is inside us.

The second is accusation. The name “Satan” means adversary, accuser; Revelation calls him the one “who accuses them before our God day and night.” So when we count up a brother’s faults day and night, whose shift are we working? When Jesus faced the woman thrown down in the middle of the crowd, the one person there who had every right to pick up a stone was the one person who didn’t. He said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more” (John 8:11). His order is: first forgiveness, then change; first acceptance, then teaching. We so often reverse it.

The third is looking at others through a magnifying glass and at ourselves through a flattering filter. Psychology recorded it long ago: we explain other people’s failures by their character and our own by our circumstances. In 1977 the social psychologist Lee Ross called it the “fundamental attribution error.” The Lord Jesus said it earlier and more weightily: “First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.” He didn’t say, “Never mind the speck in your brother’s eye.” He spoke about the order.
Three causes, three roads, all leading to one word — “self.”
We are different precisely so that we can work together

California’s coast redwoods can grow to more than a hundred metres, yet their roots go down only two or three metres. How can such shallow roots stand against the wind? Because redwoods never grow alone. Underground, their roots intertwine into a web; the whole grove stands hand in hand.

The church is the same. Paul says, “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you.’” The eye and the hand can need each other precisely because they are different. If the whole body were an eye, it wouldn’t be a body; it would be a heap of eyes.

So 321’s 920 practice says: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; in front of them we practise living out the selfless life and bearing the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Notice that every one of these nine graces needs an “other person” in order to grow. Patience needs someone difficult to get along with; gentleness needs someone who makes you angry. That brother you don’t quite get along with isn’t your obstacle; he’s your training ground.
Three actions for this week

1. Recognise the motive of self-interest. Think of a strained relationship and honestly ask: Do I care too much about my own interests? Am I unwilling to give up even a little of my sovereignty? Am I only willing to associate with people who are useful to me?

2. Put down the stone, pick up the rope. Three don’ts: don’t condemn, don’t gossip, don’t judge by your own standards. Three do’s: cover with love, build up with words, support with action. We don’t need more hands of judgement; we need more shoulders like Barnabas’s.
3. Appreciate someone you “don’t quite get along with”: list three of their strengths, and tell them one to their face.
The root of separation lies not in the differences between people, but in whether “self” takes first place in our hearts. Unity isn’t forced endurance; it is a decision made out of love.

The disciples experienced this moment on the mountain: Moses withdrew, Elijah withdrew, Peter’s plans withdrew. Scripture says, “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).
They saw no one — not my interests, not other people’s faults, not my own superiority. Jesus alone — he is King, and he receives all the glory.
Reflection question: This week, whose name stands on the other side of the wall in your heart? Which specific interest, standard or comment are you willing to lay down first?

notes: Tearing Down the Wall of Self-Centredness
Self-Interest, Accusation and Fault-Finding
“They saw no one, except Jesus alone”
Matthew 17:8
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 19
Greet the brothers and sisters and introduce today’s theme: separation is Satan’s scheme; unity is Jesus’ mission.
Explain that this lesson covers the fourth, fifth and sixth causes in the series “Why Separation Happens”: self-interest, accusation and fault-finding.
Read the theme verse, Matthew 17:8, stressing that “they saw no one, except Jesus alone” is the answer to the whole lesson.
Preview: all three causes share one root — “self”; live self-centred and there is a wall; live selfless and the wall falls.
Walls are built from the inside
The Berlin Wall stood for 28 years
Concrete comes down; the heart’s wall is harder
Isolation raises the risk of death by half
Separation is Satan’s scheme
Tell the Berlin Wall story: built overnight on 13 August 1961, fallen on 9 November 1989 — twenty-eight years.
Point out the German phrase “the wall in the head”: concrete can be removed in months; the wall in people’s hearts can’t.
Cite the data: Julianne Holt-Lunstad’s 2010 meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine — 148 studies, over 300,000 people; those with weak social connections had about a 50 per cent higher risk of death.
Compare the Harvard Study of Adult Development (begun 1938): the quality of relationships predicts happiness in later life.
Back to the Bible: Genesis 2:18, “It is not good for the man to be alone”; in Genesis 3:5 Satan creates separation.
That moment on the mountain: only one remained
Peter wanted three tents; the Lord wants one
“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”
“Listen to him” Matthew 17:5
All else withdraws — Jesus alone
The author, Matthew, was formerly a tax collector in Capernaum (Matthew 9:9) — himself someone who had been shut out.
Context: Matthew 16:16, Peter’s confession; 16:23, the Lord’s rebuke, “Get behind me, Satan!”; 16:24, “let him deny himself.”
Six days later, the Transfiguration; Peter offers to make three tents (Matthew 17:4) — zealously arranging the Lord’s place for him is the self-centred life.
The cloud overshadows them, and the Father says only one thing: listen to him (Matthew 17:5).
Greek μόνον (only): they saw no one, except Jesus himself alone.
Self-interest · selfish desire · separation
No permanent friends, only interests
Inheritance, coldness, position, gifts
“Your pleasures that war in your members”
James 4:1
Quote Lord Palmerston’s speech to Parliament on 1 March 1848: no eternal allies, only eternal interests.
The lesson’s four scenes: siblings fighting over an inheritance, marriages growing cold, small groups fighting over position, churches dividing over compared gifts.
Read James 4:1–2 in full: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?”
Original words: pleasures, ἡδονή (enjoyment); war, στρατεύομαι (to encamp, draw up for battle) — selfish desire has pitched camp in our members.
The Pharisee’s prayer (Luke 18:11): it opens with “God,” but its whole content is “I.”
Self-centred, a wall; selfless, it falls
“Let him deny himself, and take up his cross”
Matthew 16:24
Christ emptied himself, taking a servant’s form
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
The Prisoner’s Dilemma: devised in 1950 by Flood and Dresher at RAND, named by Tucker; when each seeks his own advantage, both end up worse off.
321: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Use the picture of two goats on a narrow log bridge.
Deny, ἀπαρνέομαι in the original: say to the old self, “I don’t know you.”
Galatians 2:20: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; selflessness is entering into fullness.
Philippians 2:5–8, emptied himself, κενόω (to empty out); 2:3–4, each counting others better than himself.
Accusation · condemnation · separation
Satan’s very name means “accuser”
“Accuses them before our God day and night”
Revelation 12:10
When we speak, whose shift are we working?
Hebrew שָׂטָן (satan) means adversary, accuser; Greek διάβολος means slanderer, one who tears apart.
Read Revelation 12:10 and point out that accusation is Satan’s job description.
Contrast Romans 8:33–34: there are two voices in heaven — one accuses day and night, the other intercedes day and night.
Ask: when we count up a brother’s faults day and night, whose shift are we working?
Facing someone who has done wrong, do we want to lift him up, or distance ourselves from him?
Put down the stone, pick up the rope
“Neither do I condemn you. Go your way”
John 8:11
Forgive, then change; accept, then teach
Not hands of judgement — Barnabas’s shoulders
Tell John 8:1–11: Jesus says, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her,” and they leave one by one, beginning with the oldest.
The one person there who had every right to pick up a stone was the one person who didn’t.
The order: first forgiveness, then change; first acceptance, then teaching. We so often get it backwards.
John 3:17: not to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him; Luke 15:2, sharing a table is a sign of acceptance.
Galatians 6:1, restore, καταρτίζω (mend nets, set bones); Barnabas takes in Saul (Acts 9:26–27).
Gottman’s research: of the Four Horsemen, “contempt” best predicts divorce, and “stonewalling” is separation itself.
A magnifying glass for others, a filter for me
“First remove the beam out of your own eye”
Matthew 7:5
Others by character, myself by circumstance
One event, two rulers
The lesson’s three attitudes: feeling others aren’t as good as me, being unable to stand someone’s personality, being unwilling to work with people who think differently.
Original words: speck, κάρφος, a wood chip; beam, δοκός, a roof timber — a carpenter’s humour.
The Lord didn’t say, “Never mind your brother’s speck”; he spoke about the order: first remove your own beam, and then you can see clearly.
The fundamental attribution error, named by Lee Ross in 1977: others by character, ourselves by circumstance.
The better-than-average effect: Ola Svenson’s 1981 study in Acta Psychologica found about 88 per cent of American drivers surveyed rated themselves above the median.
Different, so that we can work together
“The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you’”
1 Corinthians 12:21
Redwoods: shallow roots, standing intertwined
920: bear ninefold fruit with every “2”
Read 1 Corinthians 12:20–21 in full: “But now they are many members, but one body. The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you.’”
1 Corinthians 12:22, the weaker members are necessary; 12:25–26, members caring for one another, suffering together, rejoicing together.
Redwoods grow over a hundred metres tall with roots only two or three metres deep, standing because their roots intertwine into a web.
Geese in a V: Lissaman and Shollenberger’s 1970 analysis in Science — twenty-five birds could gain about 70 per cent more range.
The 920 practice: everyone we relate to is our “2”; practise selflessness and bear the nine fruits of Galatians 5:22–23; then go on to 235 relationships.
Three steps to tear down the wall
Recognise the motive of self-interest
Put down the stone, pick up the rope
Appreciate someone you don’t get along with
Eight stages: Implementation, Evaluation, Correction
Practice 1: reflect on a strained relationship and ask three questions — too concerned with my interests? Unwilling to give up sovereignty? Only mixing with useful people?
Practice 2: three don’ts — don’t condemn, don’t gossip, don’t judge by your own standards; three do’s — cover with love, build up with words, support with action (Ephesians 4:29).
Practice 3: list three of that person’s strengths, and tell them one to their face.
Go deeper with the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Reminder: three minutes each evening to review — did I pick up a stone today, or a rope?
From self at the centre to Christ
Unity isn’t endurance; it’s a decision of love
“They saw no one, except Jesus alone”
Matthew 17:8
Let Jesus be King; all glory to him
Back to Berlin: the wall fell, but the wall in the head remained. We have three bricks in our hearts, each stamped with “self.”
The lesson’s conclusion: the root of separation lies not in our differences, but in whether “self” takes first place in our hearts.
Unity isn’t forced endurance; it is a decision made out of love.
Psalm 133:1: how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity.
Call: lift up your eyes — put down interests, put down stones, put down the magnifying glass; let Jesus be King, all glory to him.
Response Prayer and Blessing
Lord, I lay myself down; be the centre
Make me one with others, a witness to you
“How good it is for brothers to live in unity”
Psalm 133:1
Lead the brothers and sisters in a response prayer together: confess the walls in our hearts, and ask the Lord to change me first, not others first.
Ask the Holy Spirit to shine on the beam in our own eye, and the Lord to give gentle hearts to restore our brothers.
Declare together the lesson’s declaration of faith: Lord, I lay myself down; may you become the centre.
Blessing: may the Lord make us children of peace and vessels of unity; may the glory go to Jesus.

What the Germans call “the wall in the head”: no bulldozer can push it over.
Bring it close to home: a couple under one roof who don’t talk, brothers in court over an inheritance, a small group that nods at the door but detours in the heart.

Isolation raises the risk of death by about half

“It is not good for the man to be alone” Genesis 2:18

Genesis 2:18 is the first “not good” since creation.
In Eden Satan first created separation: Genesis 3:5 made people suspicious of God, and then Adam shifted the blame to Eve.
Recap the first three causes — comparison, suspicion, unforgiveness; today we look at the fourth, fifth and sixth.

Peter wanted three tents; the Lord wants one
“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”

Greek μόνον: Jesus alone

Generally dated AD 50–70, written for Jewish Christians; its theme is “Jesus is King.”
Context: Matthew 16:16, the confession; 16:23, “Get behind me, Satan!”; 16:24, “let him deny himself.”
Six days later, the Transfiguration; Moses stands for the Law, Elijah for the Prophets; Peter’s three tents (17:4) are zealous self-centredness.
The cloud overshadows them, and the Father says only, “Listen to him”; the result is 17:8 — they saw no one, except Jesus alone.

No permanent friends, only interests
Siblings at odds, marriages gone cold
Groups fight for position; gifts become rulers
It starts not outside, but inside
Quote Lord Palmerston’s speech to Parliament on 1 March 1848: no eternal allies and no perpetual enemies, only eternal interests.
The lesson’s four scenes: siblings falling out over an inheritance, a marriage growing cold, a small group quarrelling over position, a church dividing over compared gifts.
Stress: not one of these four begins with outward circumstances; every one begins on the inside.
Ask the brothers and sisters: which of these four scenes is closest to you?
Selfish desire pitches its camp within us
“Your pleasures that war in your members”
James 4:1
Pleasures, ἡδονή: “make me happy” above all
War, στρατεύομαι: encamp, draw up for battle
Read James 4:1–2 in full: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?”
ἡδονή means pleasure, the root of the English word hedonism; when “make me happy” becomes the highest rule, the war begins.
The root of στρατεύομαι is “army”; it means to encamp — the battlefield isn’t the meeting room; it is inside us.
James 4:2b: “You don’t have, because you don’t ask.” Fighting is relying on ourselves; asking is relying on God.
321: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you rejoice; rely on the brain and ourselves, and you worry.

“God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men”
Luke 18:11
“They all seek their own” Philippians 2:21
First mark of the last days: lovers of self
The Pharisee’s prayer opens with “God,” but its whole content is “I”; he stood in the temple, but his eyes were on other people.
Luke 15:2: they murmured, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them”; in Middle Eastern culture, sharing a table is a sign of acceptance and covenant.
Philippians 2:21 is Paul’s sigh late in life.
2 Timothy 3:2 lists nineteen marks of end-time corruption, and the first is “lovers of self,” φίλαυτοι in the original — those who love themselves.
321: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.
From self-centred to selfless
“Let him deny himself, and take up his cross”
Matthew 16:24
Christ emptied himself, taking a servant’s form
Count others better than yourself · Philippians 2:3
The Prisoner’s Dilemma: devised in 1950 by Flood and Dresher at RAND, named by Princeton’s Tucker; when each seeks his own advantage, both end up worse off.
321: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. The picture of two goats on a narrow log bridge.
Deny, ἀπαρνέομαι in the original: the very word used when Peter denied the Lord — say to the old self, “I don’t know you.”
Galatians 2:20: no longer I, but Christ lives in me; selflessness is entering into fullness, like a cup of water poured into the ocean.
Philippians 2:5–8, emptied himself, κενόω (to empty out); life first, then relationships, then ministry — people matter more than tasks.
5. Accusation is Satan’s line of work
Satan, שָׂטָן: adversary, accuser
“Accuses them before our God day and night”
Revelation 12:10
Two voices in heaven: accusing and interceding
Hebrew שָׂטָן means adversary, accuser; Greek διάβολος means slanderer, one who tears apart.
Read Revelation 12:10: “the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them before our God day and night.”
Ask: when we count up a brother’s faults day and night and spread word of his failures, whose shift are we working?
Romans 8:33–34: Christ is at the right hand of God, and also makes intercession for us.
Every day, when we open our mouths, we are choosing whether to join the side that accuses or the side that intercedes.
Neither do I condemn you
“He who is without sin, let him throw the first stone”
John 8:7
“Neither do I condemn you. Go your way”
John 8:11
Describe the scene in John 8:1–11: stones in their hands, the law on their lips; what they wanted wasn’t justice but to trap Jesus.
They left one by one, beginning with the oldest — the longer you’ve lived, the better you know your own hands aren’t clean.
The one person there who had every right to pick up a stone was the one person who didn’t.
Condemn, κατακρίνω in the original, means to pass sentence; the Lord didn’t say, “You have no sin” — he said, “Neither do I condemn you,” then, “sin no more.”
The order: first forgiveness, then change; first acceptance, then teaching; John 3:17 — not to judge the world.
Judging is a usurpation
“Who are you who judge another’s servant?”
Romans 14:4
Only one is the lawgiver · James 4:12
“No condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus”
Romans 14:4: to his own lord he stands or falls.
James 4:11–12: only one is the lawgiver and judge; who are you to judge another?
321: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position.
Romans 8:1: there is now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus — we ourselves are people who have been forgiven.
Optionally cite Matthew 18:23–35: someone let off ten thousand talents has no business seizing a fellow servant who owes a hundred denarii.
Put down the stone, pick up the rope
“Restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness”
Galatians 6:1
Restore, καταρτίζω: mend nets, set bones
Only Barnabas took him in · Acts 9:27
Galatians 6:1: those who are spiritual restore in a spirit of gentleness, looking to themselves.
In Matthew 4:21 καταρτίζω is “mending” nets; in medicine it means setting a dislocated bone back in place.
Barnabas took in Saul (Acts 9:26–27) and later insisted on taking Mark (Acts 15:37–39); in 2 Timothy 4:11 Paul says Mark is useful to him.
Gottman and Levenson’s marriage research: of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, “contempt” best predicts divorce, and “stonewalling” is separation itself.
Mother Teresa is generally credited with saying: if you judge people, you have no time to love them. The church is a hospital, not a courtroom.

Others are never quite good enough
I can’t stand their personality or ways
I won’t work with people who think differently
Sentence by sentence, a wall goes up

“First remove the beam out of your own eye”
Matthew 7:5

Geese in a V: Lissaman and Shollenberger’s 1970 analysis in Science — twenty-five birds could gain about 70 per cent more range; not one had stronger wings, they were simply in the right position.

Bonhoeffer, Life Together: whoever loves his dream of community more than the real community will end up destroying it.

Read the nine fruits of Galatians 5:22–23; point out that each one needs an “other person” in order to grow.
The person you don’t quite get along with isn’t an obstacle; he’s a training ground.
235 relationships: spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades; the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Am I unwilling to give up any sovereignty?
Do I only mix with people who are useful?
Lord, for your sake I lay myself down

Link to the first three of the eight stages: Information (what we learned today), Revelation (the Spirit pointing to a particular face), Conviction (no longer defending myself).

Three do’s: cover, build up, support

Practice 3: deliberately observe someone you tend to criticise, list three strengths, and tell them one to their face.
Repetition and Multiplication: keep changing the way you see; take someone with you to practise — one person tearing down their wall is salvation; a whole group tearing down walls is revival.
321 summary: no one, but Jesus alone
Three causes, one root: self
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan
Let Jesus be King and receive all the glory
Trade the earthly and temporary for the eternal
Self-interest puts my advantage at the centre; accusation puts me on the judgement seat; fault-finding makes me the standard.
The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.
The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; the Goal: establish God’s system.
Shifts of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly.
The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the order can’t be skipped.

Matthew 17:8
