script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re reading Lesson 19 together: Tearing Down the Wall of Self-Centredness. These are the fourth, fifth and sixth causes of “Why Separation Happens”: self-interest, accusation and fault-finding. Separation is Satan’s scheme; unity is Jesus’ mission. Let me put today’s answer right at the start — it’s our theme verse: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” Matthew 17:8. Brothers and sisters, remember this line: they saw no one, except Jesus alone.

In the small hours of 13 August 1961, a barbed-wire fence appeared in the middle of Berlin’s streets. The same city, the same people — cut in two overnight. That wall stood for twenty-eight years. But the Germans tell us that after the wall fell, there was another one even harder to tear down: “the wall in the head.” Brothers and sisters, every separation you can see on the outside was first built on the inside. How high is the cost of separation? A 2010 analysis pooling 148 studies and more than 300,000 people found that those with weak social connections had roughly a 50 per cent higher risk of death. God said it long ago: “It is not good for the man to be alone.”

Let’s go up the mountain and watch a scene. After six days, Jesus took three disciples up a high mountain, and Moses and Elijah appeared. Peter said: Lord, I’ll make three tents — one for you, one for Moses, one for Elijah. It sounds very devout, but in fact it reduces the Lord to one-third and puts his own arrangements above the Lord’s plan. That is the self-centred life. How did God respond? The cloud came down, and a voice said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” Then the disciples lifted up their eyes — and saw no one, except Jesus alone. Brothers and sisters, when everything else has withdrawn, the one who remains is everything.

The fourth cause: self-interest. The world says, “In business there are no permanent friends, only permanent interests.” That saying moved from diplomacy into business, and from business it has quietly moved into the family and the church. Siblings fall out over a plot of land, couples grow cold through self-protection, small groups quarrel over position, churches divide over compared gifts. Where’s the root? James says, “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” James 4:1. The word “war” in the original means to encamp, to draw up in battle array. Brothers and sisters, the battlefield isn’t the meeting room; the battlefield is inside us.

So what’s the cure? Not living for yourself a little less, but changing the centre. The Lord said, “let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” Matthew 16:24. The word “deny” in the original is the very word used when Peter denied the Lord — say to the old self: I don’t know you. Paul says: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. Brothers and sisters, selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness. Pour a cup of water into the ocean, and it hasn’t vanished; it has gained the whole ocean. So: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The fifth cause: accusation. Brothers and sisters, accusation isn’t a neutral habit; accusation has a pedigree. The name “Satan” means adversary, accuser. Revelation says, “the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them before our God day and night.” Revelation 12:10. That is Satan’s job description. So let me ask a piercing question: when we count up a brother’s faults day and night, spreading word of his failures everywhere we go, whose shift are we working? There are two voices in heaven: one accuses day and night, the other intercedes day and night. Which side will we join today?

The scribes and Pharisees threw a woman down in the middle, stones in their hands. Jesus said, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.” And they went out one by one, from the oldest to the youngest. Then the Lord said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” John 8:11. Brothers and sisters, the one person there who had every right to pick up a stone was the one person who didn’t. His order is: first forgiveness, then change; first acceptance, then teaching. We don’t need more hands of judgement; we need more shoulders like Barnabas’s.

The sixth cause: looking at others through a magnifying glass and at ourselves through a flattering filter. The Lord Jesus put it vividly: “First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.” Matthew 7:5. A speck is a tiny chip of wood; a beam is the great timber that holds up a whole house. Psychology has found the same thing: we explain other people’s failures by their character, and our own by our circumstances. One event, two rulers. Brothers and sisters, the Lord didn’t say, “Never mind your brother’s speck.” He spoke about the order: deal with yourself first, and then you can see clearly.

God made each of us different precisely so that we would work together. Paul says, “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you.’” 1 Corinthians 12:21. The eye and the hand can need each other precisely because they are different. If the whole body were an eye, it wouldn’t be a body. California’s redwoods can grow a hundred metres tall, yet their roots are only two or three metres deep; they stand because their roots intertwine. Brothers and sisters, this is the 920 practice: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; in front of them we practise selflessness and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. The person you don’t get along with isn’t an obstacle; he’s a training ground.

Now here are this week’s three practices. First, recognise the motive of self-interest: think of a strained relationship and honestly ask yourself — Do I care too much about my own interests? Am I unwilling to give up even a little of my sovereignty? Am I only willing to associate with people who are useful to me? Second, put down the stone and pick up the rope: three don’ts — don’t condemn, don’t gossip, don’t judge by your own standards; three do’s — cover with love, build up with words, support with action. Third, appreciate someone you don’t quite get along with, and list three of their strengths. Then: Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition.

Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to Berlin. The wall fell, but the wall in the head remained. We have walls in our hearts too, and today we’ve seen three of their bricks: self-interest, accusation and fault-finding. Every one of those bricks is stamped with the same word — “self.” The root of separation lies not in the differences between people, but in whether “self” takes first place in our hearts. Unity isn’t forced endurance; it is a decision made out of love. The psalm says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” This morning, let’s lift up our eyes together: put down our interests, put down the stones, put down the magnifying glass.

Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that there are walls in our hearts. We have sacrificed relationships for our own interests; we have picked up stones to condemn our brothers; we have looked at others through a magnifying glass and at ourselves through a flattering filter. Please forgive us. Lord, we don’t ask you to change others first; we ask you to change us first. When I lift up my eyes, may I see no one, but you alone standing there. Let’s declare together: Lord, I lay myself down; may you become the centre; make me one with others, a witness to you! We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus. Amen. May the Lord bless you, and may you be a child of peace today.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re reading Morning Devotion 321, Lesson 19 together: Tearing Down the Wall of Self-Centredness. This lesson covers the fourth, fifth and sixth causes of “Why Separation Happens”: self-interest, accusation and fault-finding. Let’s remember one sentence: separation is Satan’s scheme; unity is Jesus’ mission. Let me put today’s answer right at the start. Our theme verse is Matthew 17:8: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” They saw no one, except Jesus alone — that is the key to tearing down walls.

Let me begin with some history. In the small hours of 13 August 1961, the people of Berlin went to sleep as usual. When day broke, there was a barbed-wire fence running down the middle of their streets. The same city, the same people — cut in two overnight. Later the barbed wire became concrete, a wall 3.6 metres high and 155 kilometres long. It stood for twenty-eight years, until it finally fell on 9 November 1989. But the Germans tell us that what was truly hard to tear down was the wall that remained in people’s hearts after the concrete had gone. They call it “the wall in the head.” Brothers and sisters, a bulldozer can push over concrete, but it can’t push over the human heart.

We don’t need to go to Berlin for examples. A husband and wife under one roof who barely exchange three sentences a day. Brothers who grew up together, now facing each other in court over an inheritance. Brothers and sisters in a small group who nod and smile at the door, while in their hearts they’ve long since taken a detour around each other. A wall doesn’t need concrete; one thought is enough. How high is the cost? A 2010 analysis pooling 148 studies and more than 300,000 people found that those with weak social connections had roughly a 50 per cent higher risk of death. A Harvard study that has followed people for more than eighty years since 1938 found that the best predictor of happiness in later life is the quality of our relationships. In Eden, God had already said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” We’ve already looked at comparison, suspicion and unforgiveness; today we look at three more.

First let’s go up the mountain and watch a scene. Matthew, who wrote this Gospel, had been a tax collector in Capernaum; he himself had once stood on the other side of that wall, and it was Jesus who walked past the tax office and tore the wall down. The Transfiguration follows straight on from chapter 16. Peter had just said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” yet a few verses later he tried to stop the Lord going to the cross, and the Lord said, “Get behind me, Satan!” Then the Lord gave his great summary: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself.” Six days later, the Lord took three disciples up the mountain, and Moses and Elijah appeared. Peter said: Lord, I’ll make three tents — one for you, one for Moses, one for Elijah. It sounds devout, but it reduces the Lord to one-third and puts his own arrangements above the Lord’s plan. How did God respond? The cloud came down, and a voice said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” The disciples lifted up their eyes, and they saw no one, except Jesus alone.

Now let’s look at the fourth cause: self-interest. When someone cares only about what benefits him and pursues only his own advantage, it becomes all too easy to sacrifice relationships and sever unity. People often say, “In business there are no permanent friends, only permanent interests.” The saying is generally traced to the British Prime Minister Lord Palmerston’s speech to Parliament in 1848. It moved from diplomacy into business, and from business it has quietly moved into the family and the church. Siblings fall out over a plot of land, couples grow cold through self-protection, small groups quarrel over position, churches divide over compared gifts. Brothers and sisters, notice this: not one of these four begins with outward circumstances. Every one of them begins on the inside.

James puts it very bluntly: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” James 4:1. The word for “pleasures” in the original means enjoyment; the English word hedonism comes from it. James isn’t saying that having desires is sin. He’s saying that when “make me happy” becomes the highest rule, the war begins. The other word is even more vivid: the root of “war” is the word for “army,” and it means to pitch camp. Brothers and sisters, selfish desire isn’t an occasional visitor; it has pitched its camp among our members. The battlefield isn’t the meeting room; the battlefield is inside us. And James adds: “You don’t have, because you don’t ask.” Fighting is relying on ourselves; asking is relying on God.

The most dangerous self-interest is the kind dressed in the robes of piety. The Lord Jesus recorded the Pharisee’s prayer: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.” Luke 18:11. What makes this prayer so frightening isn’t how wicked it is, but how much it sounds like a prayer. It opens with “God,” but its whole content is “I.” So when Jesus sat at table with tax collectors and sinners, they couldn’t bear it, and murmured: This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them. In Middle Eastern culture, sharing a table is a sign of acceptance and covenant. Jesus chose to sit down; they chose to stand further off. Paul sighed late in life, “For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.” He foretold that in the last days people would be lovers of self — of nineteen marks of corruption, the very first is loving oneself.

Brothers and sisters, where does self-interest end? In 1950 researchers at the RAND Corporation devised a scenario later named the “Prisoner’s Dilemma”: two people are questioned separately; if both stay silent, both get a light sentence; if they betray each other, both get a heavy one. And the most common result? The two betray each other, and both end up worse off than if they had cooperated. That is exactly what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Two goats meet on a narrow log bridge; neither will give way, so both fall in. If one is willing to lie down, both can cross. That’s why the Lord said, “let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” Paul says: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness.

The fifth cause: accusation. Brothers and sisters, accusation isn’t a neutral habit; accusation has a pedigree. The name “Satan” in Hebrew means adversary, accuser. Revelation says, “the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them before our God day and night.” Revelation 12:10. That is Satan’s job description. So let me ask a piercing question: when we count up a brother’s faults day and night, spreading word of his failures everywhere we go, whose shift are we working? By contrast, Scripture says Christ is at the right hand of God, and also makes intercession for us. There are two voices in heaven: one accuses day and night, the other intercedes day and night. Every day, when we open our mouths, we are choosing which side to join.

John chapter 8 records a scene that will never go out of date. The scribes and Pharisees threw a woman down in the middle, stones in their hands and the law on their lips. Jesus said only one thing: “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.” And they went out one by one, from the oldest to the youngest. Why did the oldest leave first? Because the longer you’ve lived, the better you know your own hands aren’t clean. Then the Lord said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” The one person there who had every right to pick up a stone was the one person who didn’t. Notice his order: first forgiveness, then change; first acceptance, then teaching. We so often reverse it — first condemn, and only accept the person once they’ve sorted themselves out. The result: the wall goes up, and the person walks away.

The Bible speaks very seriously about judging, because judging is usurping a position that isn’t ours. Paul says, “Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls.” Romans 14:4. Brothers and sisters, 321 puts it clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. To judge is to climb up onto the judgement seat ourselves, and that seat isn’t ours. What’s more, the gospel declares: there is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus. We ourselves are people who have been forgiven. Someone who has just been let off a debt of ten thousand talents really has no business seizing a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii.

So when we come across a brother who really has done wrong, what should we do? The Bible doesn’t ask us to pretend we haven’t seen it; it gives us a completely different action: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” Galatians 6:1. In the Gospels, this word “restore” is fishermen “mending” their nets; in medicine it means setting a dislocated bone back in place. Not throwing away the torn net, but mending it. And Scripture gives us a living role model: when Saul had just come to faith, all the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of him, and only Barnabas took him in and brought him to the apostles; later, when Mark had turned back halfway, Barnabas was still willing to take him again. Had there not been someone willing to give him another chance, the church might have been without a Gospel of Mark. Brothers and sisters, we don’t need more hands of judgement; we need more shoulders like Barnabas’s.

The sixth cause is a distortion in the way we see: looking at other people’s faults through a magnifying glass, and at our own strengths through a flattering filter. This attitude commonly takes three forms: feeling that others are never quite good enough, not as good as me; being unable to stand someone’s personality or way of doing things; being unwilling to work with people who think differently. Brothers and sisters, all three sound so slight — so slight that we often think we’re simply “a person of principle,” or that we just “have high standards.” But that’s exactly how walls get built: one sentence at a time, one day at a time. Have you noticed that the standards we set for others are always stricter than the ones we set for ourselves?

The Lord Jesus said something wonderfully vivid about this: “First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.” Matthew 7:5. A “speck” is a tiny chip of wood; a “beam” is the great timber that holds up a whole house. The Lord Jesus had worked as a carpenter; he knew exactly how different those two are. A man with a roof beam sticking out of his eye leans in to pick a wood chip out of someone else’s — what an absurd picture! Psychology has a record of this too. In 1977 Lee Ross named the “fundamental attribution error”: when someone else is late, we say he has no sense of time; when we’re late, we say the traffic was bad. A 1981 study by Ola Svenson found that about 88 per cent of the American drivers surveyed believed they drove more safely than the median driver. Mathematically, that’s impossible. But that is the human heart: the magnifying glass points outwards, the flattering filter points inwards.

God made each of us different precisely so that we would work together and make up for one another’s lack. Paul says, “But now they are many members, but one body. The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you.’” 1 Corinthians 12:20–21. And he says that the members which seem to be weaker are necessary. Brothers and sisters, the eye and the hand can need each other precisely because they are different. If the whole body were an eye, it wouldn’t be a body; it would be a heap of eyes. The natural world says the same. California’s coast redwoods can grow to more than a hundred metres, yet their roots go down only two or three metres; they stand because underground their roots intertwine into a web. Then there are geese: research shows that twenty-five birds flying in a V can fly about 70 per cent further than a bird flying alone. Not one of them had stronger wings. They were simply in the right position.

The theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer left us a piercing sentence: whoever loves his dream of community more than the real people in the community in front of him will end up destroying that community. Brothers and sisters, it often isn’t that we don’t love the church; it’s that we love “the church of my ideals” too much. So 321 gives us the 920 practice: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; in front of them we practise living out the selfless life and bearing the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Notice that every one of these nine graces needs an “other person” in order to grow. Patience needs someone difficult to get along with; gentleness needs someone who makes you angry. That brother you don’t quite get along with isn’t your obstacle; he’s your training ground. One step further on are 235 relationships: spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, and a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Now here are this week’s practices. Practice 1: recognise the motive of self-interest. Reflect on a relationship of yours that is strained or has gone silent, and honestly ask yourself three questions. Do I care too much about my own interests? Am I unwilling to give up even a little of my own sovereignty? Am I only willing to associate with people who are “useful” to me? When you find traces of self-interest, turn to Jesus at once and say, “Lord, for your sake I am willing to lay myself down.” Brothers and sisters, the hardest part of this step isn’t answering the questions; it’s being still and letting the Holy Spirit shine his light. What we’ve heard today is Information; when the Holy Spirit points to one particular face, that is Revelation; when I stop defending myself, that is Conviction.

Practice 2: put down the stone, pick up the rope. This week, practise the three don’ts: don’t condemn, don’t gossip, don’t judge by your own standards; and the three do’s: cover with love, build up with words, support with action. Paul says: let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up. Implementation means this: at least once this week, when that comment is already on the tip of your tongue, swallow it and turn it into a word of blessing. Practice 3: deliberately observe someone you have tended to criticise, list three of their strengths, and tell them one to their face. Each evening, take three minutes to review: did I pick up a stone today, or a rope? Then correct, and repeat. The last step is Multiplication: take someone with you and practise this together. One person tearing down their own wall is salvation; a whole group tearing down walls together is revival.

Brothers and sisters, put today’s three causes side by side and you’ll discover they grow from the same root. Self-interest puts my own advantage at the centre; accusation puts me up on the judgement seat; fault-finding makes me the standard. Three roads, all leading to one word — “self.” So the way to tear down the wall isn’t to try harder to love that difficult person; it’s to let “self” step aside. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself, he didn’t condemn, he sat at table with sinners. The Bible is my standard — not my feelings or my face. The Holy Spirit is my guide — only he can make me see the beam in my own eye. Then let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Our perspective must shift too: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly.

Let’s go back to Berlin. The wall fell, but the wall in the head remained. Brothers and sisters, we have walls in our hearts too. Today we’ve seen three of their bricks: self-interest, accusation and fault-finding, and every one is stamped with the same word — “self.” The lesson puts it well: the root of separation lies not in the differences between people, but in whether “self” takes first place in our hearts. Unity isn’t forced endurance; it is a decision made out of love. The psalm says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” This morning, let’s lift up our eyes together. Put down our interests, put down the stones, put down the magnifying glass. When all of that has withdrawn, we will see the Lord who has been standing there all along: lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You are the Lord who broke down the middle wall of separation. We confess that there are walls in our hearts. We have sacrificed relationships for our own interests; we have picked up stones to condemn our brothers; we have looked at others through a magnifying glass and at ourselves through a flattering filter. Please forgive us. Lord, we don’t ask you to change others first; we ask you to change us first. Holy Spirit, shine your light and let us see the beam in our own eye. Give us gentle hearts to restore brothers who have fallen. Give us new eyes to see the gifts you have placed in every person. When I lift up my eyes, may I see no one, but you alone standing there. Let’s declare together: Lord, I lay myself down; may you become the centre; make me one with others, a witness to you! We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus. Amen. May the Lord bless you, and make you a child of peace.

sections.heading: Introduction: A Drop of Water, and an Ocean
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Tomorrow morning, when you wash your face, try one small thing. Turn the tap down as low as it will go, and let the water slowly gather into a single drop that hangs at the mouth of the tap. You will see a bead of water, crystal clear; the light passes through it, and it shines brighter than a diamond.

That one drop holds about 0.05 millilitres, and inside it are some 1.7 × 10²¹ water molecules. Every molecule clings tightly to its neighbours by hydrogen bonds, and that is why the drop can hold itself up as a round, full bead instead of spreading out flat.

It is beautiful. It is also pure.

But if you let it fall onto the kitchen counter and go and have your breakfast, by the time you come back it is gone. A little sun, a little breeze, and in less than half an hour it has evaporated without leaving a trace.

A drop of water, however pure, however precious, so long as it insists on remaining a single drop, has only one possible end: it disappears.

And yet it is the same water. At its mouth, the Amazon pours roughly two hundred thousand cubic metres of water into the Atlantic every second. That is the volume of eighty standard swimming pools, every second. It cuts across an entire South American continent and sustains the richest ecosystem on earth.

The water of the Amazon and that drop on your tap are the same thing. The molecular formula is identical: H2O. There is only one difference — one chose to stay inside itself, the other chose to flow out and to flow in.

Brothers and sisters, that is the whole of today’s lesson.

The lesson opens with a sentence that cuts to the heart: the separation between people is very often not because of different languages, different habits or different backgrounds, but because “I am not willing to lay myself down.”

Look at the brothers and sisters who have not spoken to each other for years, the ministry teams that in the end no longer have anything to do with one another, the families who live under one roof and yet each go their own way. Ask them why, and every one of them will give you a set of reasons: what he said back then, how she handled that matter, how I simply cannot cope with his personality.

But keep listening, listen right to the end, and you will hear the same sentence every time: “Why should I be the one to back down first?”

Separation never comes from the distance being too great. Separation comes because an “I” is standing in the middle.

When we cling to our own feelings, our interests, our opinions, our grievances and our hurts, we are like that drop of water that refuses to flow in. We guard ourselves, but we also guard our own loneliness; we keep ourselves intact, and leave ourselves out in the sun, waiting to evaporate.

So the key to unity has never been “changing other people”.

The key to unity is “laying ourselves down”.

The lesson puts it very clearly: when we are willing to place ourselves in Jesus’ hands and let him become our centre, we are no longer an isolated drop of water; we can be one with the body of Christ and enter his abundant kingdom.

Today we are going to look at three things together: first, to lay ourselves down is to choose to be separated no longer; second, what it actually means to lay ourselves down; third, how Jesus himself laid himself down. Then we will step together into three very concrete practices.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter of Unity Sent from Prison
sections.html:
Our theme passage comes from Philippians chapter 2.

The writer is the apostle Paul. The letter is generally dated to AD 61–62, during Paul’s first imprisonment in Rome. He says in the letter itself, “so that it became evident to the whole palace guard, and to all the rest, that my bonds are in Christ” (Philippians 1:13). In other words, this letter, so full of joy, so full of unity, so full of hope, was not written on the lawn at a retreat. It was written in chains.

The church that received it was in Philippi. Philippi was a city in the province of Macedonia. In 42 BC Octavian and Antony defeated the forces of Caesar’s assassins there, and afterwards the city was raised to the rank of a Roman colony. What did it mean to be a colony? It meant that although the people of this city lived far away in northern Greece, they held Roman citizenship, enjoyed Roman law and freedom from certain taxes, and took great pride in being Romans.

This was a city that set enormous store by “status” and “standing”.

The Philippian church was the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16). In it were Lydia, the wealthy dealer in purple cloth; a slave girl possessed by a spirit, of the very lowest standing; and a jailer and his household from inside the Roman system. A businesswoman of high society, a slave girl once treated as a money-spinner, a military man in charge of a prison — sitting at the same table breaking bread. In the Roman society of the day, those three kinds of people could never have shared a table.

So from its very first day, the church at Philippi was a church that “could only exist because people laid themselves down”.

But people are people. By the time Paul wrote this letter, this church — the one he loved most and gave thanks for most — had developed cracks. In chapter 4 Paul names names: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.” (Philippians 4:2) Two sisters who had laboured side by side with Paul in the gospel were at odds.

It was in exactly this situation that Paul wrote, in chapter 2, the passage that has come to be called the “Christ hymn”. Scholars widely believe that Philippians 2:6–11 may have been a hymn sung in the early church. Paul brings this song out not to teach some lofty Christology, but to deal with a very practical matter —

he is dealing with separation in the church.

Look at what comes just before the passage: “If therefore there is any exhortation in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any tender mercies and compassion, make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind; doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:1–4)

Do you see it? The prescription Paul writes is not “you need to communicate more”, nor “you need to spend more time together”, but “each counting others better than himself” and “not just looking to his own things”.

Then he says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5)

And straight after that comes the hymn: who, existing in the form of God … emptied himself.

Brothers and sisters, please remember this order. Faced with a church that had cracks in it, Paul did not first tell people to go and repair their relationships. He first turned their eyes to Jesus. Because unity is not a technique; unity is a life. And the name of that life is “emptying oneself”.

sections.heading: 1. To Lay Ourselves Down Is to Choose to Be Separated No Longer
sections.html:
The lesson’s first key point uses a very beautiful picture: the picture of water — choose the ocean, and be no longer just a drop.

Two endings for a drop of water

The lesson says: if a drop of water insists on itself and refuses to merge, then however pure and however precious it may be, in the end it will still evaporate and vanish. But when that drop is willing to let itself go, to flow into a great river and on into the sea, it is no longer small; it becomes one with a mighty current and has enormous influence and worth.

There is a very deep truth in this picture: the nature of the water does not change; what changes is where it is.

The same you, placed inside “yourself”, is a drop of water that may evaporate at any moment; placed inside “the kingdom of God”, you are part of a river of living water.

The Bible really does have such a river. God took the prophet Ezekiel to see the temple, and he saw water flowing out from under the threshold of the house, growing deeper and deeper — ankle-deep, then knee-deep, then waist-deep, and at last “a river that could not be walked through” (Ezekiel 47:5). This river flowed eastward all the way down and into the Dead Sea. Scripture says: “It will happen, that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, will live. Then there will be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea will be healed, and everything will live wherever the river comes.” (Ezekiel 47:9)

Why is the Dead Sea called the Dead Sea? Here is a real geographical fact: the Dead Sea has an inlet but no outlet. The water of the Jordan flows in and can never flow out again; it can only evaporate. Day after day, year after year, the salt keeps concentrating, until today the Dead Sea is close to ten times as salty as ordinary sea water — so salty that fish cannot live in it, and not a blade of grass grows on its shores.

Brothers and sisters, the Dead Sea did not die for lack of water. The Dead Sea died because “everything goes in and nothing comes out”.

Some Christians are like that. They come to the meetings, they hear the messages, they receive the grace — but nothing ever flows out of them: no serving, no giving, no forgiving, no welcoming. Over time the grace in them does not become living water; instead it crystallises into something salty and bitter — fault-finding, comparing, judging, defensiveness.

Take in and never give out, and you become a Dead Sea. Be willing to flow out and to flow in, and you become a river of living water.

The one thing that was “not good”

Why must people be one? Because God laid this down when he made humankind.

In Genesis chapter 2, when God had finished making the heavens and the earth and everything in them, he called each thing “good” — until he looked at Adam on his own. Scripture records: “Yahweh God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.’” (Genesis 2:18)

Notice: there was no sin yet. Everything in Eden was perfect. And yet God said, “Not good.” In Genesis chapters 1 and 2, “not good” appears only this once; the one and only thing God called “not good” was being alone.

Separation is not a neutral state. Separation is the state God called “not good” from the very beginning.

So when did separation really come in? In Genesis chapter 3. Satan said to them, “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) The moment humankind reached out and grasped at “I can be like God”, three layers of separation appeared at once. They hid from God — separation from God. Adam said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree” — separation from one another. They sewed fig leaves together to cover themselves — separation from themselves.

Isaiah puts it with great precision: “But your iniquities have separated you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he will not hear.” (Isaiah 59:2)

So the root of separation is sin, and the core of sin is the self-centred life. We want to grasp hold of ourselves, to leave our originally intended position, to take God’s place. This is exactly what 321 says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

By Genesis chapter 11, humanity’s collective self-centredness reached its peak: “They said, ‘Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.’” (Genesis 11:4)

Brothers and sisters, look at the motive behind the tower of Babel — “let’s make a name for ourselves”. And the result? Their language was confused, and humanity was scattered over the whole earth.

This is one of Scripture’s weightiest lessons: any unity built in order to “make a name for ourselves” will in the end always turn into separation. Because a crowd of self-centred people, even when they are packed onto the same building site, are not one; they simply happen to share the same interests for a while. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.

There is only one kind of true unity: a company of people who have laid themselves down, before one and the same Lord.

Supporting evidence from science and psychology

The harm that isolation does to people is not just a matter of mood.

In 2010, Julianne Holt-Lunstad of Brigham Young University and her colleagues published a meta-analysis in the journal PLoS Medicine, drawing together 148 studies and data on more than 300,000 participants. They found that people with stronger social connections had about a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up period. The research team pointed out that the health risk of weak social connection is comparable to well-known risk factors such as smoking and heavy drinking.

Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years. Its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger, sums up its conclusion in one sentence: what keeps people healthy and happy through life is neither wealth nor fame, but good relationships.

What science has measured is exactly what God said at the very start: “It is not good for the man to be alone.”

The English poet John Donne, who was also Dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, wrote some words in 1624 that are still quoted today: “No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main.”

No one is an island. And no drop of water can become an ocean on its own.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal is: establish God’s system.

Notice that the order itself deals with the self-centred life.

Why am I willing to lay myself down? Because Jesus is my role model; he laid himself down first. On what basis do I judge whether I ought to lay something down? Because the Bible is my standard, not my feelings. By what power can I let it go? Because the Holy Spirit is my guide, not my willpower. Once I have laid myself down, who takes the seat? Jesus reigns as King. Once I have laid myself down, who gets the glory? Jesus receives all the glory — not me, earning a fine reputation as someone “so big-hearted”.

A drop of water enters the ocean not because it has suddenly become great, but because it has finally agreed to leave the cup.

sections.heading: 2. What Does It Mean to “Lay Ourselves Down”?
sections.html:
This is the lesson’s second key point, and the most practical part of it.

The lesson begins with a very important definition: laying ourselves down does not mean denying our own worth; it means choosing not to make “self” our starting point.

This has to be made clear, or it is very easy to go astray.

The Bible never tells us to despise ourselves. God says we are made in his image, and to the people he chose he says, “you have been precious and honored in my sight, and I have loved you” (Isaiah 43:4). So “laying ourselves down” is not low self-esteem; it is not trampling ourselves underfoot; it is not becoming someone with no voice, no boundaries and no worth.

321 puts it exactly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out.

What does Paul say? “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

“It is no longer I who live” — that is laying down. “But Christ lives in me” — that is entering into fullness.

A drop of water placed in the sea has not disappeared; it has become the sea.

The Lord Jesus said the same thing with another picture: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

A grain of wheat that clings to itself will only ever be one grain. A grain of wheat that lets itself go bears much fruit.

Very well — so what, concretely, are we to lay down? The lesson lists six things. Let’s take them one at a time.

(1) Lay down comparison; stop trying to prove yourself by what you achieve

Comparison is one of the most draining things there is.

Because comparison never has a finish line. Beat this person, and there is another one ahead. Win this time, and next time you have to win again. Your worth turns into a proof that never ends.

Paul says: “For I say through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3)

“To think reasonably” is the Greek sōphronein — to be clear-headed, sound-minded, to think in line with reality. The most frightening thing about comparison is that it robs us of clear thinking: it magnifies others and distorts ourselves, until in the end there is no truth left in our eyes, only rankings.

The cure for comparison is not “actually I’m not so bad”, but “my worth is not found here”.

Brothers and sisters, your worth is not what you have achieved; it is what the Lord has done for you. The cross has already put a price on you — the life of God’s only Son. That price will not go up because you had a good year at work, and it will not go down because you were weak this quarter.

321 says: change the mindset and you change the life. When your mindset turns from “I have to prove myself” to “I have already been proved”, your life loosens. Only someone who no longer needs to prove himself can truly rejoice at someone else’s good news.

(2) Lay down suspicion; put both yourself and others into God’s hands

Suspicion is separation’s favourite building material.

Psychology has a very well-known phenomenon called the “fundamental attribution error”, formally named by the social psychologist Lee Ross in 1977. It describes how, when we explain other people’s behaviour, we tend to put it down to their character, but when we explain our own, we tend to put it down to our circumstances.

He hasn’t answered my message because he’s a cold sort of person. I haven’t answered his because I’ve just been so busy lately.

The same thing, measured with two rulers.

Brothers and sisters, a great many of the misunderstandings in the church grow in exactly this way. We mean no harm; it’s just that without realising it we explain others by the worst assumption and ourselves by the best excuse.

What is the Bible’s standard? “Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.” (Romans 14:4)

The Lord Jesus says it more sharply still: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3)

Laying down suspicion does not mean naively believing there is nothing wrong with anyone; it means handing the judgement seat back to God. Suspicion is so exhausting because we are holding three jobs at once: prosecutor, judge and victim. 321 says: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. The judgement seat is God’s place; no wonder we can’t sit comfortably when we climb into it.

So put yourself into God’s hands, and put that person into God’s hands too. You will find that you have not only let him go; you have let yourself go as well.

(3) Lay down hurt; choose to forgive and to reconnect

This is the hardest of them all, because the hurt is real.

Let me first say something as a pastor: the Bible never says “that was nothing”. Forgiveness actually starts by admitting there is a debt. If there is no debt, there is nothing to cancel.

Paul teaches us: “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.” (Colossians 3:13)

Look at the standard at the end — “even as Christ forgave you”. The measure of our forgiving is not whether the other person deserves it, but how the Lord has already treated me.

One frequently cited study is an experiment by Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet and colleagues, published in 2001 in the journal Psychological Science. The researchers asked participants to call to mind, in turn, an unforgiving frame of mind and a forgiving one, while measuring their physiological responses. They found that when people dwelt on grudges and imagined revenge, their blood pressure, heart rate and facial muscle tension all rose markedly; when they entered a frame of mind of empathy and forgiveness, these measures settled down.

Brothers and sisters, this shows one thing: when you will not forgive, you are the one bearing the consequences of the other person’s sin. Someone has put it well — refusing to forgive is like drinking poison yourself and waiting for the other person to drop.

But the lesson does not stop at “forgive”. What it says is “forgive and reconnect”.

Forgiveness is one-sided; I can complete it on my own before God. Reconnection is two-sided; it takes time, it takes wisdom, and sometimes it takes boundaries. But a Christian should not use “I’ve already forgiven him” as a reason to put that person in the freezer of his heart for good. Forgiveness with no willingness to move towards reconnection can easily become nothing more than a more respectable form of separation.

What did the Lord Jesus do on the cross? He came that he “might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it” (Ephesians 2:16). He did not only pardon; he made the two into one body.

(4) Lay down self-interest; learn to think of others

Paul’s words are still ringing in our ears: “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:4)

Notice that Paul did not say “don’t look to your own things”; he said “not just”. The Bible is not asking us to be irresponsible; it is asking us to widen our field of vision.

Adam Grant, an organisational psychologist at the Wharton School, divides people in his 2013 book Give and Take into three types: givers, takers and matchers. He points out a fascinating finding: in many workplace performance rankings, the people at the bottom are often givers — but the people who climb to the very top are givers too. The difference is that successful givers know how to give wisely and give with boundaries, rather than being drained until they run dry.

That bears out exactly the Bible’s order: life first, then ministry; first be connected with God, and then you can keep on giving.

Brothers and sisters, 321 says: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.

When our service goes wrong, it is often not because we are not trying hard enough but because the order has been turned upside down. We put ministry ahead of relationships, so to get the job done we are willing to hurt people; we put relationships ahead of life, so to keep the peace we refuse to face ourselves.

Laying down self-interest means putting the order back where it belongs.

(5) Lay down your standards; stop criticising and finding fault with others

This one needs careful discernment, so we must say it precisely.

“Laying down standards” in the lesson never means giving up the standard of biblical truth. The Bible is our standard; that will never change. What the lesson means is the standards we make up ourselves and then use to measure other people — how I think worship should be sung, what time I think children should go to bed, how many minutes I think a co-worker should take to reply to a message, what I think a spiritual person should look like.

Faced with arguments over eating or not eating, keeping days or not keeping them, Paul says: “But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you again, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.” (Romans 14:10)

The Lord Jesus also says, “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.” (Matthew 7:1)

Fault-finding has a secret: the people who find fault with others are in fact the least forgiving towards themselves. They carry a very strict ruler in their hearts; they measure themselves with it first, and then everyone else. They spend all day doing God’s performance reviews for him, yet they have never once enjoyed God’s grace.

Brothers and sisters, if you notice that lately you are especially quick to find other people irritating, don’t rush to deal with that person. First come before the Lord and ask: Lord, is there a place in me that your grace has not yet touched?

(6) Lay down pride; be willing to make up what others lack, and work hand in hand

The last one is really the root of the other five. Comparison, suspicion, holding grudges, self-interest, fault-finding — behind every one of them is the same thing: pride.

Scripture says, “Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is with people who take advice.” (Proverbs 13:10) And again, “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)

321 puts it with great precision: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

And God’s attitude towards these two kinds of people is very clear: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

Notice the word “resists”. The original, antitassomai, is a military term for an army drawn up in battle array against an enemy. It is not merely that God does not like proud people; God has drawn up his battle lines and stands facing them. A proud person finds that every effort he makes has to face God’s army.

So what does humility actually look like in the church? Paul says, “For as the body is one, and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ.” (1 Corinthians 12:12) “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” (1 Corinthians 12:21)

Here is the mystery of the body: no member is complete, so every member needs the others. The hand is deft, but the hand cannot see; the eye can see, but the eye cannot pick anything up. God deliberately made us incomplete, so that we cannot do without working hand in hand.

The phrase the lesson uses is “make up what others lack”. What a beautiful phrase that is. When a humble person sees a brother’s lack, his first reaction is not to comment on it, but to fill it.

Ecclesiastes says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10) “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Ecclesiastes 4:12)

When three strands are twisted around one another, the friction makes them hold each other up, and their strength is far more than three times that of one. This is exactly the principle of 321’s “235 relationships”: two selfless people becoming spiritual companions — that is your “2”; bringing forth spiritual parents and spiritual children — that is the “3”; the fivefold ministries working hand in hand to become a team of spiritual comrades — that is the “5”.

One person can go fast; only a company of people can go far. And what keeps a company of people walking together is not ability but humility.

sections.heading: 3. Jesus Our Role Model: He Laid Himself Down, and It Was for Us
sections.html:
The lesson’s third key point takes us to the highest place, which is also the lowest — the cross.

The lesson quotes Philippians chapter 2. Let us read the whole passage now:

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

Seven steps down

Brothers and sisters, walk down with me, one step at a time.

The first step: “existing in the form of God.” The Greek word for “form” is morphē. It does not mean outward appearance but the expression of one’s essential nature — he was God from the beginning, and all the glory of God’s very being was his.

The second step: “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped.” The original word, harpagmos, means a prize to be clutched tightly and kept for oneself. What Satan grasped at in the beginning, what Adam and Eve grasped at in the beginning, was precisely “equality with God”. Yet the One who was equal with God from the start did not treat it as something he had to cling to.

The third step: “but emptied himself.” The original is ekenōsen, from the verb kenoō, “to empty”. Notice that what he emptied was not his divinity — he never stopped being God. What he emptied himself of was his way of using his rights, the display of his glory, his entitlement to be served.

The fourth step: “taking the form of a servant.” Here again is morphē. He did not “play the part” of a servant; he truly and really took on the nature of a servant — from Lord of all things to doulos, a slave.

The fifth step: “being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form.” He became truly human, knowing weariness, hunger and tears.

The sixth step: “he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death.” He obeyed to the very end, until his last breath. In Gethsemane he said, “not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42)

The seventh step: “yes, the death of the cross.”

To the Philippians, this seventh step landed like a hammer blow.

In the Roman Empire the cross was a punishment reserved for slaves, rebels and non-citizens. By law, Roman citizens could not be crucified. The Roman statesman Cicero, in his speech in defence of Rabirius, said that the very word “cross” should be kept far not only from the body of a Roman citizen, but even from his thoughts, his eyes and his ears.

What the Philippians were proudest of was their Roman citizenship; and one of the greatest guarantees of that citizenship was “I will never have to go to a cross”.

Yet Paul tells them: the One you worship came all the way down from the highest place there is, right down to the place you dare not even think about.

Brothers and sisters, this is the perfect answer to what it means to “lay ourselves down”.

The way down is the way up

But the story does not stop at verse 8. Paul goes on:

“Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:9–11)

Do you see it? When the seven steps down were complete, God himself raised him to the highest place.

This is an unchanging law in the kingdom of God: God does not compete with those who grab for power; God lifts up those who let go.

The Lord Jesus said it himself: “even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28)

And he lived it out before our eyes. At the Last Supper, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, he got up, laid aside his outer garments, wrapped a towel around his waist, and washed his disciples’ feet one by one — including the feet that were about to walk out and betray him.

He let go, and we gained. He came down, and we were lifted up. He was shut out from his Father’s face and cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46) — so that we would never be separated again.

Ephesians puts it in the plainest terms: “For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation.” (Ephesians 2:14)

In the temple in Jerusalem there really was a stone wall between the Court of the Gentiles and the inner courts, and on it was carved a warning: any foreigner who passes this barrier will have himself to blame for his death. That wall was the most concrete symbol of human separation.

On the cross, the Lord Jesus tore that wall down.

Brothers and sisters, what are all our separations today compared with that wall? The Lord has already torn down the greatest wall of all, the wall between God and humankind — and here we are, over one remark, one incident, one misunderstanding, building new walls between brothers.

The lesson says: if we say we want to follow Christ’s example, we must learn to lay ourselves down. Not in order to disappear, but in order to take part in a greater, eternal plan.

321 says: Jesus is my role model. A role model is not something you hang on the wall to admire; a role model is someone you follow. The way he walked is the way we walk.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness, from Separation to Unity
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us look at today’s message once more within the framework of 321.

First, the heart of this lesson is the very heart of 321’s message: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.

The root of separation is the self-centred life. The door to unity is selflessness. The whole Bible, from Genesis chapter 3, “you will be like God”, to the New Jerusalem in Revelation, where “God himself will be with them”, is about one thing: when people snatch themselves back, God is pushed out; when people lay themselves down, God moves in.

Second, humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

One of Satan’s specialities is manufacturing separation. In Eden he set humankind against God; in Cain he set man against man; in the church he sets brother against brother. His strategy is always the same: first make you feel you have been wronged, then make you feel you have every right to hold on to that grievance.

And there is only one way to break it: lay yourself down. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Third, the fourfold shift of perspective.

From the human perspective to God’s perspective — not “how could he treat me like this?” but “Lord, what do you want to do in this?” From the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal — however great this grievance, it lasts a few decades at most; but if this relationship is reconciled, it will stretch on into eternity. From the worldly to the godly — not settling it by human methods, but overcoming by God’s methods.

Fourth, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Notice the order. Unity belongs to “relationships”, the fourth item. You cannot skip the first three and go straight to it. Someone whose mindset has not changed will not have a changed life; someone whose life has not changed will not have changed daily living; and someone whose daily living has not changed will never manage to mend their relationships.

So today’s real lesson is not “whom do I need to make peace with?” but “will I let my mindset be changed?” Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Fifth, the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

Many people who cannot get along with others actually cannot get along with themselves; and they cannot get along with themselves because they have not yet truly come into line with God.

Sixth, the 920 practice.

Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. The 920 practice is this: in front of that “2”, live a selfless (0) life and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice: of those nine graces, at least six can only grow within relationships. Shut away in a room on your own, you cannot learn patience, you cannot learn kindness, you cannot learn gentleness. God has placed that “difficult” person beside you not to wear you down, but so that you will bear fruit.

Seventh, the 235 relationships.

With a selfless person, become a “2” — spiritual companions who hold each other up; build the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally become the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working hand in hand. “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” (Ephesians 4:11–12)

Eighth, the Goal: establish God’s system.

The lesson’s closing words put it superbly: the kingdom of God is not a human organisation, not someone’s personal platform, but the realm where Jesus reigns as King. God’s system is not about gathering people under a name; it is about gathering people under a King.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Steps into a Life of Unity
sections.html:
The lesson gives three practices. We’ll take them one by one, and we’ll go deeper with each by using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice one: Where will I put this drop of water that I am?

The lesson asks us to meditate on three questions every day and pray over them:

First, am I still “clinging to myself”?

Second, is my choice to protect my feelings, my reputation, my position, my church — or am I willing to lay myself down and enter the kingdom of God?

Third, am I willing to say, “Lord, I want to put myself into your ocean, to be one with you and one with my brothers and sisters”?

The lesson also gives a very concrete action: draw a drop of water on a piece of paper, write inside it one thing you are willing to lay down today, and offer it to God.

Brothers and sisters, don’t underestimate this action. Writing it down turns something vague into something definite. Vague repentance never changes anything; repentance that has been written down gives the Holy Spirit something to work on.

Now let’s walk it through the eight stages.

Information: you have heard it today — separation is clinging to yourself; unity is laying yourself down.

Revelation: information does not change people; revelation does. So please stop and pray: Lord, show me what it really is that I am clinging to right now. When the Holy Spirit points out in your heart that name, that matter, that scene, you have received revelation.

Conviction: once you have seen it, you must say “yes”. Not “but he was in the wrong too”, but “Lord, on this one I submit.”

Implementation: write it inside that drop of water and offer it up concretely.

Evaluation: a week later, look back — did I really let it go, or did I only push it down for a while?

Correction: if you find you have taken it back again, don’t condemn yourself; simply let it go once more.

Repetition: do it again every morning. Laying yourself down is not a one-time decision; it is a daily choice.

Multiplication: when you have truly experienced it, go and tell someone else. Let the story of your drop of water become someone else’s invitation into the ocean.

Practice two: Choose unity, not independence

The lesson asks us this week to do one thing deliberately that will bring us into unity:

First, take the initiative to contact someone with whom you have had a misunderstanding.

Second, in your team, take the initiative to cooperate rather than insisting on your own way.

Third, at home or in your service, choose to “take a step back” so that someone else can flourish.

Fourth, refuse to complain; choose praise and thanksgiving.

The lesson says: you will find that the moment you lay down “self”, God’s glory and power begin to flow.

On that last point, psychology offers good confirmation too. In 2003 Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Participants were divided into three groups, which each week wrote down, respectively, things they were grateful for, things that troubled or annoyed them, and neutral events. After several weeks the group that wrote about gratitude not only rated their lives as a whole more positively, but also complained of fewer physical symptoms.

Complaint and gratitude look at the same world, but they end up with two different lives.

Brothers and sisters, please pay special attention to the words “take the initiative”. Unity never happens by itself. Unity always needs someone to move first.

And the one who moves first is very often the one who is more like Jesus.

How do the eight stages work here? Revelation: Lord, whom do you want me to step out towards first this week? — usually a name comes to mind at once, and you will very much want to swap it for another. Conviction: all right, it is him. Implementation: within this week, send that message, make that phone call. Evaluation: am I going to repair the relationship, or to prove that I am the more spiritual one? Correction: if my motive is not pure, I adjust it before God first, and then go. Multiplication: carry this culture of taking the initiative into your small group, your family, your team.

Practice three: Live for the kingdom of God

The lesson asks us to meditate on two questions:

First, am I willing to give myself for the kingdom of God, and not only for my church or for myself?

Second, am I willing to lay down the boundaries between churches and the labels on ministries, and to work for the vision of unity?

Then the lesson gives a crucial sentence: the kingdom of God is not a human organisation, not someone’s personal platform, but the realm where Jesus reigns as King. When you live for the kingdom, you will bring about limitless influence.

Brothers and sisters, there is a very important distinction here.

The prayer the Lord Jesus taught us does not begin with “May my ministry flourish”, but “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) He also said, “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33)

Social psychology has a famous experiment. In 1954, at a camp called Robbers Cave in Oklahoma, Muzafer Sherif divided a group of boys who did not know one another into two teams. After a few competitions, fierce hostility quickly sprang up between the two teams — calling each other names, fighting over territory, damaging each other’s belongings.

Next the researchers had the two teams eat together and watch films together, hoping that “spending more time together” would dissolve the hostility. It failed. Simply putting people together only gave them more opportunities to attack each other.

What really turned things around was a “higher shared goal” that the researchers deliberately set up: the camp’s water supply line broke, and the two teams had to work together to fix it; the truck bringing the food broke down, and the two teams had to pull on the rope together to get it moving. Only when the two teams had a shared goal that neither could achieve alone did the hostility begin to crumble.

Brothers and sisters, this experiment tells us one thing: unity does not come from “spending more time together”; unity comes from “a shared, higher goal”.

Unity between churches is the same. We will not become one just by holding a few more joint meetings. We are one because we have one King, one kingdom, and one charge that will not change until death.

“There is one body and one Spirit, even as you also were called in one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all, and in us all.” (Ephesians 4:4–6)

Going deeper with the eight stages here: Revelation — Lord, have I secretly mistaken my platform for your kingdom? Implementation — this month, pray specifically, at least once, for another church and another ministry. Evaluation — when someone else is flourishing more than I am, what is my first reaction inside? Correction — bring the envy to the cross. Repetition — until rejoicing at someone else’s revival becomes your instinct.

A Gentle Reminder: To choose unity is to choose to let Jesus be King

After the practices, the lesson adds a gentle reminder. I want to read it out in full:

You are no longer that lonely drop of water, but the drop that is willing to enter the ocean. You no longer live for yourself, but for Christ. Jesus will be glorified in you.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the logic here.

Unity is not a social goal; unity is a question of kingship.

Why can two people not get along? Because inside each of them sits a king. When I let Jesus be King, and you let Jesus be King, there is only one King left between us — and then unity is not something forced; it simply happens.

Paul says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” (2 Corinthians 5:15)

These are the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

John the Baptist summed up the lesson of a whole life in a single short sentence: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

sections.heading: Closing Word: Only by Laying Ourselves Down Can We Enter True Revival
sections.html:
The lesson closes with very powerful words: revival is not an event, nor an atmosphere, but a company of people willing to let Jesus be Lord, willing to lay themselves down, to enter God’s kingdom, to be one with each other and to walk with God.

But what does revival look like in the Bible? Acts chapter 2 tells us: “All who believed were together, and had all things in common.” (Acts 2:44) “Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God, and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.” (Acts 2:46–47)

Look at the order: first “together”, first “with one accord”, and only then “the Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved”.

Unity comes first; revival comes after.

The Lord Jesus’ own prayer runs the same way: “that they may all be one … that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) The key to the world believing is not our eloquence, nor our venues, but our unity.

The psalm says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” And then, “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (Psalm 133:1, 3)

The blessing God commands comes down “there” — on the place where brothers live together in unity.

So the lesson says: if each of us is willing to lay ourselves down, separation will have nowhere left to stand, and the glory of Jesus will be greatly revealed.

Brothers and sisters, this morning the Lord sets a very simple choice before you.

Will this drop of water that you are stay in the cup, or flow into the ocean?

Will you go on being the one who says, “Why should I be the one to back down first?” — or will you be the one who steps out first?

Will you live for your own name, or for the kingdom of Jesus?

A drop of water placed in the ocean does not disappear. It becomes part of the ocean, and goes to places it could never have reached on its own in a whole lifetime.

May each of us say to the Lord today: Lord, I am willing. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)
“that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21)
practices: Choose unity, not independence
Live for the kingdom of God
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we worship you.

Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and were obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. You laid everything down, and it was for us. You broke down the middle wall of separation, reconciling us to God and reconciling us to one another.

Lord, forgive us. So often we cling to our own feelings, our interests, our opinions, our grievances and our hurts, and will not let go. We wear ourselves out with comparison, judge others with suspicion, build high walls out of our hurts, and condemn our brothers by our own standards. Have mercy on us, we pray.
Holy Spirit, shine your light on me and name it plainly; show me the one thing I must lay down today. Give me the courage to write it down, to offer it up, and never to take it back.
Lord, I want to put this drop of water that I am into your kingdom. Let me be separated no longer, but bear witness to your glory in unity.
Make me the one who takes the initiative first, the one who makes up what others lack, the one who rejoices for the kingdom.
Let your kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: The lesson says, “The separation between people is very often not because of different languages, different habits or different backgrounds, but because ‘I am not willing to lay myself down.’” Set this beside Philippians 2:3–4: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” Share: of the six things the lesson lists — comparison, suspicion, hurt, self-interest, standards and pride — which one has the Holy Spirit touched most deeply in you today? What, specifically, are you willing to lay down?

The Lord Jesus prayed, “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) Share: towards which brother or sister will you take the first step this week? How do you plan to do it? Ask the group to pray together about this, and follow up with one another at the next meeting.
