brief12.title: By Whom? For Whom?
notes: Slide text:
Adjusting our focus back to Jesus
“In him we live, move, and have our being.”
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 22
Key points:
1. Theme of the lesson: adjust our focus back to Jesus; two questions run through the whole lesson.
2. Theme verse: Acts 17:28; supported by Romans 11:36, “of him, and through him, and to him are all things”.
3. Open with a warm greeting; make clear we ask only two questions today: by whom? for whom?
4. Preview: the anchor answers “by whom”, the star answers “for whom”.

brief12.title: Introduction: The Ship’s Anchor and the Ship’s Star
notes: Slide text:
Anchor: on whom am I relying to live?
Star: for whom am I living?
The key to overcoming: focus back in place.
“As an anchor of the soul” (Hebrews 6:19)
Key points:
1. Image: a sailing ship at night; the old sailor does two things — drops anchor and looks for a star.
2. Scientific fact: the North Star sits almost directly above the earth’s axis, so its position is constant; sailors of old steered by it.
3. Scripture: Hebrews 6:19, “This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast and entering into that which is within the veil.”
4. Application: our emotions rise and fall not because the waves are big, but because the anchor is in the wrong place.

brief12.title: Theme Verse and Background
notes: Slide text:
Paul’s declaration on the Areopagus in Athens
“In him we live, move,
and have our being.” (Acts 17:28)
Life, movement, being — none self-given
Key points:
1. Background: the author is Luke, a doctor and Paul’s co-worker, writing around AD 60 to Theophilus.
2. Setting: Paul’s second missionary journey (around AD 50–51), at the Areopagus in Athens.
3. Acts 17:16, “his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols”; 17:23, “to an unknown god”.
4. The original: live (zōmen), move (kinoumetha), have our being (esmen) — the three most basic things, none of which we gave ourselves.

brief12.title: 1. By Whom? What You Fear Losing
notes: Slide text:
Whatever you panic about losing
is what you are relying on to live.
“Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh,
whose confidence is in Yahweh!” (Jeremiah 17:7)
Key points:
1. The test: whatever you panic about losing is what you are relying on to live.
2. Scripture: Jeremiah 17:5–6, the bush in the desert; 17:7–8, the tree planted by the waters.
3. Emphasis: the text doesn’t say there will be no heat or drought; the difference is where the roots go down.
4. Everyday examples: losing a job, losing someone’s support, losing savings — and falling apart.

brief12.title: 1. Jesus Is Our Threefold Source
notes: Slide text:
Source of wisdom: he knows all (Colossians 2:3)
Guarantee of protection: ever present (Psalm 139:7)
Wellspring of power: almighty (Jeremiah 32:17)
“I can do all things” (Philippians 4:13)
Key points:
1. Colossians 2:3, “in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.”
2. Psalm 139:7–10, “Where could I go from your Spirit?” — the same truth sounds like a threat to the rebellious and a guarantee to the obedient.
3. Jeremiah 32:17, “There is nothing too hard for you.”
4. Read Philippians 4:13 with 4:12 on being humbled and abounding: not obtaining all things, but standing firm in all things.

brief12.title: 1. Hold Fast to Jesus and Possess All
notes: Slide text:
No need to chase the anointing, rely on circumstances
or cling to connections — just hold fast to Jesus.
“As having nothing, and yet possessing all things”
(2 Corinthians 6:10)
Key points:
1. The lesson’s point: no need to chase the anointing, rely on circumstances or cling to connections; just hold fast to Jesus.
2. The root disease: we want “the things of God” more than God himself.
3. Scripture: read the full verse, 2 Corinthians 6:10; having the Lord who owns all things, in him we possess all things.
4. Quotation: Augustine, Confessions — our heart is restless until it rests in you.
5. Psychology: Bowlby’s attachment theory and Ainsworth’s Strange Situation — the steadier the base, the further we dare to go.

brief12.title: 2. For Whom? No Longer for Self, Only for the Lord
notes: Slide text:
The lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes,
the pride of life — not the Father’s.
They share just one thing: self.
Key points:
1. Two probing questions: for whom do we live? for whom do we serve? We drift most easily when life goes smoothly.
2. Scripture: 1 John 2:15–17; “the pride of life” is alazoneia tou biou in the original, literally “the boasting of life”.
3. The threefold parallel: Genesis 3:6, good for food, a delight to the eyes, desired to make one wise.
4. Three times in the wilderness the Lord answered, “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10).
5. They share just one thing: self.

brief12.title: 2. Please the Lord, Not People
notes: Slide text:
“No longer live to themselves” (2 Corinthians 5:15)
“If I were still pleasing men,
I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10)
Focus on people, drained; on the Lord, filled.
Key points:
1. 2 Corinthians 5:14–15: Christ died for me, so I no longer live for myself — the conclusion love draws, not a heavy-handed command.
2. Galatians 2:20, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”
3. Galatians 1:10; Matthew 6:1, don’t do your charitable giving before men.
4. Psychology: Deci and Ryan’s 1985 self-determination theory — burnout comes most easily when extrinsic motivation dominates.
5. Illustration: the two people mopping the floor; Colossians 3:23, “as for the Lord”.

brief12.title: 3. For Whom Is Revival?
notes: Slide text:
Not numbers, not social change,
not signs and wonders — but Jesus glorified.
“He will glorify me” (John 16:14)
Don’t look for a formula — look for Jesus!
Key points:
1. Revival is not growing numbers, social change, or signs and wonders — these may be results, but cannot be the focus.
2. John 6:15 and 6:26, “you seek me … because you ate of the loaves, and were filled”.
3. John 16:14, “He will glorify me”; 12:32, first lifted up, then all people drawn.
4. History: the Herrnhut revival of 1727 — reconciliation first, then the outpouring, then a century-long prayer watch.
5. Science: Kepler’s first law — the sun at the focus keeps the orbit steady.

brief12.title: Practice: Three Turns of Focus
notes: Slide text:
List what you rely on; hand it back.
Realign your heart for service: for whom?
Five minutes a day gazing on Jesus alone.
Declare: I live relying on you, for you!
Key points:
1. Exercise one: write down three things you most easily lean on, and hand them back to the Lord in prayer.
2. Exercise two: when discouraged in service, stop and ask — for whom am I doing this?
3. Exercise three: five minutes a day, not for needs, not for service, only worshipping and gazing on Jesus.
4. Deepen with the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
5. Declaration of faith: I do not rely on circumstances, I do not live for myself; I live relying on you and living for you!

brief12.title: Closing and Call: Return to the Focus, Enter Victory
notes: Slide text:
Whom you rely on decides how far you go;
whom you live for decides if it’s worth it.
“Yet I will rejoice in Yahweh”
(Habakkuk 3:18) Let Jesus be King!
Key points:
1. Whom you rely on decides how far you can go; whom you live for decides whether the journey is worth it.
2. Read the whole of Habakkuk 3:17–19; the key is that word “yet”.
3. Habakkuk’s circumstances did not change; his focus did.
4. Call: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, not relying on circumstances, not for myself,
but relying on you and living for you!
May Jesus have the preeminence in all things,
and may all the glory be his. Amen.
Key points:
1. Lead the congregation in prayer together, slowly and warmly.
2. Content of the prayer: confession, forgiveness, refocusing, asking the Holy Spirit to work.
3. Declare that Jesus reigns as King in our homes, our work and our church.
4. Close with “May all the glory be yours” and a blessing.

brief21.title: By Whom? For Whom?
notes: Slide text:
Adjusting our focus back to Jesus
“In him we live, move, and have our being.”
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 22
Key points:
1. Theme of the lesson: adjust our focus back to Jesus.

brief21.title: Introduction 1: The Ship’s Anchor and the Ship’s Star
notes: Slide text:
In a night storm a sailor does two things:
drops anchor onto the immovable bedrock;
looks up for the unmoving North Star.
An anchor and a star.
Key points:
1. Image: a sailing ship at night; in the storm the old sailor does two things.
2. The anchor must sink to the seabed and lock onto immovable bedrock, not be hooked onto a boat alongside.
3. Scientific fact: the North Star sits almost directly above the earth’s axis, so its position is constant.
4. Sum up the picture in one line: an anchor and a star.

brief21.title: Introduction 2: Two Questions
notes: Slide text:
The anchor asks: on whom am I relying?
The star asks: for whom am I living?
Rely on the wrong thing — disappointment;
aim at the wrong thing — weariness.
Key points:
1. The anchor and the star correspond to the two questions.
2. Everyday example: someone praises us and we soar; someone misunderstands us and we sink.
3. Rely on the wrong thing and you will surely be disappointed; aim at the wrong thing and you will surely grow weary.
4. Hebrews 6:19, “as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast and entering into that which is within the veil”.

brief21.title: Theme Verse and Background
notes: Slide text:
Written by Luke: Paul on the Areopagus
“In him we live, move,
and have our being.” (Acts 17:28)
“Of him … are all things” (Romans 11:36)
Key points:
1. The author is Luke, a doctor (Colossians 4:14), writing to Theophilus around AD 60.
2. Second missionary journey, around AD 50–51; Acts 17:16, 17:21, 17:23.
3. The Areopagus was the council hill and highest court of Athens.
4. The original: live, move, have our being — the three most basic things, none of which we gave ourselves.
5. Romans 11:36, “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things.”

brief21.title: 1.1 What You Fear Losing Is What You Rely On
notes: Slide text:
Panic at losing relationships, resources, chances
shows our reliance is in the wrong place.
“Cursed is the man who trusts in man …”
(Jeremiah 17:5)
Key points:
1. The test: whatever you panic about losing is what you are relying on.
2. Everyday examples: losing a job, losing support, losing savings.
3. Jeremiah 17:5–6: trusting in the strength of flesh is like a bush in the desert.
4. Stress: this isn’t a question of weakness; it’s a question of focus.

brief21.title: 1.2 A Tree Planted by the Waters
notes: Slide text:
“As a tree planted by the waters, roots by the river,
will not fear when heat comes” (Jeremiah 17:8)
The heat will come, the drought will come;
the difference is where the roots go down.
Key points:
1. Read the whole of Jeremiah 17:7–8: planted by the waters, spreading its roots by the river.
2. The text plainly says “when heat comes” and “the year of drought” — trouble is not cancelled.
3. Contrast: salt land versus riverside; one withers, one stays green.
4. Application: don’t ask for circumstances to change; ask for your roots to go down in the right place.

brief21.title: 1.3 Jesus Is Our Threefold Source
notes: Slide text:
Source of wisdom: he knows all (Colossians 2:3)
Guarantee of protection: ever present (Psalm 139:7)
Wellspring of power: almighty (Jeremiah 32:17)
“I can do all things” (Philippians 4:13)
Key points:
1. Colossians 2:3: all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him.
2. Psalm 139:7–10: he is present everywhere; the obedient hear it as a guarantee.
3. Jeremiah 32:17, “There is nothing too hard for you.”
4. Philippians 4:12–13: doing all things means bearing all things and standing firm in all things.

brief21.title: 1.4 Hold Fast to Jesus and Possess All
notes: Slide text:
No need to chase the anointing, rely on circumstances

“As having nothing, and yet possessing all things”
(2 Corinthians 6:10)
Key points:
1. The lesson’s point: no need to chase the anointing, rely on circumstances or cling to connections.
2. The root disease: wanting “the things of God” more than God himself.
3. Read the full verse, 2 Corinthians 6:10.
4. Quotation: Augustine, Confessions, Book One — our heart is restless until it rests in God.

brief21.title: 1.5 The Secure Base and the Three Foundations
notes: Slide text:
Bowlby and Ainsworth: the steadier the base,
the further we dare to go. (Attachment theory)
Jesus my role model, the Bible my standard,
the Spirit my guide: the Three Foundations are our anchor.
Key points:
1. Psychology: Bowlby’s attachment theory; Ainsworth’s Strange Situation experiments in the 1970s.
2. The key: how far a child dares to venture depends on how stable the base behind him is.
3. The spiritual parallel: if our base is other people’s opinion we shrink back; if it is Jesus we can go forward.
4. Isaiah 41:10, “Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God”; Hebrews 13:8.
5. 321: the Three Foundations are our anchor.

brief21.title: 2.1 Living for Whom? Serving for Whom?
notes: Slide text:
“Don’t love the world or the things in the world”
The lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes,
the pride of life (1 John 2:15–16)
They share just one thing: self.
Key points:
1. The second question: for whom do we live? for whom do we serve?
2. We drift most easily when life goes smoothly: when ill, it’s easy to rely on the Lord; when praised, it’s easy to forget him.
3. Read the whole of 1 John 2:15–17.
4. The original: “the pride of life” is alazoneia tou biou, literally “the boasting of life”.

brief21.title: 2.2 From Eden to the Wilderness
notes: Slide text:
Good for food, a delight to the eyes,
desired to make one wise (Genesis 3:6)
Tempted, the Lord said: “It is written …”
The content of temptation has never changed.
Key points:
1. The threefold parallel in Genesis 3:6: good for food, a delight to the eyes, desired to make one wise.
2. The wilderness temptations: stones into bread, leaping from the temple, worshipping Satan for the glory of the kingdoms.
3. Three times the Lord answered, “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10).
4. Conclusion: the content of temptation has never changed; they share just one thing — self.

brief21.title: 2.3 No Longer Living for Ourselves
notes: Slide text:
“He died for all, that those who live
should no longer live to themselves” (2 Corinthians 5:15)
“It is no longer I who live, but Christ
lives in me” (Galatians 2:20)
Key points:
1. 2 Corinthians 5:14–15: Christ died for me, so I no longer live for myself.
2. Romans 14:7–8: whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.
3. Read the full verse, Galatians 2:20.
4. 321: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; selflessness is not having nothing, but entering into the infinite and living out the infinite.

brief21.title: 2.4 Please the Lord, Not People
notes: Slide text:
“If I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t
be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10)
Deci and Ryan: motivation from outside approval
burns out fastest. Work “as for the Lord”
Key points:
1. Galatians 1:10; Matthew 6:1.
2. Deci and Ryan’s 1985 self-determination theory: burnout comes most easily when extrinsic motivation dominates.
3. Colossians 3:23–24, “as for the Lord”.
4. Illustration: the two people mopping the floor — polishing for people’s eyes versus cleaning the Lord’s house.
5. The 920 practice: everyone is our “2”; live out the “0” and bear the ninefold fruit of Galatians 5:22–23.

brief21.title: 3.1 Revival Is Not Those Three Things
notes: Slide text:
Not growing numbers, not social change,
not signs and wonders.
“You seek me … because you ate of the loaves”
(John 6:26)
Key points:
1. Revival is not growing numbers, social change, or signs and wonders.
2. All three may be results but cannot be the focus; otherwise we compare, measure results, and chase phenomena.
3. John 6:15, the Lord withdrew to the mountain; 6:26, “because you ate of the loaves, and were filled”.
4. The sign was right before their eyes, yet all they remembered was the taste of the bread.

brief21.title: 3.2 Revival Is Jesus Glorified
notes: Slide text:
“He will glorify me” (John 16:14)
“If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw
all people to myself” (John 12:32)
“In all things … the preeminence” (Colossians 1:18)
Key points:
1. John 16:14: the Holy Spirit glorifies Jesus — the touchstone for discerning all spiritual work.
2. John 12:32, the order: first lifted up, then all people drawn.
3. Psalm 115:1: not to us, give glory.
4. Colossians 1:18, “that in all things he might have the preeminence” — that is the definition of revival.

brief21.title: 3.3 History and Focus
notes: Slide text:
Herrnhut 1727: reconciled first, then the outpouring;
a century of prayer, missionaries sent out.
Kepler’s first law: the sun at the focus
keeps the orbit steady. Focus decides orbit.
Key points:
1. Herrnhut, 13 August 1727: reconciliation first, then the outpouring; a century-long prayer watch; missionaries sent out.
2. Zinzendorf: generally attributed with the saying, “I have one passion: it is he, he alone.”
3. The 1857 Fulton Street midday prayer meeting in New York, started by Jeremiah Lanphier — only six people came on the first day.
4. Kepler’s first law: the orbit is an ellipse, with the sun at a focus.
5. Extension: an aeroplane one degree off course is more than ten kilometres off after an hour’s flight.

brief21.title: Practices One and Two

3. Five minutes a day: only worship and gaze on Jesus.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Slide text:

brief21.title: Closing and Call: Return to the Focus, Enter Victory
notes: Slide text:
Whom you rely on decides how far you go;
whom you live for decides if it’s worth it.
“Yet I will rejoice in Yahweh”
(Habakkuk 3:18) Let Jesus be King!
Key points:
1. Whom you rely on decides how far you go; whom you live for decides whether it’s worth it.
2. Some rely on themselves and go fast, but not far; some live for themselves and do a great deal, but it isn’t worth it.
3. Read the whole of Habakkuk 3:17–19; the key is “yet”.
4. Call: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing

Lord, not relying on circumstances, not for myself,

May Jesus have the preeminence in all things,
and may all the glory be his. Amen.

2. Confession, forgiveness, refocusing, asking the Holy Spirit to work.
3. Declare that Jesus reigns as King in our homes, our work and our church.
4. Close with “May all the glory be yours, for ever and ever” and a blessing.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 22: By Whom? For Whom? Our theme verse is Acts 17:28: “In him we live, move, and have our being.” It is one short sentence, yet this morning it will bring our focus back to Jesus.

First, picture a scene. A ship is caught in wind and waves at night, and an old sailor does two things: he lets down the anchor to lock onto the immovable bedrock on the seabed; then he looks up and finds that unmoving star, the North Star. An anchor and a star. The anchor answers one question: on whom am I relying? The star answers another: for whom am I living? Brothers and sisters, our emotions so often rise and fall not because the waves are too big, but because the anchor has been dropped in the wrong place and we’ve mistaken the star we’re steering by. Hebrews says our hope is “an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast and entering into that which is within the veil”. This anchor isn’t locked onto the seabed; it is locked onto Jesus, seated on the throne in the Most Holy Place.

Paul spoke this theme verse on the Areopagus in Athens, to a crowd of people who were the world’s finest thinkers and relied on their own minds more than anyone. Standing among them, Paul said: you are alive, you move, you exist — all because of him. Brothers and sisters, of the three most basic things we possess, not one did we give ourselves. Today’s lesson asks us two questions: on whom am I relying to live? And for whom am I living?

The first question: on whom am I relying? There is a very reliable test — whatever you panic about losing is what you have been relying on to live. Jeremiah says, “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh.” Notice that the text doesn’t say we will never meet the heat, nor that there will be no drought. The difference isn’t the weather; the difference is where the roots go down. The desert bush has its roots in salt land; the tree by the waters has its roots by the river. The same sun beats down on both: one withers, one stays green.

Who is Jesus? He is the source of our wisdom, because he knows all things; he is the guarantee of our protection, because he is present everywhere; he is the wellspring of our power, because he can do all things. Paul says, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” Brothers and sisters, that doesn’t mean we can obtain all things; it means we can stand firm in all things.

So we don’t need to strain after the anointing, we don’t need to wait for circumstances to change, we don’t need to cling to our connections. If we simply hold fast to Jesus, we have everything. Paul says, “as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.” Because when you have the Lord who owns all things, in him you possess all things.

The second question: for whom am I living? John says that the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life are not the Father’s. I want to feel, I want to have, I want to be seen. Brothers and sisters, these three share just one thing — self. In the Garden of Eden, Eve saw that the fruit was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desired to make one wise; and the temptations the Lord faced in the wilderness were the very same three. From Eden until today, the content of temptation has never changed.

Paul says the Lord died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves. And he says: if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ. Pleasing people is a road that never ends, because applause never lasts long enough. Focus on people and you’ll be drained; focus on the Lord and you’ll be filled. Even if others don’t understand, don’t support me and don’t respond, I still press on, because the one I seek to please is the Lord.

The third question: for whom is revival? The focus of true revival is not growing numbers, not social change, not signs and wonders, but that Jesus be glorified. Speaking of the Holy Spirit, the Lord said, “He will glorify me.” Brothers and sisters, the starting point of the Herrnhut revival in 1727 was not a strategy; it was a group of people coming back before Jesus and being reconciled to one another. So don’t look for a secret formula; look for Jesus. Kepler tells us that a planet’s orbit is steady because the sun sits at its focus. Brothers and sisters, whether your orbit is steady depends not on how hard you try but on who is at your focal point.

Today there are three exercises. First, write down three things you most easily lean on, hand them back to the Lord in prayer, and declare: I’m not relying on these; I’m relying on you. Second, when you are discouraged in your service, stop and ask: for whom am I doing this? Third, spend at least five minutes a day not praying about your needs, not praying about your service, simply worshipping Jesus and gazing on Jesus. Let your heart come back to its focus — Jesus. And then declare: Lord, I do not rely on circumstances, and I do not live for myself; I live relying on you and living for you!

Brothers and sisters, whom you rely on decides how far you can go; whom you live for decides whether the journey is worth it. In his darkest hour Habakkuk said, “Yet I will rejoice in Yahweh.” His circumstances didn’t change; his focus did. Today let us adjust our focus together — not to satisfy ourselves, not to please people, but simply and solely for Jesus. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Morning Devotion 321, Lesson 22: By Whom? For Whom? Our theme verse is Acts 17:28: “In him we live, move, and have our being.” It is one short sentence, yet this morning it will bring our focus back to Jesus. Today we ask just two questions, but these two questions will decide how we live our whole life.

First, I’d like you to picture a scene. An ocean-going sailing ship sails at night into unfamiliar waters. The wind begins to rise, and the waves roll in one after another. At a moment like this, an old sailor will do two things. First, he lets down the anchor. The anchor isn’t tossed onto the surface of the water, nor hooked onto another boat alongside; it sinks all the way to the bottom of the sea and locks onto the immovable bedrock. Second, he looks up for a star. Every sailor in the northern hemisphere knows the North Star; because the axis of the earth’s rotation points almost directly at it, however the night sky wheels around, it stays fixed in its place in the north. An anchor and a star.

Brothers and sisters, the anchor answers one question: on whom am I relying? The star answers another: for whom am I living? Our emotions so often rise and fall — someone praises us and we soar; someone misunderstands us and we sink. Why? Not because the waves are too big, but because the anchor has been dropped in the wrong place and we’ve mistaken the star we’re steering by. If what I rely on is not Jesus but people, resources or circumstances, I will surely be disappointed; if my aim is not Jesus but achievement, applause or control, I will surely grow weary.

Paul spoke this theme verse on the Areopagus in Athens. The author of Acts is Luke, a doctor and Paul’s co-worker, who wrote this book around AD 60. Around AD 50, on his second missionary journey, Paul came to Athens and saw that the city was full of idols, and his spirit was provoked within him. Athens was the city of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, the intellectual capital of the world. Standing among them, Paul said: you are alive, you move, you exist — all because of him. And Romans says: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things.”

Now we come to the first question: on whom am I relying? There is a very reliable test — whatever you panic about losing is what you have been relying on to live. Lose a job, and the sky falls in; lose one person’s support, and you can’t go another step. Brothers and sisters, this isn’t a question of weakness; it’s a question of focus. Jeremiah 17:5 says: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh.”

But two verses later it says: “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes.” Notice that the text doesn’t say we will never meet the heat, nor that there will be no drought. The heat will come, the drought will come; that is certain. Where is the difference? The difference is where the roots go down. The desert bush has its roots in salt land; the tree by the waters has its roots by the river. The same sun beats down on both: one withers, one stays green.

So what exactly is Jesus to us? First, he is the source of our wisdom, because he knows all things — Colossians says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him. Second, he is the guarantee of our protection, because he is present everywhere — Psalm 139 says, where could I go from your Spirit? Third, he is the wellspring of our power, because he can do all things. Paul says, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” Brothers and sisters, that doesn’t mean we can obtain all things; it means we can bear all things and stand firm in all things.

So we don’t need to strain after the anointing, we don’t need to wait for circumstances to change, we don’t need to cling to our connections. If we simply hold fast to Jesus, we have everything. We so often want the things of God more than we want God himself. But Paul says, “as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.” This isn’t some trick of positive thinking; it is a spiritual fact — when you have the Lord who owns all things, in him you possess all things. Augustine put it well: our heart is restless until it rests in you.

In psychology there’s a concept called the “secure base”. The British psychiatrist John Bowlby put forward attachment theory, and his colleague Mary Ainsworth confirmed it with her Strange Situation experiments: how far a child dares to venture out depends on how stable he believes the base behind him is. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the spiritual reality. If my base is other people’s opinion of me, I will certainly shrink back; if my base is Jesus, then I can go forward. 321 says: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide — these Three Foundations are our anchor.

Now we come to the second question: for whom am I living? Are we living for ourselves, or for the Lord? Are we serving to please people, or to please the Lord? 1 John says that all that is in the world — the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life — isn’t the Father’s. I want to feel, I want to have, I want to be seen. Brothers and sisters, these three share just one thing — self.

Have you noticed that these three began in the Garden of Eden? Genesis says the woman saw that the tree was good for food, that it was a delight to the eyes, and that it was to be desired to make one wise. Good for food is the lust of the flesh; a delight to the eyes is the lust of the eyes; desired to make one wise is the pride of life. When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, Satan used these same three, and three times the Lord answered, “It is written …” From Eden until today, the content of temptation has never changed.

So what is it that the gospel means to accomplish in us? Paul says: he died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again. This isn’t a heavy-handed command; it’s the conclusion that love draws. Galatians goes even deeper: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” 321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. But listen carefully: selflessness doesn’t mean erasing yourself; selflessness is exchanging a limited “I” for an infinite Lord.

Paul also says, “For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.” Why is pleasing people so dangerous? Because it never has an end. In 1985 Deci and Ryan put forward self-determination theory, and their research showed that people driven chiefly by outside approval are more prone to burn out and give up when the feedback dries up. That’s why Colossians says, whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord. Think of the two people mopping the floor: one looks up to see whether anyone is coming by; the other mops clean even the corner no one walks across. Focus on people and you’ll be drained; focus on the Lord and you’ll be filled.

The third question: for whom is revival? We all long for revival, but the focus of true revival is not growing numbers, not social change, and not signs and wonders. All three may be results of revival, but none of them can be the focus of revival. The Lord Jesus himself dealt with this. After the five thousand had eaten their fill, the crowd wanted to take him by force to make him king, but he withdrew to the mountain. The next day he said, “You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled.” The sign was right in front of their eyes, yet all they remembered was the taste of the bread.

So what is revival for? There is only one answer — that Jesus be glorified. Speaking of the Holy Spirit, the Lord said, “He will glorify me.” This is the touchstone for discerning every spiritual work: whatever truly comes from the Holy Spirit will in the end give the glory to Jesus. The Lord also said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” Look at the order: first he is lifted up, and only then are all people drawn. Yet we so often do it the other way round — we work hard designing events to attract people and forget to lift up Jesus.

Church history bears this out. In 1727, at Herrnhut in Germany, a group of Moravian brothers and sisters were on the verge of splitting apart. Count Zinzendorf went from house to house reconciling them, and led them back before Christ. On 13 August that year the Holy Spirit was poured out during a Communion service, and after that they kept a prayer watch in shifts, day and night without a break, for more than a hundred years. The starting point of revival is putting the focus back where it belongs. Kepler’s first law tells us that a planet’s orbit is an ellipse, with the sun at one of its focal points. Whether your orbit is steady depends not on how hard you try but on who is at your focal point.

Next come three exercises. First, write down your list of dependencies: list three things you most easily lean on — money, connections, reputation, or your own methods — then hand them back to the Lord one by one in prayer, and declare: Lord, I’m not relying on these; I’m relying on you. Second, realign your heart for service: when you feel discouraged, weary, or start comparing yourself with others, stop and ask yourself: for whom am I doing this? Then pray silently: Lord, I serve only you; I don’t live for people’s opinions.

Third, a daily exercise of focusing on Jesus: spend at least five minutes each day not praying about your needs, not praying about your service, simply worshipping Jesus and gazing on Jesus. The 321 eight stages of changing our mindset can help us go deeper: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. First receive the information, ask the Holy Spirit for revelation, be convinced in your heart, and then put it into practice; after a week, evaluate and correct, keep repeating it, and finally multiply it by passing it on to someone else. The psalmist says, “One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after” — to see Yahweh’s beauty.

Let’s set today’s message within 321 and look at it once more. “By whom” corresponds to the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide — this is our anchor. “For whom” corresponds to the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory — this is our star. The anchor and the star together point to the Goal: establish God’s system. From beginning to end, this lesson is really dealing with one thing — self. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan; life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Brothers and sisters, whom you rely on decides how far you can go; whom you live for decides whether the journey is worth it. Some rely on themselves and go very fast, but not very far; some live for themselves and do a great deal, but it isn’t worth it. In the darkest hour of his nation Habakkuk said, “For though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines … yet I will rejoice in Yahweh.” His circumstances didn’t change at all; what changed was his focus. That “yet” is the sound of a focus returning to its place.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, in you we live, move and have our being, yet so often we live as though everything depended on ourselves. Forgive us for casting our anchor on things that move, and for fixing our eyes on people who change. Today we are willing to adjust our focus afresh, and we declare: I do not rely on circumstances, I rely on you; I do not live for myself, I live for you. Reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our work, and have the preeminence in all things. May all the glory be yours, for ever and ever. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
